Trabeculae are the struts of spongy bone, deep inside the bone ends. Pick them for a question about the lattice that holds red marrow.
Canaliculi are tiny channels connecting lacunae inside the bone, used for exchange of nutrients and wastes. They would be the answer for a question about how osteocytes communicate.

questions.topic: Bone tissue, the long bone and bone microanatomy
questions.q: What is the opening in the shaft of a long bone where the nutrient artery enters called?
questions.why: The nutrient foramen is a small opening in the diaphysis where the nutrient artery passes through the compact bone into the medullary cavity. From there, branches supply the marrow and the inner part of the bone. You can often see this opening as a small hole on the shaft of a dry bone in lab.
notes: The central canal runs down the core of a single osteon and is microscopic. It would be the answer for a question about the canal at the center of the osteon.
Correct. The nutrient artery enters through the nutrient foramen.
The medullary cavity is the hollow core of the shaft that the nutrient artery supplies after it enters. Choose it for a question about where marrow is stored.
Perforating canals are microscopic channels running crosswise between osteons. Pick them for a question about how central canals are linked to each other.

questions.topic: Bone tissue, the long bone and bone microanatomy
questions.q: In an adult long bone, what fills the medullary cavity of the shaft?
questions.why: In an adult, the medullary cavity of the diaphysis is filled with yellow marrow, which is mostly stored fat. Red marrow, the site of blood cell formation, is found in the spongy bone of the epiphyses. Keeping the two marrow types in their places helps you map a long bone from end to end.
notes: Spongy bone fills the epiphyses under a thin compact shell, not the hollow core of the shaft. Pick it for a question about the tissue inside the bone ends.
Hyaline cartilage covers the joint surfaces and forms the growth plate. Choose it for a question about articular cartilage or the epiphyseal plate.
Correct. Yellow marrow fills the adult medullary cavity.
Red marrow fills the spaces of spongy bone in the epiphyses and makes blood cells. It would be the answer for a question about the marrow in the ends of the bone.

questions.topic: Bone tissue, the long bone and bone microanatomy
questions.q: Which region of a long bone lies between the diaphysis and the epiphysis and holds the growth plate or its remnant?
questions.why: The metaphysis is the region where the shaft widens into the expanded end of the bone. In a growing bone it holds the epiphyseal plate, and in an adult it holds the epiphyseal line. The prefix meta- means between, which matches its position between the diaphysis and the epiphysis.
notes: Articular cartilage caps the epiphysis at the joint surface, at the far end of the bone. Choose it for a question about where two bones meet.
The periosteum is the membrane covering the outer surface of the bone. Pick it for a question about the outer covering.
The medullary cavity is the hollow core of the diaphysis that holds marrow. It would be the answer for a question about the space inside the shaft.
Correct. The metaphysis lies between the shaft and the end.

questions.topic: Bone tissue, the long bone and bone microanatomy
questions.q: In which zone of the growth plate do chondrocytes divide and stack into columns?
questions.why: The zone of proliferation is the second zone of the growth plate. Here chondrocytes divide rapidly and line up in columns, like stacks of coins. This cell division is what pushes the epiphysis away from the shaft and drives growth in length.
notes: Correct. Chondrocytes divide and stack into columns in the zone of proliferation.

The zone of resting cartilage is the first zone, anchoring the plate to the epiphysis, and its cells are not dividing rapidly. It would be the answer for a question about the zone closest to the epiphysis.
The zone of ossification is the last zone, where bone replaces the cartilage next to the diaphysis. Choose it for a question about where new bone is laid down.
The zone of hypertrophy comes next, where the stacked chondrocytes enlarge. Pick it for a question about where cartilage cells swell.

questions.topic: Bone tissue, the long bone and bone microanatomy
questions.q: In which zone of the growth plate do the chondrocytes enlarge?
questions.why: The zone of hypertrophy is the third zone of the growth plate. Chondrocytes that were produced in the zone of proliferation grow larger here. Hypertrophy means enlargement, so the name tells you what happens in this zone.
notes: The zone of calcification follows hypertrophy, and there the cartilage matrix hardens. Pick it for a question about where the matrix calcifies.
Correct. Chondrocytes enlarge in the zone of hypertrophy.
The zone of resting cartilage anchors the plate to the epiphysis. Choose it for a question about the first zone of the plate.
The zone of proliferation is where chondrocytes divide and stack into columns, just before they enlarge. It would be the answer for a question about cell division in the plate.

questions.topic: Bone tissue, the long bone and bone microanatomy
questions.q: Which bone cell is the stem cell of bone tissue, dividing to produce new osteoblasts?
questions.why: The osteogenic cell is the stem cell of bone tissue. It divides to produce new osteoblasts, which build bone and later become osteocytes. This makes it the starting point of the osteogenic cell to osteoblast to osteocyte lineage.
notes: Correct. The osteogenic cell is the stem cell that produces osteoblasts.
The osteoclast comes from a blood-cell line and breaks down bone, so it is outside this lineage. Pick it for a question about bone resorption.
The osteoblast is the cell the stem cell produces, the one that builds new matrix. Choose it for a question about bone formation.
The osteocyte is a mature bone cell in a lacuna, at the end of the lineage rather than the start. It would be the answer for a question about the cell that maintains matrix.

questions.topic: Bone tissue, the long bone and bone microanatomy
questions.q: The costal cartilages that join the ribs to the sternum are made of which type of cartilage?
questions.why: The costal cartilages are bars of hyaline cartilage connecting the ribs to the sternum. Hyaline cartilage is firm but slightly flexible, which lets the chest wall move a little during breathing. It is the same type found at the ends of long bones, in the nose, and in the airways.
notes: Dense irregular connective tissue forms the dermis and the capsules around organs, not cartilage bars. Choose it for a question about tissue with collagen running in many directions.
Elastic cartilage is springy and found in the external ear and epiglottis. It would be the answer for a question about cartilage that bends and springs back.
Correct. The costal cartilages are hyaline cartilage.
Fibrocartilage is tough and shock-absorbing, found in the intervertebral discs, knee menisci, and pubic symphysis. Pick it for a question about cartilage that resists compression.

questions.topic: Bone tissue, the long bone and bone microanatomy
questions.q: What are the two ways cartilage grows?
questions.why: Cartilage has two modes of growth. Appositional growth adds new cartilage at the outer surface, starting from the perichondrium. Interstitial growth expands the cartilage from within, as chondrocytes divide inside the matrix.
notes: These are the two routes of ossification, the ways bone forms. They do not describe how cartilage itself grows.
These are two zones of the growth plate, where chondrocytes divide and then enlarge. They are steps in bone lengthening, not the two modes of cartilage growth.
Correct. Cartilage grows by adding at its outer surface (appositional) and by expanding from within (interstitial).
Compact and spongy are the two kinds of bone tissue. They are not growth modes, and cartilage is neither.

questions.topic: Bone tissue, the long bone and bone microanatomy
questions.q: Appositional growth of cartilage begins in which structure?
questions.why: The perichondrium is the connective tissue sheath wrapped around most cartilage. Appositional growth starts there, laying new cartilage onto the outer surface, so the cartilage gets thicker at its edge.
notes: Correct. Appositional growth starts from the perichondrium and adds new cartilage at the outer surface.
Lacunae are the small cavities in the matrix that hold the chondrocytes. Growth from cells inside the matrix is interstitial growth, not appositional.
The periosteum covers the outer surface of a bone, and a bone grows wider beneath it. The cartilage version of that covering is the perichondrium.
The epiphyseal plate is the disc of hyaline cartilage where a long bone grows longer. It is not the starting point of appositional cartilage growth.

questions.topic: Bone tissue, the long bone and bone microanatomy
questions.q: Which phrase describes interstitial growth of cartilage?
options: New cartilage is added at the outer surface.
Bone replaces a hyaline cartilage model.
Bone forms within a connective tissue membrane.
questions.why: Interstitial means within the tissue. Chondrocytes sitting in their lacunae divide inside the matrix, so the cartilage enlarges from the inside. This is the opposite of appositional growth, which adds new cartilage at the outer surface.
notes: This describes appositional growth, which starts from the perichondrium. Interstitial growth happens inside the matrix.
Correct. In interstitial growth, chondrocytes divide inside the matrix and the cartilage expands from within.
This describes endochondral ossification, the way most bones form. It is about bone forming, not cartilage growing.
This describes intramembranous ossification, which builds the flat bones of the skull. It does not involve cartilage growth.

questions.topic: Bone tissue, the long bone and bone microanatomy
questions.q: One cartilage gets thicker as new cartilage is laid down at its edge from the surrounding sheath. A second cartilage enlarges as chondrocytes divide inside its matrix. Which pair names the two growth modes, in that order?
options: Appositional in both, at different rates.
questions.why: Sort each case by where the growth begins. The first starts at the perichondrium and adds to the outer surface, which is appositional growth. The second starts with chondrocytes dividing inside the matrix, which is interstitial growth.
notes: Correct. Growth from the sheath at the edge is appositional, and growth from dividing chondrocytes inside is interstitial.
This reverses the two. Interstitial growth comes from dividing chondrocytes inside the matrix, and appositional growth adds at the surface.
These are the two routes of bone formation. Neither describes cartilage enlarging from its edge or from within.
Only the first case adds at the surface. Chondrocytes dividing inside the matrix is a different mode, interstitial growth.

questions.topic: Bone tissue, the long bone and bone microanatomy
questions.q: Fibrocartilage has no perichondrium. Using that fact, which mode of growth would a knee meniscus be unable to use?
options: Interstitial growth, which starts from the perichondrium.
Interstitial growth, since a meniscus has no chondrocytes.
Neither mode, since fibrocartilage cannot grow at all.
Appositional growth, which starts from the perichondrium.
questions.why: First recall that the knee menisci are fibrocartilage, which has no perichondrium. Then recall where each growth mode begins. Appositional growth starts from the perichondrium, so a meniscus cannot use it, but it still has chondrocytes in its matrix, so interstitial growth remains possible.
notes: Interstitial growth starts with chondrocytes dividing inside the matrix, not from the perichondrium. A meniscus still has chondrocytes.
Fibrocartilage does have chondrocytes in lacunae. What it lacks is a perichondrium, which affects appositional growth.
Losing the perichondrium removes only appositional growth. The chondrocytes inside the matrix can still divide.
Correct. Appositional growth starts from the perichondrium, so cartilage without one cannot grow that way.
questions.answerText: Appositional growth, which starts from the perichondrium.

questions.topic: Bone tissue, the long bone and bone microanatomy
questions.q: A long bone grows longer by interstitial growth at the epiphyseal plate and wider by appositional growth beneath the periosteum. Why are the same two names used for cartilage growth?
options: Interstitial always makes tissue wider, and appositional makes it longer.
Both names mean growth that starts from the perichondrium.
Interstitial needs a covering sheath, and appositional needs cells inside.
Interstitial works from within, and appositional adds at the covered surface.
questions.why: The names describe where growth happens, not which tissue is growing. In cartilage, interstitial growth comes from chondrocytes dividing inside the matrix, and appositional growth adds new cartilage from the perichondrium at the surface. The long bone follows the same pattern, lengthening inside the cartilage plate and widening at its surface beneath the periosteum.
notes: This reverses the bone example. In a long bone, interstitial growth lengthens it and appositional growth widens it.
Only appositional cartilage growth starts from the perichondrium. Interstitial growth starts with chondrocytes inside the matrix.
This swaps the two. Appositional growth works from the covering sheath, and interstitial growth relies on cells dividing inside.
Correct. In both tissues, interstitial growth works from within and appositional growth adds at the outer surface under a covering.
questions.answerText: Interstitial works from within, and appositional adds at the covered surface.

questions.topic: Bone tissue, the long bone and bone microanatomy
questions.q: In a damaged region of hyaline cartilage, the chondrocytes deep in the matrix have died, but the perichondrium around the cartilage is intact. Which growth can still happen there?
options: Interstitial growth, from within the matrix.
Neither, since cartilage grows only from lacunae.
questions.why: Link each growth mode to the structure it needs. Interstitial growth needs living chondrocytes dividing inside the matrix, and those are gone. Appositional growth starts from the perichondrium and adds cartilage at the surface, so it can still occur.
notes: Interstitial growth needs chondrocytes dividing inside the matrix. With those cells dead, this mode is lost.
Interstitial growth does not start at the perichondrium. Growth from the perichondrium is appositional.
Correct. The perichondrium is intact, so new cartilage can still be added at the outer surface.
Lacunae only house chondrocytes. Cartilage can also grow from the perichondrium, which is still intact here.

questions.topic: Bone tissue, the long bone and bone microanatomy
questions.q: Which list gives the correct shape class for a vertebra, a rib, and a carpal, in that order?
questions.why: Match each bone to its shape class. Vertebrae have complex shapes that fit no other group, so they are irregular. Ribs are thin and curved, which makes them flat bones even though they are long and narrow. Carpals are roughly cube-shaped, which makes them short bones.
notes: Correct. Vertebrae are irregular, ribs are flat, and carpals are short.
Vertebrae are irregular, not short, and carpals are short, not irregular. Ribs look long, but they are thin and curved, so they are flat.
The rib is the trap here. It is thin and curved, so it is flat rather than long, and carpals are short bones, not bones formed in a tendon.
The rib and carpal are right, but a vertebra is irregular. Flat bones are thin and often curved, like the sternum and most skull bones.

questions.topic: Bone tissue, the long bone and bone microanatomy
questions.q: In lab, a student holds a roughly cube-shaped bone that sits with seven others to form the wrist. The student labels it a long bone because it is in a limb. What is the correct class, and why was the label wrong?
options: Long, because every bone in a limb is a long bone.
Short, because shape class depends on shape, not location.
Sesamoid, because small wrist bones form within tendons.
Irregular, because the wrist bones fit no other group.
questions.why: Bones are classified by their shape, not by the region they sit in. A roughly cube-shaped bone is a short bone, and the carpals of the wrist are the standard example. Being in a limb does not make a bone long; a long bone needs a shaft with two ends.
notes: Limbs hold long bones like the femur and humerus, but also short bones like the carpals and tarsals. Location does not set the class.
Correct. A cube-shaped carpal is a short bone, since classes are set by shape.
Sesamoid bones form within a tendon, like the patella. The carpals are short bones, not sesamoid bones.
Irregular bones, like vertebrae and hip bones, have complex shapes that fit no group. A cube-shaped carpal fits the short class.
questions.answerText: Short, because shape class depends on shape, not location.

questions.topic: Bone tissue, the long bone and bone microanatomy
questions.q: The femur and the patella both sit at the knee, yet they belong to different shape classes. What explains the difference?
options: The femur has a shaft with two ends; the patella forms in a tendon.
The femur is thin and curved; the patella is roughly cube-shaped.
The femur fits no other group; the patella is a long bone with a shaft.
The femur forms in a tendon; the patella has a shaft with two ends.
questions.why: Classify each bone on its own features. The femur is longer than it is wide, with a shaft and two ends, so it is a long bone. The patella is a small bone formed within the quadriceps tendon, so it is a sesamoid bone. Sitting near each other does not put them in the same class.
notes: Correct. The femur is a long bone with a shaft and two ends, and the patella is a sesamoid bone formed within a tendon.
Thin and curved describes flat bones, and cube-shaped describes short bones. Neither fits the femur or the patella.
Fitting no other group describes irregular bones. The femur is a long bone and the patella is a sesamoid bone.
This swaps the two. The patella is the bone that forms within a tendon, and the femur is the one with a shaft.
questions.answerText: The femur has a shaft with two ends; the patella forms in a tendon.

questions.topic: Bone tissue, the long bone and bone microanatomy
questions.q: A lab tray holds a sternum, a vertebra, and a hip bone. A student says all three are flat bones because they have broad surfaces. Which correction is right?
options: All three are irregular, because none has a shaft.
The sternum and hip bone are flat; the vertebra is short.
Only the sternum is flat; the vertebra and hip bone are irregular.
Only the hip bone is flat; the sternum and vertebra are irregular.
questions.why: Check each bone against the class definitions. The sternum is thin and flat, so it is a flat bone along with the ribs and most skull bones. Vertebrae and hip bones have complex shapes that fit no other group, so both are irregular, even though the hip bone has a broad surface.
notes: Having no shaft rules out a long bone, not a flat one. The sternum is thin and flat, so it is a flat bone.
The hip bone looks broad, but its complex shape makes it irregular. Vertebrae are irregular too, not short like the carpals.
Correct. The sternum is a flat bone, while vertebrae and hip bones are irregular.
This reverses the sternum and hip bone. The sternum is the flat bone here, and the hip bone is irregular.
questions.answerText: Only the sternum is flat; the vertebra and hip bone are irregular.

questions.topic: Bone tissue, the long bone and bone microanatomy
questions.q: An adult long bone is cut lengthwise in lab. One expanded end holds a lattice of bony struts filled with red tissue, and the hollow of the shaft holds yellow, fatty tissue. What are you looking at?
options: Epiphysis compact bone with yellow marrow; medullary cavity with red marrow.
Epiphysis spongy bone with red marrow; medullary cavity with yellow marrow.
Diaphysis spongy bone with red marrow; metaphysis with yellow marrow.
Epiphyseal plate with red marrow; periosteum with yellow marrow.
questions.why: Name the region first, then the marrow. The expanded end is the epiphysis, and its lattice of trabeculae is spongy bone, whose spaces hold red marrow. The hollow of the shaft is the medullary cavity of the diaphysis, which in an adult stores fat as yellow marrow.
notes: This swaps the marrows and the bone type. A lattice of struts is spongy bone, which holds red marrow, while the adult shaft holds yellow marrow.
Correct. The epiphysis holds spongy bone with red marrow, and the adult shaft's medullary cavity holds yellow marrow.
The diaphysis is the shaft, not the expanded end, and the metaphysis is the region holding the growth plate or its remnant. The hollow of the shaft is the medullary cavity.
The epiphyseal plate is hyaline cartilage where a bone lengthens, and the periosteum is the outer membrane. Neither holds marrow.
questions.answerText: Epiphysis spongy bone with red marrow; medullary cavity with yellow marrow.

questions.topic: Bone tissue, the long bone and bone microanatomy
questions.q: A surgeon drills into the middle of an adult femur's shaft from the outside to reach the marrow. Which layers does the drill pass, in order, and what does it reach?
options: Periosteum, compact bone, endosteum, then yellow marrow.
Endosteum, compact bone, periosteum, then yellow marrow.
Periosteum, spongy bone, endosteum, then red marrow.
Articular cartilage, compact bone, endosteum, then red marrow.
questions.why: Picture the shaft from the outside in. The periosteum covers the outer surface, the wall of the diaphysis is a tube of compact bone, and the endosteum lines the internal surface. Inside is the medullary cavity, which in an adult shaft holds yellow marrow.
notes: Correct. The drill crosses the periosteum, the compact bone wall, and the endosteum into the yellow marrow of the medullary cavity.
This swaps the two membranes. The periosteum is on the outer surface and the endosteum lines the inside.
The shaft wall is compact bone, not spongy bone. Spongy bone with red marrow fills the epiphyses at the ends.
Articular cartilage caps the epiphysis at a joint, not the shaft. The adult shaft holds yellow marrow, not red.
questions.answerText: Periosteum, compact bone, endosteum, then yellow marrow.

questions.topic: Bone tissue, the long bone and bone microanatomy
questions.q: A fall peels the periosteum away at two spots on an adult long bone: the middle of the shaft and the side of one expanded end. Which bone tissue lies just under the periosteum at each spot?
options: Shaft: spongy bone; end: a thin spongy shell over compact bone.
Shaft: compact bone; end: a thin compact shell over spongy bone.
Shaft: compact bone; end: spongy bone with no compact shell.
Shaft: articular cartilage; end: compact bone over yellow marrow.
questions.why: Name each region, then its tissue. The middle of the shaft is the diaphysis, a tube of compact bone around the medullary cavity, so compact bone lies right under the periosteum there. The expanded end is the epiphysis, which is spongy bone under a thin compact shell, so the periosteum sits on that shell with spongy bone just beneath it.
notes: This flips the two tissues. The shaft wall is compact bone, and spongy bone fills the inside of each end under a compact shell.
Correct. The diaphysis is a tube of compact bone, and each epiphysis is spongy bone under a thin compact shell.
The shaft is right, but the epiphysis is not bare spongy bone. A thin shell of compact bone covers the spongy bone inside it.
Articular cartilage caps the epiphysis where it meets another bone, not the shaft. The spongy bone of the ends holds red marrow, while yellow marrow fills the adult shaft.
questions.answerText: Shaft: compact bone; end: a thin compact shell over spongy bone.

questions.topic: Bone tissue, the long bone and bone microanatomy
questions.q: Which bone cell is a large cell with many nuclei?
questions.why: The osteoclast is a large, multinucleated cell that comes from a blood-cell line. That origin sets it apart from the other three bone cells, which form one lineage, and it is the only one that breaks down bone matrix.
notes: The osteocyte is a mature osteoblast sitting alone in a lacuna, maintaining the matrix. It is not a large multinucleated cell.
Correct. The osteoclast is a large multinucleated cell that resorbs bone.
The osteoblast builds and secretes new bone matrix and later becomes an osteocyte. It is not the multinucleated cell.
The osteogenic cell is the stem cell of bone that divides to make osteoblasts. It is not the large multinucleated cell.

questions.topic: Bone tissue, the long bone and bone microanatomy
questions.q: On a bone slide, a single cell sits in a lacuna between lamellae, linked to neighboring cells by tiny channels. A student calls it an osteoblast. What is the cell, and what does its position tell you?
options: An osteoblast, still building matrix at the bone surface.
An osteoclast, a blood-line cell that resorbs the lamellae.
An osteogenic cell that will soon become an osteoblast.
An osteocyte, a former osteoblast now walled in by matrix.
questions.why: Start with the location. A cell sitting in a lacuna between lamellae, linked by canaliculi, is an osteocyte. Then trace its history: an osteoblast secretes matrix, and once it is surrounded by that matrix it becomes an osteocyte, which maintains the bone day to day.
notes: Osteoblasts build new matrix, but once a cell is enclosed in a lacuna it has become an osteocyte. That is the student's mistake.
Osteoclasts are large multinucleated cells that break down bone. A single cell resting in a lacuna and linked by canaliculi is an osteocyte.
Osteogenic cells are the stem cells that divide to make osteoblasts. A cell enclosed in a lacuna is further along the lineage, an osteocyte.
Correct. A cell in a lacuna between lamellae is an osteocyte, an osteoblast that became surrounded by its own matrix.
questions.answerText: An osteocyte, a former osteoblast now walled in by matrix.

questions.topic: Bone tissue, the long bone and bone microanatomy
questions.q: What are the two routes of ossification?
questions.why: Ossification is the formation of bone, and it follows one of two routes. Intramembranous ossification forms bone directly within a connective tissue membrane and builds the flat bones of the skull. Endochondral ossification replaces a hyaline cartilage model and builds most bones of the body.
notes: These are the two ways cartilage and bone grow, at the surface or from within. They are not the routes by which bone first forms.
These are two zones of the growth plate. They describe steps in lengthening a bone, not the two routes of ossification.
Correct. Bone forms either directly in a membrane (intramembranous) or by replacing a cartilage model (endochondral).
These are the two kinds of bone tissue. They describe what bone looks like, not how it forms.

questions.topic: Bone tissue, the long bone and bone microanatomy
questions.q: Which zone of the growth plate lies closest to the diaphysis?
questions.why: The five zones run from the epiphysis to the diaphysis: resting cartilage, proliferation, hypertrophy, calcification, and ossification. The zone of ossification is at the diaphysis end, where cartilage is replaced by bone.
notes: Resting cartilage is the first zone, at the epiphysis end, where it anchors the plate. It is the farthest zone from the diaphysis.
Proliferation is the second zone, where chondrocytes divide and stack into columns. It sits near the epiphysis end.
Correct. The zone of ossification is the last zone, where cartilage is replaced by bone next to the diaphysis.
Hypertrophy is the middle zone, where chondrocytes enlarge. Two more zones lie between it and the diaphysis.

questions.topic: Bone tissue, the long bone and bone microanatomy
questions.q: What does the zone of resting cartilage do in the growth plate?
options: Its chondrocytes divide and stack into columns.
It anchors the growth plate to the epiphysis.
Its cartilage is replaced by bone.
questions.why: The zone of resting cartilage sits at the top of the growth plate, next to the epiphysis. Its job is to anchor the plate to the epiphysis, while the zones below it carry out division, enlargement, calcification, and replacement by bone.
notes: This happens in the zone of proliferation, the second zone. Resting cartilage anchors the plate instead.
Correct. The zone of resting cartilage is the first zone and anchors the plate to the epiphysis.
Enlarging chondrocytes mark the zone of hypertrophy, the third zone. They are not the job of the resting zone.
This happens in the zone of ossification, at the diaphysis end. The resting zone is at the opposite end.
questions.answerText: It anchors the growth plate to the epiphysis.

questions.topic: Bone tissue, the long bone and bone microanatomy
questions.q: The epiphyseal plate, where a long bone grows longer, is a disc of which tissue?
questions.why: The epiphyseal plate is a disc of hyaline cartilage between the epiphysis and the diaphysis, and it is where a long bone lengthens. When growth ends, the plate closes and leaves the bony epiphyseal line.
notes: Correct. The epiphyseal plate is a disc of hyaline cartilage.
Fibrocartilage, with thick collagen bundles, forms the intervertebral discs, menisci, and pubic symphysis. The growth plate is hyaline.
Compact bone forms the shaft wall. The plate only becomes bone, as the epiphyseal line, after growth ends.
Elastic cartilage is found in the external ear and the epiglottis. The growth plate is hyaline cartilage.

questions.q: How many bones make up the skull, not counting the hyoid bone?
questions.why: The skull has 22 bones in two groups. Eight cranial bones form the braincase that encloses the brain, and fourteen facial bones frame the face and hold the teeth. The hyoid bone in the neck is associated with the skull but is counted separately.
notes: Eight is the number of cranial bones alone. It would be the answer if the question asked how many bones enclose the brain.
Fourteen is the number of facial bones alone. Pick it for a question about how many bones form the facial skeleton.
Correct. The skull has 22 bones, eight cranial and fourteen facial.
Twenty-six is the number of bones usually counted in the adult vertebral column, the 24 vertebrae plus the sacrum and coccyx. Choose it for a question about the spine, not the skull.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Which group of skull bones encloses and protects the brain?
questions.why: The eight cranial bones form the cranium, the braincase that encloses and protects the brain. They are the frontal, two parietal, two temporal, occipital, sphenoid, and ethmoid bones. The fourteen facial bones form the front of the skull instead.
notes: Correct. The cranial bones enclose the brain.
The auditory ossicles are the tiny bones of the middle ear, housed inside the temporal bone. Pick them for a question about the bones that transmit sound.
The cervical vertebrae form the neck and surround the spinal cord, not the brain. Choose them for a question about the bones below the skull.
The facial bones frame the face, form the jaws, and hold the teeth. They would be the answer for a question about the bones of the face and upper and lower jaws.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: How many cranial bones are there?
questions.why: There are eight cranial bones. Four are single (frontal, occipital, sphenoid, and ethmoid) and two are paired (parietal and temporal), which gives 4 plus 4 for a total of eight. Together they form the braincase.
notes: Correct. There are eight cranial bones.
Twenty-two is the total for the whole skull, cranial plus facial. Pick it for a question about how many bones form the skull.
Six is the number of different cranial bone names. Students arrive at six by forgetting that the parietal and temporal bones each come as a pair.
Fourteen is the number of facial bones. It would be the answer for a question about the facial skeleton.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Which cranial bone forms the forehead?
questions.why: The frontal bone forms the forehead with its broad squamous part. It also forms the roof of the orbits and the floor of the anterior cranial fossa, and it contains the frontal sinus above the eyes. It is a single bone that meets the two parietal bones at the coronal suture.
notes: Correct. The frontal bone forms the forehead.
The parietal bones form most of the superior and lateral walls of the cranium, behind the forehead. They would be the answer for a question about the top and sides of the skull.
The occipital bone forms the back of the skull and much of the cranial base. Pick it for a question about the back of the head or the foramen magnum.
The temporal bones form the lower sides of the cranium and house the ear. Choose them for a question about the region around the ear.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Which cranial bone contains the foramen magnum?
questions.why: The occipital bone forms the back of the skull and much of the cranial base. Its foramen magnum, the large central opening, is where the brainstem continues into the spinal cord. The occipital condyles beside it meet the atlas, the first cervical vertebra.
notes: The parietal bones form the top and sides of the cranium and have no major foramen for the spinal cord. Choose them for a question about the sagittal suture.
The temporal bones contain the carotid canal and the ear openings. Pick them for a question about the external acoustic meatus or the mastoid process.
Correct. The foramen magnum is in the occipital bone.
The sphenoid bone sits in the center of the cranial base and contains the sella turcica, the optic canal, and the foramen ovale. It would be the answer for a question about any of those.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Which cranial bone houses the structures of the ear?
questions.why: The temporal bones form the lower sides of the cranium. Each one has the external acoustic meatus, the opening of the ear canal, and a dense petrous part that houses the middle and inner ear. The mastoid process behind the ear is also part of the temporal bone.
notes: The parietal bones form the top and upper sides of the cranium, above the temporal bones. They would be the answer for a question about the skull roof.
The sphenoid bone is the central wedge of the cranial base. Choose it for a question about the sella turcica or the bone that touches every other cranial bone.
The ethmoid bone lies deep between the orbits and forms part of the nasal cavity. Pick it for a question about the cribriform plate or the nasal septum.
Correct. The temporal bone houses the ear.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Which facial bone is the only freely movable bone of the skull?
questions.why: The mandible, or lower jaw, is the only skull bone that moves freely. Its condylar process meets the mandibular fossa of the temporal bone at the temporomandibular joint, a synovial joint that allows chewing and speaking. All the other skull bones are locked together by sutures.
notes: The zygomatic bone is the cheekbone, fixed in place by sutures. Choose it for a question about the bone forming the prominence of the cheek.
The maxilla forms the upper jaw and is fixed to the other skull bones by sutures. It would be the answer for a question about the bone that holds the upper teeth.
The vomer is a single facial bone that forms the inferior part of the nasal septum. Pick it for a question about the bony nasal partition.
Correct. The mandible is the only freely movable skull bone.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Which facial bones are the cheekbones?
questions.why: The zygomatic bones are the cheekbones, forming the prominence of each cheek and part of the lateral wall and floor of the orbit. Each one meets the zygomatic process of the temporal bone to complete the zygomatic arch.
notes: Correct. The zygomatic bones are the cheekbones.
The palatine bones form the posterior part of the hard palate. Choose them for a question about the back of the roof of the mouth.
The nasal bones form the bridge of the nose. They would be the answer for a question about the bones between the eyes at the top of the nose.
The lacrimal bones are tiny bones in the medial wall of the orbit, grooved for the tear duct. Pick them for a question about where tears drain.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Which suture joins the two parietal bones along the midline of the skull roof?
questions.why: The sagittal suture runs along the midline of the skull roof, front to back, joining the right and left parietal bones. Its name matches the sagittal plane, which also runs front to back and divides the body into right and left.
notes: The lambdoid suture joins the parietal bones to the occipital bone at the back of the skull. Pick it for a question about the suture shaped like an upside-down V at the back of the head.
Correct. The sagittal suture joins the two parietal bones in the midline.
The coronal suture runs across the top of the skull, side to side, joining the frontal bone to the parietal bones. It would be the answer for the suture behind the forehead.
The squamous suture joins a parietal bone to a temporal bone on each side. Choose it for a question about the suture on the lower side of the skull.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: What is the largest fontanelle of the infant skull?
questions.why: The anterior fontanelle is the largest of the soft spots on an infant's skull. It sits where the frontal bone meets the two parietal bones and is the last to close, at about 18 to 24 months. Its size and location make it the one clinicians check on a newborn.
notes: Correct. The anterior fontanelle is the largest.
The anterolateral fontanelles, also called the sphenoidal fontanelles, are small paired spots on the sides of the skull. Choose them for a question about the fontanelles near the sphenoid bone.
The posterolateral fontanelles, also called the mastoid fontanelles, are small paired spots behind the ears. Pick them for a question about the fontanelles near the mastoid region.

The posterior fontanelle, also called the occipital fontanelle, is smaller and sits where the parietal bones meet the occipital bone. It closes early, at about 2 months, so pick it for a question about the first fontanelle to close.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Which paranasal sinuses are the largest?
questions.why: The maxillary sinuses are the largest paranasal sinuses. They fill much of the body of each maxilla in the cheek region, just above the roots of the upper teeth. Like all the paranasal sinuses, they lighten the skull and drain into the nasal cavity.
notes: The sphenoidal sinus lies within the body of the sphenoid bone, deep in the skull. Choose it for a question about the sinus just below the sella turcica.
The frontal sinuses sit in the frontal bone above the orbits. They would be the answer for a question about the sinuses behind the forehead.
Correct. The maxillary sinuses are the largest.
The ethmoidal sinuses are many small air cells in the ethmoid bone between the orbits. Pick them for a question about the sinuses made of small air cells.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Which bone is U-shaped, sits in the anterior neck below the mandible, and does not articulate with any other bone?
questions.why: The hyoid bone is a U-shaped bone in the front of the neck, just below the mandible. It is the only bone that does not form a joint with any other bone; instead, ligaments suspend it from the styloid processes of the temporal bones. It anchors the tongue and several muscles of the neck and larynx.
notes: The mandible is U-shaped too, which is why students confuse them, but it articulates with the temporal bones at the jaw joints. Pick it for a question about the lower jaw.
Correct. The hyoid bone touches no other bone.

The atlas is the first cervical vertebra, a ring-shaped bone that articulates with the occipital condyles above and the axis below. Choose it for a question about the vertebra that holds up the skull.
The vomer is a thin bone forming the lower part of the nasal septum, and it articulates with several bones. It would be the answer for a question about the bony nasal partition.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Which marking of the sphenoid bone is the saddle-shaped seat that cradles the pituitary gland?
questions.why: The sella turcica, which means Turkish saddle, is a saddle-shaped depression on the body of the sphenoid bone. Its deep seat holds the pituitary gland in the middle of the cranial base. The sphenoidal sinus lies just below it within the body of the sphenoid.
notes: The glabella is the smooth area of the frontal bone between the eyebrow ridges. Pick it for a question about the spot between the eyebrows.
The cribriform plate is the perforated plate of the ethmoid bone that olfactory nerve filaments pass through. Choose it for a question about the sense of smell.
The crista galli is an upright ridge on the ethmoid bone where the falx cerebri attaches. It would be the answer for a question about the attachment of that fold of the brain covering.
Correct. The sella turcica cradles the pituitary gland.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Which marking of the temporal bone is the bump you can feel behind the ear?
questions.why: The mastoid process is the rounded bump of the temporal bone just behind the ear. It is an attachment point for neck muscles, and inside it is filled with small air cells. You can feel it easily by pressing behind your earlobe.
notes: The zygomatic process of the temporal bone runs forward to meet the cheekbone and form the zygomatic arch. Pick it for a question about the bar of bone in front of the ear.
The coronoid process belongs to the mandible, not the temporal bone, and is the anterior process where the temporalis muscle attaches. Choose it for a question about the jaw.
Correct. The mastoid process is the bump behind the ear.

The styloid process is a slender spike pointing down below the ear, too deep to feel easily. It would be the answer for a question about the anchor for tongue and neck muscles and the ligaments that hold the hyoid.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Which one cranial bone articulates with every other cranial bone?
questions.why: The sphenoid bone is the central wedge of the cranial base, shaped somewhat like a bat with its wings spread. Because it sits in the middle of the skull floor, it touches every other cranial bone. It contains the sella turcica, the optic canals, and the sphenoidal sinus.
notes: The occipital bone forms the back of the skull and much of the cranial base, but it does not touch the frontal or ethmoid bones. Pick it for a question about the foramen magnum.
Correct. The sphenoid touches every other cranial bone.
The ethmoid bone lies deep between the orbits and forms part of the nasal cavity. It would be the answer for a question about the deepest cranial bone or the cribriform plate.
The frontal bone forms the forehead and orbital roofs, but it does not reach the occipital bone. Choose it for a question about the forehead.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Which cranial bone is the deepest, lying between the orbits and forming part of the nasal cavity?
questions.why: The ethmoid bone is the deepest cranial bone, tucked between the orbits behind the nose. It forms the roof and part of the walls of the nasal cavity, the upper part of the nasal septum through its perpendicular plate, and it holds the ethmoidal air cells. Its cribriform plate lets the olfactory nerve filaments through.
notes: The sphenoid bone lies just behind the ethmoid as the central wedge of the cranial base. It would be the answer for a question about the bone that touches every other cranial bone.
The temporal bones form the lower sides of the cranium and house the ear. Pick them for a question about the bones around the ear canal.
The frontal bone forms the forehead and roof of the orbits, in front of and above the ethmoid. Choose it for a question about the forehead or the frontal sinus.
Correct. The ethmoid is the deepest cranial bone, between the orbits.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Which cranial bones come in pairs rather than as single bones?
questions.why: Of the eight cranial bones, only the parietal and temporal bones are paired, one on each side of the head. The frontal, occipital, sphenoid, and ethmoid bones are single bones that cross the midline. Two pairs plus four single bones gives the total of eight.
notes: Correct. The parietal and temporal bones are the paired cranial bones.
The occipital and sphenoid bones are both single bones of the cranial base. Choose this pair for a question about bones that form much of the skull floor.
The sphenoid and ethmoid bones are single bones that sit in the midline of the cranial base. Pick this pair for a question about the two deep, single cranial bones near the orbits.

The frontal and occipital bones are single midline bones at the front and back of the skull. This pair would be the answer if the question asked for two single cranial bones at opposite ends of the skull.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Which marking of the occipital bone articulates with the atlas, the first cervical vertebra?
questions.why: The occipital condyles are the paired knobs beside the foramen magnum. They rest on the superior articular facets of the atlas to form the atlanto-occipital joint. This is the joint that lets you nod your head yes.
notes: The external occipital protuberance is the midline bump on the back of the head and does not form a joint. Pick it for a question about the bump you can feel at the back of the skull.
Correct. The occipital condyles articulate with the atlas.
The mastoid process is a bump on the temporal bone behind the ear, used for muscle attachment, and it does not form a joint. Pick it for a question about the bump you can feel behind the ear.

The condylar process belongs to the mandible, and its head meets the temporal bone at the jaw joint. Students confuse it with the occipital condyles because of the similar name. Choose it for a question about the temporomandibular joint.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Which marking of the temporal bone forms the socket of the temporomandibular joint?
questions.why: The mandibular fossa is a shallow socket on the underside of the temporal bone, just in front of the ear canal. The condylar process of the mandible fits into it, forming the temporomandibular joint (TMJ), the jaw joint.
notes: The external acoustic meatus is the opening of the ear canal, just behind the mandibular fossa. Pick it for a question about where sound enters the skull.
The mastoid process is the bump behind the ear where neck muscles attach. It would be the answer for a question about the bump you can feel behind the earlobe.
The styloid process is a slender spike below the ear that anchors tongue and neck muscles. Choose it for a question about the bony point the hyoid is slung from.
Correct. The mandibular fossa is the socket of the jaw joint.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Which marking of the maxilla forms the anterior part of the hard palate?
questions.why: The palatine process is a horizontal shelf on each maxilla. The right and left palatine processes meet in the midline to form the front part of the hard palate, the bony roof of the mouth. The palatine bones complete the hard palate behind them.
notes: The frontal process projects upward beside the nose to meet the frontal bone. Pick it for a question about the part of the maxilla that reaches toward the forehead.
The alveolar process is the ridge of the maxilla that holds the upper teeth. It would be the answer for a question about the tooth sockets.
Correct. The palatine processes of the maxillae form the anterior hard palate.
The zygomatic process of the maxilla projects laterally to meet the cheekbone. Choose it for a question about where the maxilla joins the zygomatic bone.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Which two facial bones are single rather than paired?
options: The zygomatic bones and the mandible
The maxillae and the palatine bones
The nasal bones and the vomer
questions.why: Of the fourteen facial bones, twelve come in six pairs and only two are single: the vomer and the mandible. Both cross the midline. The vomer forms the lower part of the nasal septum, and the mandible is the lower jaw.
notes: Correct. The vomer and the mandible are the single facial bones.
The mandible is single, but the zygomatic bones are paired cheekbones. Choose the zygomatic bones for a question about the cheeks.
The maxillae and palatine bones are both paired, together forming the hard palate. This choice would fit a question about the bones of the roof of the mouth.
The vomer is single, but the nasal bones are paired, meeting at the bridge of the nose. Pick the nasal bones for a question about the bridge of the nose.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Which suture joins the frontal bone to the two parietal bones?
questions.why: The coronal suture runs across the top of the skull from side to side, just behind the forehead. It joins the frontal bone in front to the two parietal bones behind. It runs in the same direction as the coronal (frontal) plane, which is how it got its name.
notes: The squamous suture joins a parietal bone to a temporal bone on each side. Choose it for a question about the suture on the lower side of the cranium.
The sagittal suture joins the two parietal bones to each other along the midline. It would be the answer for the suture running front to back on top of the skull.
Correct. The coronal suture joins the frontal bone to the parietal bones.
The lambdoid suture joins the parietal bones to the occipital bone at the back of the skull. Pick it for a question about the back of the head.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: The pterion is the junction of which four bones?
questions.why: The pterion is an H-shaped junction on the side of the skull, in the temple region, where the frontal, parietal, temporal, and sphenoid (greater wing) bones meet. It is the thinnest part of the skull. The middle meningeal artery runs just beneath it, so a blow here can tear the artery.
notes: Correct. The frontal, parietal, temporal, and sphenoid bones meet at the pterion.
The occipital bone is at the back of the skull and is too far back to reach the temple. Swap it for the temporal bone and the set is correct.
The occipital bone is at the back and the ethmoid bone is deep inside the skull, so neither reaches the temple. This set leaves out the frontal and sphenoid bones that actually form the pterion.
This set drops the parietal bone and adds the occipital bone, which sits at the back of the skull. The parietal bone is needed to form the upper part of the H.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Which marking of the ethmoid bone is the perforated plate that the olfactory nerve filaments pass through?
questions.why: The cribriform plate is a horizontal plate of the ethmoid bone, full of small holes, that forms the roof of the nasal cavity. Filaments of the olfactory nerve, cranial nerve I, pass up through these holes from the nasal lining to the brain. Cribriform means sieve-like.
notes: Correct. The cribriform plate is perforated for the olfactory nerve filaments.
The crista galli is the upright ridge on top of the cribriform plate where the falx cerebri attaches. It would be the answer for a question about that attachment point.
The perpendicular plate is the vertical plate forming the upper part of the nasal septum. Pick it for a question about the bony nasal partition.
The lateral masses are the side portions of the ethmoid that contain the ethmoidal air cells. Choose them for a question about the ethmoidal sinuses.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Which structure passes through the foramen magnum?
questions.why: The foramen magnum is the large opening in the occipital bone where the medulla oblongata of the brainstem continues into the spinal cord. The vertebral arteries and the spinal accessory nerve also pass through it. It is the one large opening between the brain and the spinal cord.
notes: The internal jugular vein leaves the skull through the jugular foramen, between the temporal and occipital bones. Choose it for a question about the jugular foramen.
Correct. The spinal cord passes through the foramen magnum.
The optic nerve passes through the optic canal of the sphenoid bone. It would be the answer for a question about the opening from the orbit to the brain.
The internal carotid artery enters the skull through the carotid canal of the temporal bone. Pick it for a question about the carotid canal.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Which opening transmits the optic nerve?
questions.why: The optic canal is an opening in the sphenoid bone at the back of the orbit. The optic nerve, cranial nerve II, passes through it from the eye to the brain. It sits just medial to the superior orbital fissure.
notes: The foramen ovale, in the sphenoid bone, passes a branch of the trigeminal nerve to the lower jaw. Pick it for a question about that nerve branch.
Correct. The optic nerve passes through the optic canal.
The jugular foramen, between the temporal and occipital bones, passes the internal jugular vein. Choose it for a question about where the main vein leaves the skull.
The superior orbital fissure, also in the sphenoid bone, passes the nerves that move the eye. It would be the answer for a question about the opening for the eye-moving nerves.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Which opening transmits the internal carotid artery into the skull?
questions.why: The carotid canal is a passage through the temporal bone that carries the internal carotid artery into the cranial cavity. The internal carotid is one of the main arteries supplying the brain. Its name matches the vessel it carries.
notes: Correct. The internal carotid artery enters through the carotid canal.
The jugular foramen carries the internal jugular vein out of the skull. It would be the answer for a question about the main vein draining the brain.
The stylomastoid foramen is the exit of the facial nerve between the styloid and mastoid processes. Choose it for a question about where that nerve leaves the skull.
The foramen magnum carries the spinal cord and the vertebral arteries, not the internal carotid. Pick it for a question about the vertebral arteries entering the skull.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Which bone forms part of the medial wall of the orbit and is grooved for the tear duct?
questions.why: The lacrimal bones are the smallest facial bones, one in the medial wall of each orbit. Each has a groove that holds the passage carrying tears from the eye toward the nasal cavity. Lacrimal means related to tears.
notes: The nasal bones form the bridge of the nose, in front of the orbit rather than inside its wall. They would be the answer for a question about the bridge of the nose.
The zygomatic bone forms the lateral wall and part of the floor of the orbit, on the opposite side from the tear duct. Pick it for a question about the cheekbone.
The palatine bone contributes only a small piece to the back of the orbit floor and mostly forms the posterior hard palate. Choose it for a question about the back of the roof of the mouth.
Correct. The lacrimal bone is grooved for the tear duct.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: What is the domed roof of the cranium, the skullcap, called?
questions.why: The calvaria is the domed skullcap, the roof of the cranium. It is formed mainly by the frontal, parietal, and occipital bones. The floor beneath the brain is a different region called the cranial base.
notes: The cranial base is the floor of the cranium, beneath the brain. It would be the answer for a question about the part of the skull divided into anterior, middle, and posterior fossae.
Correct. The calvaria is the skullcap.
The glabella is the small smooth area of the frontal bone between the eyebrows. Pick it for a question about that single landmark.
A cranial fossa is one of the three depressions in the cranial base that hold parts of the brain. Choose it for a question about the floor of the cranium.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Which part of the mandible is the vertical portion that rises on each side?
questions.why: The ramus is the vertical part of the mandible on each side, rising from the angle of the jaw up toward the skull. At its top it splits into the condylar process behind and the coronoid process in front. The mandibular foramen opens on its inner surface.
notes: The body is the horizontal, U-shaped part of the mandible that holds the lower teeth. It would be the answer for a question about the part of the jaw at the chin.
The angle is the corner where the body turns upward into the ramus. Pick it for a question about the corner of the jaw below the ear.
The alveolar process is the ridge that holds the lower teeth. Choose it for a question about the tooth sockets.
Correct. The ramus is the vertical portion.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Which process of the mandible is the anterior process where the temporalis chewing muscle attaches?
questions.why: The coronoid process is the thin, pointed anterior process at the top of the mandibular ramus. The temporalis, a chewing muscle that fans out over the side of the skull, attaches to it. The mandibular notch separates it from the condylar process behind.
notes: The condylar process is the posterior process whose head meets the temporal bone at the jaw joint. It would be the answer for a question about the part of the mandible that forms the TMJ.
The alveolar process is the ridge that holds the lower teeth. Pick it for a question about the tooth sockets.
Correct. The temporalis attaches to the coronoid process.
The styloid process belongs to the temporal bone, not the mandible. Choose it for a question about the slender spike below the ear.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Which opening, located between the styloid and mastoid processes, is the exit of the facial nerve from the skull?
questions.why: The stylomastoid foramen lies on the underside of the temporal bone, between the styloid process and the mastoid process. Its name simply joins the two landmarks it sits between. The facial nerve leaves the skull here on its way to the face.
notes: The carotid canal carries the internal carotid artery into the skull. Pick it for a question about that artery.
The internal acoustic meatus is where the facial nerve enters the temporal bone from the cranial cavity. It would be the answer if the question asked for the entry point rather than the exit.
The jugular foramen carries the internal jugular vein out of the skull. Choose it for a question about the vein draining the brain.
Correct. The facial nerve exits at the stylomastoid foramen.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: A student finds an immovable fibrous joint at the back of the skull joining the parietal bones to the occipital bone. Which suture is this?
questions.why: The lambdoid suture is at the back of the skull, where the two parietal bones meet the occipital bone. Its shape resembles the Greek letter lambda, an upside-down V, which is how it got its name. Like all sutures, it is an immovable fibrous joint.
notes: The sagittal suture joins the two parietal bones along the midline on top of the skull. Pick it for the suture running front to back.
The squamous suture joins a parietal bone to a temporal bone on the side of the skull. Choose it for the suture above the ear.
The coronal suture is at the front, joining the frontal bone to the parietal bones. It would be the answer for the suture behind the forehead.
Correct. The lambdoid suture joins the parietal and occipital bones.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: An anatomist examines the deep saddle-shaped seat on the body of the sphenoid bone. Which gland normally rests in this seat?
questions.why: The seat is the sella turcica, the Turkish saddle of the sphenoid bone. It cradles the pituitary gland, which hangs from the base of the brain by a stalk. Its position in the middle of the cranial base protects this small gland.
notes: The lacrimal gland sits in the upper lateral part of the orbit and produces tears. Choose it for a question about where tears are made.
The thyroid gland is in the anterior neck, wrapped around the trachea, far from the skull. It would be the answer for a question about the gland below the larynx.

The pineal gland is in the brain itself, at the back of the diencephalon, and does not sit in a bony seat. Students sometimes confuse it with the pituitary because both are small glands near the brain. Pick it for a question about the epithalamus.
Correct. The pituitary gland sits in the sella turcica.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: On an infant's skull, a clinician feels a fibrous membrane gap where the frontal bone meets the two parietal bones. Which fontanelle is this?
questions.why: The anterior fontanelle is at the junction of the frontal bone and the two parietal bones, on the top of the head toward the front. It is the largest fontanelle and closes at about 18 to 24 months. In the adult, the same spot is where the coronal and sagittal sutures meet.
notes: The posterolateral (mastoid) fontanelles are behind the ears on each side. Pick them for a question about a soft spot near the mastoid region.
The posterior fontanelle is where the parietal bones meet the occipital bone, at the back of the head. It would be the answer if the gap were at the back of the skull.
Correct. The frontal and parietal bones meet at the anterior fontanelle.
The anterolateral (sphenoidal) fontanelles are on the sides of the skull near the sphenoid bone. Choose them for a question about a soft spot at the side of the head.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: A dentist needs to numb the nerve that supplies the lower teeth. Which mandibular opening is the target for the injection?
questions.why: The mandibular foramen opens on the inner surface of the mandibular ramus. The nerve to the lower teeth enters the mandible here, so dentists inject anesthetic near this opening to numb the lower teeth on that side. This is the standard dental block.
notes: The mental foramen is on the outer surface of the mandibular body, below the premolars, and passes the nerve to the chin and lower lip. It would be the answer for a question about numbness of the chin.
The supraorbital foramen is in the frontal bone above the orbit. Choose it for a question about the nerve and vessels to the forehead.
The infraorbital foramen is on the maxilla, below the orbit, and passes the infraorbital nerve to the face. Pick it for a question about the upper face and cheek.
Correct. The mandibular foramen is the target for the lower dental block.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: A view of the skull base shows an opening between the temporal and occipital bones that carries a large vein. Which opening is this?
questions.why: The jugular foramen lies between the temporal and occipital bones in the skull base. The internal jugular vein, which drains blood from the brain, leaves the skull through it. It sits just behind the carotid canal, so the main artery in and the main vein out are close neighbors.
notes: The foramen ovale is in the sphenoid bone and passes a branch of the trigeminal nerve to the lower jaw. Pick it for a question about that nerve branch.
The hypoglossal canal is in the occipital bone and passes the hypoglossal nerve, cranial nerve XII. Choose it for a question about that nerve.
The carotid canal is in the temporal bone and carries the internal carotid artery into the skull. It would be the answer if the opening carried the major artery rather than the vein.
Correct. The jugular foramen carries the internal jugular vein.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: A clinician studies the thin H-shaped junction on the side of the skull where four bones meet. Which region is this?
questions.why: The pterion is the H-shaped junction in the temple region where the frontal, parietal, temporal, and sphenoid bones meet. It is the thinnest part of the skull. Because the middle meningeal artery runs just beneath it, a blow here can cause dangerous bleeding inside the skull.
notes: The external occipital protuberance is the midline bump at the back of the head, on the occipital bone alone. Choose it for a question about the back of the skull.
The glabella is the smooth area of the frontal bone between the eyebrows, a single-bone landmark. It would be the answer for a question about the spot between the eyebrows.
The mastoid process is a thick bump of the temporal bone behind the ear, not a junction of bones. Pick it for a question about the bump behind the ear.
Correct. The pterion is the four-bone junction on the side of the skull.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: A probe runs down the bony nasal septum from its upper part to its lower part. Which bones does it cross, in order?
options: The nasal bone, then the vomer
The vomer, then the perpendicular plate
The perpendicular plate, then the vomer
The cribriform plate, then the vomer
questions.why: The nasal septum is the partition between the right and left nasal cavities. Its upper bony part is the perpendicular plate of the ethmoid bone, and its lower bony part is the vomer. Septal cartilage completes the front of the septum.
notes: The nasal bones form the bridge of the nose on the outside, not the septum. Choose them for a question about the bony bridge.
This is the correct pair in reverse. The vomer is the lower part of the septum, so it would come first only if the probe ran from bottom to top.
Correct. The perpendicular plate is above, and the vomer is below.
The cribriform plate is horizontal and forms the roof of the nasal cavity, not part of the septum. Pick it for a question about where the olfactory nerve filaments pass.
questions.answerText: The perpendicular plate, then the vomer
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Which statement correctly names the cranial bone that forms the roof of the orbit, the cranial bone whose greater wings help form the orbit and lateral skull wall, and the cheekbone that helps form the orbit?
options: Occipital roofs it, sphenoid has the wings, zygomatic is the cheekbone
Parietal roofs it, ethmoid has the wings, maxilla is the cheekbone
Frontal roofs it, temporal has the wings, nasal is the cheekbone
Frontal roofs it, sphenoid has the wings, zygomatic is the cheekbone
questions.why: The orbit is built from seven bones. The frontal bone forms its roof through its orbital plates. The sphenoid bone contributes through its greater wings, which also form part of the lateral skull wall. The zygomatic bone, the cheekbone, forms the lateral wall and part of the floor.
notes: The occipital bone is at the back of the skull and does not reach the orbit. The rest of this set is right, so swap in the frontal bone for the roof.
The parietal bones form the top and sides of the cranium, far from the orbit. The greater wings belong to the sphenoid, not the ethmoid, and the maxilla is the upper jaw, not the cheekbone.
The frontal bone is right, but the temporal bone has no greater wings, and the nasal bones form the bridge of the nose. Greater wings belong only to the sphenoid.
Correct. Frontal, sphenoid, and zygomatic.
questions.answerText: Frontal roofs it, sphenoid has the wings, zygomatic is the cheekbone
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Which statement correctly describes the bones of the hard palate from front to back?
options: The palatine bones in front, then the maxillae behind
The maxillae in front, then the palatine bones behind
The maxillae in front, then the vomer behind
The vomer in front, then the maxillae behind
questions.why: The hard palate is the bony roof of the mouth and the floor of the nasal cavity. The palatine processes of the two maxillae form its larger front part, and the horizontal plates of the two palatine bones form the back part. Despite their name, the palatine bones form only the posterior palate.
notes: This reverses the two bones. Students choose it because the palatine bones are named for the palate, but they form only the back portion.
Correct. Maxillae in front, palatine bones behind.
The maxillae are right for the front, but the vomer stands upright in the septum and does not form the back of the palate. The palatine bones complete the palate.
The vomer is a vertical bone in the nasal septum, sitting above the palate rather than forming it. Pick it for a question about the lower nasal septum.
questions.answerText: The maxillae in front, then the palatine bones behind
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Which statement correctly matches each opening to what it transmits: the optic canal, the foramen magnum, and the carotid canal?
options: Optic canal: spinal cord; foramen magnum: carotid artery; carotid canal: optic nerve
Optic canal: optic nerve; foramen magnum: spinal cord; carotid canal: internal carotid
Optic canal: carotid artery; foramen magnum: optic nerve; carotid canal: spinal cord
Optic canal: optic nerve; foramen magnum: carotid artery; carotid canal: spinal cord
questions.why: Most of these openings are named for what passes through them. The optic canal in the sphenoid bone carries the optic nerve, the foramen magnum in the occipital bone carries the spinal cord, and the carotid canal in the temporal bone carries the internal carotid artery.
notes: This scrambles all three. The spinal cord is far too large for the optic canal and passes only through the foramen magnum.
Correct. Optic nerve, spinal cord, and internal carotid artery.
This shifts every match by one. The names give the answer away: the optic canal carries the optic nerve, and the carotid canal carries the carotid artery.
The optic match is right, but the other two are swapped. The spinal cord passes through the foramen magnum, and the internal carotid passes through the carotid canal.
questions.answerText: Optic canal: optic nerve; foramen magnum: spinal cord; carotid canal: internal carotid
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Trace the facial nerve through the temporal bone from the cranial cavity to the outside of the skull base. Where does it enter and where does it exit?
options: Enters at the stylomastoid foramen, exits at the internal acoustic meatus
Enters at the external acoustic meatus, exits at the carotid canal
Enters at the jugular foramen, exits at the stylomastoid foramen
Enters at the internal acoustic meatus, exits at the stylomastoid foramen
questions.why: The facial nerve leaves the brainstem and enters the temporal bone through the internal acoustic meatus, along with the nerve for hearing. It travels through the bone and exits on the underside of the skull at the stylomastoid foramen, between the styloid and mastoid processes, before spreading across the face.
notes: This is the right pair in reverse. The internal acoustic meatus opens toward the brain, so it must be the entry point for a nerve coming from the brainstem.
The external acoustic meatus is the outer ear canal, which carries sound inward and no nerve from the brain. The carotid canal carries the internal carotid artery.
The exit is right, but the jugular foramen carries the internal jugular vein out of the skull. The facial nerve enters through the internal acoustic meatus instead.
Correct. In at the internal acoustic meatus, out at the stylomastoid foramen.
questions.answerText: Enters at the internal acoustic meatus, exits at the stylomastoid foramen
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Which set correctly names three features of the sphenoid bone: the saddle on its body, the opening that passes the optic nerve, and the opening that passes the nerves that move the eye?
options: Glabella, optic canal, and superior orbital fissure
Crista galli, optic canal, and foramen ovale
Sella turcica, optic canal, and superior orbital fissure
Sella turcica, foramen magnum, and superior orbital fissure
questions.why: The sphenoid bone holds several key features. The sella turcica on its body cradles the pituitary gland. The optic canal passes the optic nerve from the eye, and the superior orbital fissure, just lateral to it, passes the nerves that move the eye.
notes: The glabella is a landmark of the frontal bone between the eyebrows, not a saddle. The rest of this set is right, so swap in the sella turcica.
The crista galli belongs to the ethmoid bone, and the foramen ovale passes a branch of the trigeminal nerve to the lower jaw, not the eye-moving nerves.
Correct. Sella turcica, optic canal, and superior orbital fissure.
The foramen magnum is in the occipital bone and carries the spinal cord, not the optic nerve. Swap in the optic canal and the set is correct.
questions.answerText: Sella turcica, optic canal, and superior orbital fissure
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Which statement correctly matches each paranasal sinus to the bone it occupies: the frontal sinus, the sphenoidal sinus, and the maxillary sinus?
options: Frontal: ethmoid; sphenoidal: sphenoid; maxillary: frontal bone
Frontal: frontal bone; sphenoidal: sphenoid; maxillary: maxilla
Frontal: maxilla; sphenoidal: ethmoid; maxillary: frontal bone
Frontal: frontal bone; sphenoidal: maxilla; maxillary: ethmoid
questions.why: Each paranasal sinus is named for the bone that contains it. The frontal sinus is in the frontal bone above the orbits, the sphenoidal sinus is in the body of the sphenoid, and the maxillary sinus, the largest, is in the maxilla in the cheek region. The ethmoidal sinuses, the fourth group, are air cells in the ethmoid bone.
notes: The sphenoidal match is right, but the frontal sinus is not in the ethmoid. The ethmoid holds the ethmoidal air cells instead.
Correct. Each sinus sits in the bone it is named for.
This scrambles all three. Since the sinuses are named for their bones, the frontal sinus belongs in the frontal bone and the maxillary sinus in the maxilla.
The frontal match is right, but the other two are scrambled. The sphenoidal sinus sits in the sphenoid, and the maxillary sinus sits in the maxilla.
questions.answerText: Frontal: frontal bone; sphenoidal: sphenoid; maxillary: maxilla
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: A clinician examines the air-filled cavity within the body of the sphenoid bone, just below the sella turcica. Which paranasal sinus is this?
questions.why: The sphenoidal sinus is the air space within the body of the sphenoid bone, deep in the center of the skull and just below the sella turcica that holds the pituitary. Like the other paranasal sinuses, it lightens the skull and drains into the nasal cavity.
notes: The ethmoidal sinuses are many small air cells in the lateral masses of the ethmoid bone, between the orbits. Pick them for a question about the sinuses between the eyes.
The frontal sinus is in the frontal bone above the orbits. It would be the answer for a sinus behind the forehead.
The maxillary sinus is in the maxilla, in the cheek region above the upper teeth. Choose it for a question about the largest sinus.
Correct. The cavity in the body of the sphenoid is the sphenoidal sinus.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Which marking of the frontal bone is the smooth area between the eyebrow ridges?
questions.why: The glabella is the smooth, slightly raised area of the frontal bone between the eyebrow ridges, just above the bridge of the nose. It is a common surface landmark. The name comes from a Latin word meaning smooth and hairless.
notes: The supraorbital margin is the ridge above each orbit, under the eyebrow. It would be the answer for a question about the bony rim at the top of the eye socket.
Correct. The glabella is the smooth area between the eyebrows.
The orbital plates roof the orbits and floor the anterior cranial fossa, so they lie inside the skull rather than on its surface. Choose them for a question about the roof of the eye socket.
The squamous part is the broad, flat plate that forms most of the forehead. Pick it for a question about the large forehead region of the frontal bone.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Which opening of the mandible passes the nerve and vessels to the chin and lower lip?
questions.why: The mental foramen is a small opening on the outer surface of the mandibular body, below the premolar teeth. The nerve and vessels to the chin and lower lip exit here. Mental in this case comes from the Latin for chin, not from the mind.
notes: The mandibular notch is the gap between the condylar and coronoid processes at the top of the ramus, not an opening for a nerve to the chin. Pick it for a question about the dip between those two processes.
Correct. The mental foramen serves the chin and lower lip.
The mandibular foramen is on the inner surface of the ramus, where the nerve to the lower teeth enters the bone. It would be the answer for a question about the target of a lower dental block.
The infraorbital foramen is on the maxilla below the orbit and passes a nerve to the upper face. Choose it for a question about the cheek and upper lip region.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Which facial bones form the bridge of the nose?
questions.why: The two nasal bones meet in the midline to form the bony bridge of the nose, between the orbits. Below them, the lower part of the nose is shaped by cartilage rather than bone, which is why the tip of the nose is flexible.
notes: The lacrimal bones are in the medial wall of each orbit and hold the tear duct. They would be the answer for a question about the bone grooved for tears.
Correct. The nasal bones form the bridge of the nose.
The vomer forms the lower part of the nasal septum, inside the nasal cavity. Pick it for a question about the bony partition between the nostrils.
The inferior nasal conchae are scroll-shaped bones on the lateral walls of the nasal cavity. Choose them for a question about the bones that project into the nasal airway.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: An anatomist finds an upright bony ridge on the ethmoid bone projecting up into the cranial cavity, where a fold of the brain covering attaches. Which marking is this?
