questions.why: The crista galli, meaning rooster's comb, is an upright ridge on top of the ethmoid bone. It projects up into the anterior cranial fossa, and the falx cerebri, a fold of the dura mater between the cerebral hemispheres, attaches to it.
notes: Correct. The crista galli is the ridge where the falx cerebri attaches.
The cribriform plate is a horizontal, perforated plate on either side of the crista galli. Pick it for a question about where the olfactory nerve filaments pass.
The sella turcica is on the sphenoid bone, not the ethmoid, and holds the pituitary gland. Choose it for a question about the saddle-shaped seat in the cranial base.
The perpendicular plate also runs vertically, but it projects downward into the nasal cavity to form the upper nasal septum. It would be the answer for a question about the septum.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: The orbit, the bony eye socket, is built from how many bones?
questions.why: The orbit is built from seven bones: the frontal, sphenoid, zygomatic, maxilla, lacrimal, ethmoid, and palatine. Three are cranial bones (frontal, sphenoid, ethmoid), and four are facial bones. Building it from many bones is why the orbit has both a sturdy rim and some thin walls.
notes: Four is the number of bones that meet at the pterion, a different landmark on the side of the skull. Students mix up the two counts when studying skull junctions together.
Nine overcounts by adding bones that do not reach the orbit, such as the nasal bone or the temporal bone. Neither of these forms part of the eye socket.
Correct. Seven bones form the orbit.
Five leaves out some of the smaller contributors, such as the lacrimal and palatine bones. Students who count only the bones forming the rim tend to land on a lower number.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Which list correctly names the suture between the two parietal bones, the suture between the frontal and parietal bones, and the suture between a parietal and a temporal bone, in that order?
questions.why: The sagittal suture joins the two parietal bones along the midline. The coronal suture joins the frontal bone to the parietal bones across the top of the skull. The squamous suture joins each parietal bone to the temporal bone below it on the side of the skull.
notes: Correct. Sagittal, coronal, then squamous.
The lambdoid suture joins the parietal bones to the occipital bone, not the two parietals to each other. The midline suture between the parietals is the sagittal suture.
This swaps the first two and ends with the lambdoid suture, which joins the parietal bones to the occipital bone at the back. The lambdoid would fit a question about the back of the skull.
This has the right three sutures, but the last two are swapped. The frontal and parietal bones meet at the coronal suture, and the parietal and temporal bones meet at the squamous suture.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Which bone contains the supraorbital foramen?
questions.why: The supraorbital foramen is an opening in the supraorbital margin of the frontal bone, the ridge above each orbit. It passes the supraorbital nerve and vessels to the forehead. Supra- means above, so the name places it above the orbit.
notes: Correct. The supraorbital foramen is in the frontal bone.
The zygomatic bone forms the cheek and the lateral rim of the orbit, not the upper rim. Choose it for a question about the cheekbone.
The maxilla has the infraorbital foramen, below the orbit. Students confuse the two because the names differ only by the prefix, so pick the maxilla for a question about the infraorbital foramen.
The sphenoid bone forms the back of the orbit and contains the optic canal and superior orbital fissure. Pick it for a question about openings deep in the orbit.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Which bones form the upper jaw and hold the upper teeth?
questions.why: The two maxillae form the upper jaw. Their alveolar processes hold the upper teeth, their palatine processes form the front of the hard palate, and each contains a maxillary sinus. The maxillae meet almost every other facial bone, so they are often called the keystone of the face.
notes: The palatine bones form the back of the hard palate but hold no teeth. They would be the answer for a question about the posterior roof of the mouth.
Correct. The maxillae form the upper jaw.
The zygomatic bones are the cheekbones, lateral to the maxillae. Choose them for a question about the prominence of the cheek.
The mandible is the lower jaw and holds the lower teeth. Pick it for a question about the only movable skull bone.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Which single facial bone forms the inferior part of the nasal septum?
questions.why: The vomer is a thin, single facial bone that forms the lower part of the nasal septum. The perpendicular plate of the ethmoid forms the upper part, and septal cartilage completes the front. The name means plowshare, which describes its shape.
notes: The nasal bones are paired and form the bridge of the nose, not the septum. Pick them for a question about the bony bridge.
The ethmoid bone forms the upper part of the septum through its perpendicular plate, but it is a cranial bone, not a facial one. Choose it for a question about the superior nasal septum.
The mandible is the other single facial bone, but it is the lower jaw, not part of the nose. It would be the answer for a question about the movable jaw.
Correct. The vomer forms the inferior nasal septum.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: The coronal suture joins which bones?
options: A parietal bone and a temporal bone
The two parietal bones to each other
The parietal bones and the occipital bone
The frontal bone and the two parietal bones
questions.why: The coronal suture runs across the top of the skull from side to side, just behind the forehead. It joins the frontal bone in front to the two parietal bones behind. In an infant, the anterior fontanelle sits where it crosses the sagittal suture.
notes: This describes the squamous suture on the side of the skull. Choose it if the question asked about the squamous suture.
This describes the sagittal suture, which runs along the midline of the skull roof. It would be the answer if the question named the sagittal suture.
This describes the lambdoid suture at the back of the skull. Pick it if the question asked about the lambdoid suture.
Correct. The coronal suture joins the frontal bone to the parietal bones.
questions.answerText: The frontal bone and the two parietal bones
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: The mandibular fossa, the socket of the jaw joint, is a marking of which bone?
questions.why: The mandibular fossa is a socket on the underside of the temporal bone, just in front of the ear canal. It is named for the bone that fits into it, the mandible, not for the bone it is on. The condylar process of the mandible sits in it to form the temporomandibular joint.
notes: The occipital bone forms the back of the skull and articulates with the atlas, not the mandible. Choose it for a question about the occipital condyles.

The sphenoid bone is just in front of the temporal bone in the cranial base, and its pterygoid processes anchor chewing muscles, but it does not form the jaw socket. Pick it for a question about the sella turcica.
Correct. The mandibular fossa is on the temporal bone.
The mandible supplies the condylar process that fits into the fossa, but the fossa itself is on the temporal bone. Students pick the mandible because the fossa is named after it.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: The optic canal, which passes the optic nerve, is located in which bone?
questions.why: The optic canal passes through the sphenoid bone at the back of the orbit, at the base of its lesser wing. The optic nerve, cranial nerve II, travels through it from the eye to the brain. The superior orbital fissure, also in the sphenoid, lies just beside it.
notes: Correct. The optic canal is in the sphenoid bone.
The frontal bone forms the roof of the orbit and contains the supraorbital foramen. Pick it for a question about the opening above the eye.
The maxilla forms the floor of the orbit and contains the infraorbital foramen. Choose it for a question about the opening below the eye.
The ethmoid bone forms part of the medial wall of the orbit and contains the cribriform plate for the olfactory nerve. It would be the answer for a question about the nerve of smell.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: The carotid canal of the temporal bone transmits which vessel?
questions.why: The carotid canal carries the internal carotid artery through the temporal bone into the cranial cavity, where it helps supply the brain. Its partner on the drainage side, the internal jugular vein, leaves through the nearby jugular foramen.
notes: The vertebral arteries enter the skull through the foramen magnum. Pick them for a question about the arteries that pass alongside the spinal cord.
The internal jugular vein leaves the skull through the jugular foramen, just behind the carotid canal. It would be the answer for a question about the jugular foramen.
The external carotid artery stays outside the skull and supplies the face and scalp. Choose it for a question about blood supply to the face, since only the internal carotid enters the cranium.
Correct. The internal carotid artery passes through the carotid canal.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Where on the head can the mastoid process be felt?
options: At the point of the chin
At the back of the head in the midline
questions.why: The mastoid process is a rounded bump of the temporal bone just behind and below the ear. It anchors neck muscles and is filled with small air cells. You can feel it easily by pressing behind your earlobe.
notes: The point of the chin is formed by the mandible, near the mental foramen. Pick it for a question about the front of the lower jaw.
Correct. The mastoid process is just behind the ear.
The ridge above the orbit is the supraorbital margin of the frontal bone. It would be the answer for a question about the bony rim under the eyebrow.
The midline bump at the back of the head is the external occipital protuberance of the occipital bone. Choose it for a question about that landmark.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: The occipital condyles articulate with which bone of the vertebral column?
questions.why: The occipital condyles rest on the superior articular facets of the atlas, the first cervical vertebra (C1). Together they form the atlanto-occipital joint, which lets you nod yes. The atlas, in turn, pivots on the axis below it.
notes: The seventh cervical vertebra has the prominent spinous process at the base of the neck. Pick it for a question about the vertebra prominens.
Correct. The occipital condyles articulate with the atlas.
The axis is C2, which sits below the atlas and has the dens that the atlas pivots around. It would be the answer for a question about the vertebra that allows shaking the head no.
The first thoracic vertebra is the first vertebra to articulate with a rib. Choose it for a question about where the thoracic region begins.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Which part of the temporal bone is the dense wedge that houses the middle and inner ear?
questions.why: The petrous part is the dense, wedge-shaped portion of the temporal bone that projects into the cranial base. It houses the middle and inner ear. Petrous means rock-like, which describes how hard this bone is.
notes: The zygomatic process projects forward to join the cheekbone and form the zygomatic arch. Pick it for a question about the arch in front of the ear.
Correct. The petrous part houses the middle and inner ear.
The styloid process is a slender spike below the ear that anchors tongue and neck muscles. Choose it for a question about where the hyoid ligaments attach.
The squamous part is the thin, flat portion of the temporal bone forming the lower side wall of the skull. It would be the answer for a question about the flat plate above the ear.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Which of these bones forms part of the wall of the orbit?
questions.why: The orbit is built from seven bones: the frontal, sphenoid, zygomatic, maxilla, lacrimal, ethmoid, and palatine. The lacrimal bone forms part of the medial wall and is grooved for the tear duct. None of the other three bones listed forms any of the orbit's walls.
notes: The parietal bones form the top and sides of the cranium, well behind and above the orbit. They would be the answer for a question about the skull roof.

The nasal bones form the bridge of the nose between the orbits but are not part of the orbital walls. Students choose them because they sit so close to the eyes. Choose them for a question about the bridge of the nose.
Correct. The lacrimal bone forms part of the medial wall of the orbit.
The vomer forms the lower part of the nasal septum in the midline of the nasal cavity. Pick it for a question about the bony nasal partition.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: A blow to the side of the head fractures the skull at the pterion. Which artery running just beneath this site is at risk of tearing?
questions.why: The pterion is the thinnest part of the skull, where the frontal, parietal, temporal, and sphenoid bones meet. The middle meningeal artery runs just beneath it on the inner surface, supplying the meninges. A fracture here can tear the artery and cause bleeding inside the skull, which is a medical emergency.
notes: The vertebral arteries enter through the foramen magnum at the back of the skull base. Pick them for a question about the foramen magnum.
The facial artery runs outside the skull across the face, so a pterion fracture would not tear it. Choose it for a question about blood supply to the face.
The internal carotid artery enters through the carotid canal deep in the skull base, well away from the side wall. It would be the answer for a question about the carotid canal.
Correct. The middle meningeal artery runs beneath the pterion.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: An infection at the root of an upper tooth spreads into a nearby air-filled cavity. Which sinus is most likely involved?
questions.why: The maxillary sinus fills the body of the maxilla, and its floor sits just above the roots of the upper teeth. Because the two are so close, an infection at a tooth root can spread into the sinus. The maxillary sinuses are also the largest of the paranasal sinuses.
notes: The sphenoidal sinus is deep in the body of the sphenoid bone, behind the nasal cavity. Pick it for a question about the sinus just below the pituitary gland.
The frontal sinus is in the frontal bone above the orbits, far from the teeth. It would be the answer for sinus pain in the forehead.
The ethmoidal sinuses are air cells between the orbits, above the level of the teeth. Choose them for a question about sinus pain between the eyes.
Correct. The maxillary sinus sits just above the upper tooth roots.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Rising pressure inside the rigid skull forces brain tissue toward the one large opening in the cranial base. Through which opening can the tissue be forced?
questions.why: The skull is a rigid box, so swelling or bleeding inside it raises pressure with nowhere to go. The foramen magnum is the only large opening between the cranial cavity and the vertebral canal, so brain tissue can be pushed down through it and compress the brainstem. That is why rising intracranial pressure is an emergency.
notes: The superior orbital fissure is a slit leading to the orbit that passes the nerves that move the eye. Choose it for a question about those nerves.
Correct. The foramen magnum is the large opening that brain tissue can be forced through.
The optic canal is a small opening for the optic nerve and leads into the orbit, not toward the spinal cord. It would be the answer for a question about the path of the optic nerve.
The carotid canal is a narrow passage for the internal carotid artery. Pick it for a question about how that artery enters the skull.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: A nurse checks an infant for dehydration by feeling a soft spot on the top of the skull. Which fontanelle is used for this check?
questions.why: The anterior fontanelle is the largest fontanelle and stays open the longest, until about 18 to 24 months, so it is easy to feel on top of the head. A sunken anterior fontanelle can signal dehydration, and a bulging one can signal raised pressure inside the skull.
notes: The anterolateral fontanelles are small, on the sides of the skull, and close by about 3 months. Pick them for a question about the sphenoidal fontanelles.
The posterior fontanelle is small and closes at about 2 months, so it is not useful for checks later in infancy. It would be the answer for a question about the first fontanelle to close.
Correct. The anterior fontanelle is the one checked for dehydration.
The posterolateral fontanelles are behind the ears and are not on top of the head. Choose them for a question about the mastoid fontanelles.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: A patient loses the sense of smell after a head injury. Damage to which skull structure would best explain this?
options: The mental foramen of the mandible
The mastoid process of the temporal bone
The cribriform plate of the ethmoid
The sella turcica of the sphenoid
questions.why: The olfactory nerve filaments pass from the nasal lining up through the many small holes of the cribriform plate to reach the brain. The plate is thin and perforated, so a blow to the head can fracture it and tear these filaments. That cuts the pathway for smell.
notes: The mental foramen passes the nerve to the chin and lower lip. Choose it for a question about numbness of the chin.
The mastoid process is a muscle attachment behind the ear filled with air cells. Pick it for a question about the bump behind the ear or an infection spreading from the middle ear.
Correct. Damage to the cribriform plate can tear the olfactory nerve filaments.
The sella turcica holds the pituitary gland. Damage there would be the answer for a question about injury to the pituitary, not the sense of smell.
questions.answerText: The cribriform plate of the ethmoid
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: An infant's skull bones are joined by soft fibrous fontanelles rather than fused sutures. Why does this matter at birth and in early life?
options: It makes the skull heavier so the head is more stable
It lets the skull compress at birth and expand as the brain grows
It lets the skull bones move apart freely so the jaw can open
It keeps the brain from growing until the bones have fused
questions.why: Fontanelles are fibrous membrane gaps between the bones of an infant's skull. At birth they let the skull bones shift and overlap so the head can pass through the birth canal. Afterward they leave room for the skull to enlarge as the brain grows rapidly, and they close gradually over the first two years.
notes: Membrane gaps make the skull lighter and more flexible, not heavier. This choice reverses the effect of having unfused bones.
Correct. Fontanelles allow compression at birth and growth afterward.
Jaw opening happens at the temporomandibular joint, not at the fontanelles. This choice mixes up the jaw joint with the soft spots of the cranium.
The brain grows fastest in infancy, while the fontanelles are open. This choice reverses the relationship, since the open fontanelles are what make room for that growth.
questions.answerText: It lets the skull compress at birth and expand as the brain grows
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Adult cranial bones meet at immovable, interlocking sutures. Why is an immovable joint suited to the bones around the brain?
options: Immovable joints let the cranial bones keep growing in length
Locked joints make the skull bones much lighter
Immovable joints let the cranium expand with each heartbeat
Locked joints form a stable protective case around the brain
questions.why: A suture is an immovable fibrous joint, and the wavy, interlocking edges of the cranial bones lock them together. This turns the cranium into a single rigid case that protects the brain from forces coming from any direction. Movement is needed only at the jaw, which has its own synovial joint.
notes: Skull bones do not grow in length at sutures the way long bones grow at epiphyseal plates. This choice applies the long bone growth pattern to the skull.
The type of joint does not change bone weight. The skull is lightened by its air-filled sinuses, so pick the paranasal sinuses for a question about reducing skull weight.
The adult cranium does not expand, which is exactly why rising pressure inside it is dangerous. This choice assumes the skull flexes when it does not.
Correct. Rigid sutures make a stable protective case.
questions.answerText: Locked joints form a stable protective case around the brain
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Several skull bones, such as the maxillae and the frontal bone, contain air-filled paranasal sinuses. What is one advantage of these hollow spaces?
options: They store blood that supplies the brain
They hold cerebrospinal fluid around the brain
They house the structures of the inner ear
questions.why: The paranasal sinuses are air-filled spaces within the frontal, ethmoid, sphenoid, and maxillary bones. They make the skull lighter without weakening its outer surfaces, and they add resonance to the voice. They drain into the nasal cavity, which is why a head cold can spread into them as sinusitis.
notes: The sinuses hold air, not blood. Blood reaches the brain through the internal carotid and vertebral arteries, so pick those for a question about brain blood supply.
Cerebrospinal fluid fills the ventricles and the space around the brain, inside the meninges. Choose the subarachnoid space for a question about where CSF surrounds the brain.
The inner ear is housed in the dense petrous part of the temporal bone, not in an air sinus. Pick the petrous part for a question about where the hearing organs sit.
Correct. The sinuses lighten the skull.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: The foramen magnum is a large opening in the occipital bone at the base of the skull. Why must an opening this large exist there?
options: The esophagus passes through it on its way to the stomach
The brainstem continues into the spinal cord through it
It makes room for the atlas to rotate on the skull
The internal jugular veins leave the skull through it
questions.why: The medulla oblongata, the lowest part of the brainstem, continues into the spinal cord at the foramen magnum. The cord must pass from the cranial cavity into the vertebral canal, so the skull needs a large opening directly above the spine. The vertebral arteries and spinal accessory nerve also pass through it.
notes: The esophagus runs in the neck in front of the vertebral column and never enters the skull. Pick the pharynx and esophagus for a question about the path of food.
Correct. The spinal cord passes through the foramen magnum.

The atlas rotates on the axis below it, not on the skull, and it meets the skull at the occipital condyles beside the foramen. Pick the occipital condyles for a question about the skull's joint with the spine.
The internal jugular veins leave through the jugular foramina, between the temporal and occipital bones. Choose the jugular foramen for a question about venous drainage of the brain.
questions.answerText: The brainstem continues into the spinal cord through it
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: The mandible is the only freely movable skull bone, meeting the temporal bone at the temporomandibular joint. Why does the jaw need a movable joint when the rest of the skull does not?
options: All skull bones move equally, so the mandible is not different
Chewing and speech need a moving jaw
The jaw must move to pump cerebrospinal fluid around the brain
The jaw moves to give the brain extra room as it grows
questions.why: The temporomandibular joint is a synovial joint between the condylar process of the mandible and the mandibular fossa of the temporal bone. It lets the lower jaw open, close, and slide for chewing and speaking. The cranial bones have a different job, protecting the brain, so they are locked together by immovable sutures.
notes: In the adult, every other skull bone is fixed by sutures, so the mandible really is different. This choice ignores the difference between sutures and a synovial joint.
Correct. The jaw moves for chewing and speech, while the cranium stays rigid for protection.
Cerebrospinal fluid is produced and circulated within the ventricles and meninges, independent of jaw movement. Pick the choroid plexus for a question about where CSF is made.
Room for brain growth comes from the fontanelles and sutures of the infant cranium, not the jaw. Choose the fontanelles for a question about how the skull grows with the brain.
questions.answerText: Chewing and speech need a moving jaw
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: The cribriform plate of the ethmoid bone is thin and full of small holes. Why does a hard blow to the head put this plate at special risk?
options: It fractures easily, tearing smell nerves or leaking CSF into the nose
It is the thickest skull bone and transfers the force to the brain
It is made of cartilage, so it cannot heal after a blow
Its holes carry the internal carotid arteries, which can tear
questions.why: The cribriform plate is a thin horizontal plate that separates the nasal cavity below from the brain above. Its many holes for the olfactory nerve filaments make it weak, so a blow can fracture it. A fracture can tear the filaments and cause loss of smell, and it can open a path for cerebrospinal fluid to leak into the nose.
notes: Correct. Its thin, perforated structure makes it easy to fracture.
The cribriform plate is one of the thinnest parts of the skull, not the thickest. Pick the petrous part of the temporal bone for a question about the densest region of the skull.
The cribriform plate is bone, not cartilage. Cartilage does form the front of the nasal septum, so pick septal cartilage for a question about the flexible part of the nose.
The holes carry the olfactory nerve filaments, not arteries. The internal carotid enters through the carotid canal, so choose that for a question about the artery.
questions.answerText: It fractures easily, tearing smell nerves or leaking CSF into the nose
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: The orbit is built from parts of several bones. Why can a blunt blow to the eye cause a blowout fracture of the orbital floor instead of breaking the rim?
options: The floor is formed by the frontal bone, which is very thin
The orbit is made of cartilage, which tears more easily than bone
The floor is the thickest part of the orbit, so it absorbs the force
The floor is a thin wall, so pressure breaks it before the sturdy rim
questions.why: The orbital rim is thick and strong, but the floor of the orbit, formed mainly by the maxilla above the maxillary sinus, is a thin plate of bone. A blunt object such as a ball can press the eye back into the socket and spike the pressure inside it. The pressure breaks the weakest wall, the floor, while the rim stays intact.
notes: The frontal bone forms the roof of the orbit, not the floor. The floor is formed mainly by the maxilla, so pick the frontal bone only for a question about the orbital roof.
The orbit is made entirely of bone, with no cartilage in its walls. This choice confuses the orbit with the flexible cartilage of the external nose.
This reverses the real structure. The rim is the thick, sturdy part, and the floor is thin, which is why it is the part that gives way.
Correct. The thin orbital floor breaks before the strong rim.
questions.answerText: The floor is a thin wall, so pressure breaks it before the sturdy rim
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: The inner ear sits deep within the petrous part of the temporal bone. Why is this location an advantage?
options: The delicate hearing and balance organs gain protection from dense bone
The petrous part is hollow, so it holds air for the inner ear
The petrous part is the thinnest bone, so sound reaches the ear easily
The inner ear makes new bone, so it must sit inside a bone
questions.why: The petrous part of the temporal bone is the densest, hardest region of the skull, and its name means rock-like. The inner ear holds the delicate organs of hearing and balance, and burying them inside this dense bone protects them from injury. The middle ear is housed in the same region.
notes: Correct. Dense petrous bone protects the inner ear.
The petrous part is dense, not hollow. The air spaces of the temporal bone are the mastoid air cells behind the ear, so pick those for a question about air within the temporal bone.
The thinnest part of the skull is the pterion, on the side of the cranium. This choice mixes up the densest region with the thinnest.
The inner ear does not produce bone. This choice confuses the organ with the bone cells that build bone, the osteoblasts.
questions.answerText: The delicate hearing and balance organs gain protection from dense bone
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Where on an infant's skull is the posterior fontanelle located?
options: Behind the ear near the mastoid region
On the side of the skull near the sphenoid bone
Where the frontal bone meets the parietal bones
Where the parietal bones meet the occipital bone
questions.why: The posterior fontanelle, also called the occipital fontanelle, is at the back of the infant's head, where the two parietal bones meet the occipital bone. It is small and closes early, at about 2 months. In the adult, the lambdoid suture runs through this area.
notes: This describes the posterolateral, or mastoid, fontanelles. Choose it for a question about the soft spots behind the ears.
This describes the anterolateral, or sphenoidal, fontanelles. Pick it for a question about the soft spots on the sides of the skull.
This is the location of the anterior fontanelle, the largest one. It would be the answer for a question about the fontanelle checked for dehydration.
Correct. The posterior fontanelle is at the parietal and occipital junction.
questions.answerText: Where the parietal bones meet the occipital bone
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: The hypoglossal canal, which passes cranial nerve XII, is found in which bone?
questions.why: The hypoglossal canal is a small canal in the occipital bone, just above each occipital condyle beside the foramen magnum. It passes the hypoglossal nerve, cranial nerve XII, which heads toward the tongue. Hypo- means below and glossal means tongue.
notes: The mandible contains the mandibular and mental foramina. Choose it for a question about the nerve to the lower teeth or the chin.
The sphenoid bone contains the optic canal, the superior orbital fissure, and the foramen ovale. Pick it for a question about openings passing nerves to the eye or jaw.
The temporal bone contains the carotid canal, the internal acoustic meatus, and the stylomastoid foramen. It would be the answer for a question about any of those openings.
Correct. The hypoglossal canal is in the occipital bone.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: The foramen ovale passes a branch of the trigeminal nerve to the lower jaw. In which bone is it found?
questions.why: The foramen ovale is an oval opening in the greater wing of the sphenoid bone, in the floor of the middle cranial fossa. It passes the branch of the trigeminal nerve that serves the lower jaw. Ovale simply means oval, describing its shape.
notes: Correct. The foramen ovale is in the sphenoid bone.
The occipital bone contains the foramen magnum and the hypoglossal canals. Pick it for a question about the opening for the spinal cord.
The temporal bone sits just behind the foramen ovale and has the carotid canal and the acoustic meatuses. It would be the answer for a question about the opening for the internal carotid artery.
The ethmoid bone contains the cribriform foramina for the olfactory nerve. Choose it for a question about the nerve of smell.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Which marking of the temporal bone is the slender spike below the ear that anchors tongue and neck muscles and the ligaments that hold the hyoid?
questions.why: The styloid process is a thin, pointed spike projecting down from the underside of the temporal bone, below the ear. Muscles of the tongue and neck attach to it, and ligaments run from it to suspend the hyoid bone. Stylo- means pen or pillar, which matches its shape.
notes: The zygomatic process projects forward from the temporal bone to meet the cheekbone. Pick it for a question about the zygomatic arch.
The mastoid process is the rounded bump behind the ear, an attachment for neck muscles. It would be the answer for a question about the bump you can feel behind the earlobe.
The coronoid process belongs to the mandible and anchors the temporalis muscle. Choose it for a question about the jaw.
Correct. The styloid process is the slender spike that anchors the hyoid ligaments.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: The zygomatic arch is formed where the zygomatic bone meets which marking?
options: The greater wing of the sphenoid bone
The zygomatic process of the temporal bone
The coronoid process of the mandible
The frontal process of the maxilla
questions.why: The zygomatic arch is the bony bar along the side of the face, between the cheek and the ear. It forms where the zygomatic process of the temporal bone reaches forward to join the zygomatic bone, the cheekbone. You can feel it as a ridge in front of the ear.
notes: The greater wing of the sphenoid forms part of the lateral skull wall and orbit, deep to the arch. Choose it for a question about the bones at the pterion.
Correct. The zygomatic process of the temporal bone completes the arch.
The coronoid process of the mandible sits beneath the zygomatic arch and anchors the temporalis, but it does not form the arch. Pick it for a question about the attachment of the temporalis muscle.
The frontal process of the maxilla rises beside the nose to meet the frontal bone. It would be the answer for a question about the part of the maxilla near the bridge of the nose.
questions.answerText: The zygomatic process of the temporal bone
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Which nasal conchae are separate facial bones rather than parts of the ethmoid bone?
questions.why: The nasal cavity has three pairs of scroll-shaped conchae on its lateral walls. The superior and middle conchae are projections of the ethmoid bone, but the inferior nasal conchae are separate facial bones. That is why the inferior nasal conchae are counted among the fourteen facial bones.
notes: The lateral masses are the side portions of the ethmoid that contain the ethmoidal air cells, and the superior and middle conchae hang from them. Choose them for a question about where the ethmoidal sinuses are.
The superior conchae are part of the ethmoid bone, not separate bones. They would be the answer for a question about the highest scrolls of the nasal wall.
The middle conchae are also part of the ethmoid bone. Pick them for a question about the ethmoid's scroll-shaped projections below the superior conchae.
Correct. The inferior nasal conchae are separate facial bones.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: The infraorbital foramen, which passes a nerve to the face below the eye, is found in which bone?
questions.why: The infraorbital foramen is an opening in the maxilla just below the orbit. The infraorbital nerve passes through it to supply the skin of the face below the eye. Infra- means below, so the name places it under the orbit.
notes: The zygomatic bone forms the cheekbone, lateral to the infraorbital foramen. Pick it for a question about the prominence of the cheek.
The frontal bone contains the supraorbital foramen, above the orbit. It would be the answer if the question asked about the opening above the eye.
Correct. The infraorbital foramen is in the maxilla.
The sphenoid bone forms the back of the orbit and contains the optic canal. Choose it for a question about openings deep in the orbit.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: The atlanto-occipital joint, where the occipital condyles meet the atlas, mainly allows which head movement?
questions.why: The atlanto-occipital joint forms where the occipital condyles rest on the superior articular facets of the atlas. Its shape allows the head to rock forward and back, which is the nodding yes motion. Rotation of the head, the no motion, happens at the joint between the atlas and the axis instead.
notes: Opening and closing the jaw happens at the temporomandibular joint between the mandible and the temporal bone. Pick it for a question about chewing.
Adult skull bones do not move apart, since they are locked by sutures. This choice mixes up a joint between the skull and spine with the joints between skull bones.
Correct. The atlanto-occipital joint lets you nod yes.
Shaking the head no happens at the atlantoaxial joint, where the atlas pivots around the dens of the axis. It would be the answer for a question about the joint between C1 and C2.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Which projections of the sphenoid bone point downward and anchor the chewing muscles?
questions.why: The pterygoid processes project downward from the underside of the sphenoid bone, behind the maxillae. They serve as attachment points for chewing muscles. Pterygoid means wing-shaped, which can be confusing because the sphenoid also has separate greater and lesser wings.
notes: The greater wings are broad lateral parts of the sphenoid that form part of the cranial floor, the orbit, and the lateral skull wall. They would be the answer for a question about the sphenoid at the pterion.
The styloid processes belong to the temporal bones and anchor tongue and neck muscles. Choose them for a question about where the hyoid is suspended.
The lesser wings are smaller anterior parts of the sphenoid that form part of the anterior cranial fossa. Pick them for a question about the floor beneath the frontal lobes.
Correct. The pterygoid processes anchor the chewing muscles.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: What is the midline bump felt at the back of the head called?
questions.why: The external occipital protuberance is a midline bump on the outer surface of the occipital bone. You can feel it at the back of the head, at about the level where the head meets the neck. It is an attachment point for a ligament and muscles of the back of the neck.
notes: The mastoid process is a paired bump behind each ear, on the temporal bone, not in the midline. It would be the answer for a question about the bump behind the earlobe.
Correct. The midline bump at the back of the head is the external occipital protuberance.
The parietal eminence is the rounded high point on each parietal bone, at the widest part of the skull. Choose it for a question about the sides of the skull roof.
The occipital condyles are on the underside of the skull beside the foramen magnum and cannot be felt from the outside. Pick them for a question about the joint with the atlas.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Which process of the mandible has a head that fits into the mandibular fossa of the temporal bone?
questions.why: The condylar process is the posterior process at the top of the mandibular ramus. Its rounded head fits into the mandibular fossa of the temporal bone, forming the temporomandibular joint. The mandibular notch separates it from the coronoid process in front.
notes: The coronoid process is the anterior process of the ramus, where the temporalis muscle attaches. It would be the answer for a question about that muscle attachment.
The alveolar process is the ridge that holds the lower teeth. Pick it for a question about the tooth sockets.
Correct. The head of the condylar process sits in the mandibular fossa.
The mastoid process belongs to the temporal bone, behind the ear, and is not part of the mandible. Choose it for a question about the bump behind the ear.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Which opening of the temporal bone is the entrance to the ear canal on the outside of the skull?
questions.why: The external acoustic meatus is the opening of the ear canal on the outer side of the temporal bone. Sound travels through it toward the eardrum and middle ear. Meatus means passage, and external tells you it opens on the outside of the skull.
notes: Correct. The external acoustic meatus is the opening of the ear canal.
The carotid canal carries the internal carotid artery into the skull. Choose it for a question about the main artery to the brain.
The stylomastoid foramen is on the underside of the skull, between the styloid and mastoid processes, and is where the facial nerve exits. Pick it for a question about that exit.

The internal acoustic meatus opens on the inner side of the temporal bone, facing the brain, and carries the nerves for hearing and facial movement. It would be the answer for a question about where the facial nerve enters the temporal bone.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: The floor of the cranium, the cranial base, is shaped into how many cranial fossae?
questions.why: The cranial base is shaped into three cranial fossae, which step down from front to back like a set of shelves: anterior, middle, and posterior. Each fossa cradles a different part of the brain. The frontal bone and the lesser wings of the sphenoid help form the anterior fossa, and the occipital bone forms much of the posterior fossa.
notes: Five is the number of zones in the growth plate, not the number of cranial fossae. Students sometimes carry a memorized number over from another list.
Two leaves out one level. Students who think only of front and back miss the middle cranial fossa, which holds the sella turcica and the foramen ovale.
Correct. There are three cranial fossae: anterior, middle, and posterior.
Four is the number of bones that meet at the pterion, and it is also the number of paranasal sinus groups. It would fit a question about either of those, not the cranial fossae.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: On a lateral skull, a student traces the bony bar of the zygomatic arch from the cheek back toward the ear. Which two bones does the arch join, and which group does each belong to?
options: The zygomatic bone and the maxilla, both facial bones.
The temporal bone and the sphenoid, both cranial bones.
The zygomatic bone, a facial bone, and the temporal bone, a cranial bone.
The zygomatic bone, a cranial bone, and the temporal bone, a facial bone.
questions.why: The arch is formed where the zygomatic process of the temporal bone meets the zygomatic bone. The zygomatic bone is the cheekbone, one of the fourteen facial bones. The temporal bone houses the ear and is one of the eight cranial bones, so the arch bridges the two groups.
notes: The maxilla meets the cheekbone through its own zygomatic process, but the arch running back toward the ear reaches the temporal bone.
The sphenoid forms the central wedge of the cranial base and part of the lateral wall. The arch runs to the cheekbone, a facial bone.
Correct. The zygomatic arch joins the zygomatic bone of the face to the temporal bone of the cranium.
The bones are right but the groups are swapped. The cheekbone is facial, and the temporal bone is cranial.
questions.answerText: The zygomatic bone, a facial bone, and the temporal bone, a cranial bone.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: A student sorts the skull and places the ethmoid with the facial bones because it forms part of the nasal cavity. Which correction is right?
options: It is a facial bone, since it forms the lower nasal septum.
It is counted separately, like the hyoid bone.
It is a facial bone, since its conchae are facial bones.
It is a cranial bone, one of the eight in the braincase.
questions.why: Group membership follows the bone, not the space it borders. The ethmoid is the deepest cranial bone, lying between the orbits, and it counts among the eight cranial bones. Its superior and middle conchae and perpendicular plate help build the nasal cavity, but that does not make it facial.
notes: The lower part of the nasal septum is the vomer, a facial bone. The ethmoid forms the upper part with its perpendicular plate.
The hyoid is the bone counted separately from the skull. The ethmoid is one of the eight cranial bones.
Only the inferior nasal conchae are separate facial bones. The superior and middle conchae are parts of the ethmoid.
Correct. The ethmoid is one of the eight cranial bones, even though it helps form the nasal cavity.
questions.answerText: It is a cranial bone, one of the eight in the braincase.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Which suture joins a parietal bone to a temporal bone on the side of the skull?
questions.why: The squamous suture runs along the lower side of the skull, where each parietal bone meets the temporal bone below it. There is one on each side of the head.
notes: The coronal suture joins the frontal bone to the two parietal bones, across the top of the skull behind the forehead.
The lambdoid suture joins the parietal bones to the occipital bone at the back of the skull.
The sagittal suture joins the two parietal bones along the midline of the skull roof.
Correct. The squamous suture joins a parietal bone and a temporal bone, one on each side.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: On a fetal skull, a student finds a soft membrane gap at the spot where the coronal and sagittal sutures will later meet. Which fontanelle is it, and about when does it close?
options: The anterior fontanelle, by about 18 to 24 months.
The posterior fontanelle, by about 2 months.
The anterolateral fontanelle, by about 3 months.
The anterior fontanelle, by about 2 months.
questions.why: Work from the sutures to the bones. The coronal suture joins the frontal bone to the parietals, and the sagittal suture joins the two parietals, so they meet where the frontal and parietal bones come together. That is the anterior fontanelle, the largest one, which closes at about 18 to 24 months.
notes: Correct. The coronal and sagittal sutures meet where the frontal and parietal bones meet, the site of the anterior fontanelle.
The posterior fontanelle lies where the parietal bones meet the occipital bone, at the back, where the sagittal suture meets the lambdoid suture.
The anterolateral, or sphenoidal, fontanelles are on the side of the skull, one on each side, not at the top.
The site is right, but about 2 months is when the posterior fontanelle closes. The anterior one stays open until about 18 to 24 months.
questions.answerText: The anterior fontanelle, by about 18 to 24 months.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: The ethmoidal sinuses, the ethmoid air cells, lie within which bone?
questions.why: Each paranasal sinus is named for the bone it occupies. The ethmoidal sinuses are the ethmoid air cells, held in the lateral masses of the ethmoid between the orbits.
notes: The sphenoid holds the sphenoidal sinus, within its body. The ethmoid air cells are in the ethmoid.
The frontal bone holds the frontal sinus, above the orbits. The ethmoidal sinuses lie between the orbits.
Correct. The ethmoidal sinuses are the air cells of the ethmoid, between the orbits.
The maxillae hold the maxillary sinuses, the largest sinuses, in the cheek region.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: The nasal septum is built from the vomer, the perpendicular plate of the ethmoid, and which other structure?
questions.why: The nasal septum divides the nasal cavity into two sides. Its bony part is the perpendicular plate of the ethmoid above and the vomer below, and septal cartilage completes it.
notes: Correct. The nasal septum is the vomer plus the perpendicular plate of the ethmoid plus septal cartilage.
The inferior nasal conchae are scroll-shaped bones on the lateral wall of the nasal cavity, not part of the midline septum.
The palatine bones form the posterior hard palate and part of the orbit. They do not form the septum.
The cribriform plate is the perforated horizontal plate of the ethmoid that the olfactory filaments pass through. The septum is built from the vertical perpendicular plate instead.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: A patient fractures the back part of the bony roof of the mouth. Which bone is broken, and which group of skull bones does it belong to?
options: A palatine bone, a facial bone.
questions.why: The hard palate is the bony roof of the mouth, with the maxillae in front and the palatine bones behind. A break at the back part therefore involves a palatine bone. The palatine bones are paired facial bones.
notes: Correct. The palatine bones form the posterior hard palate and are facial bones.
The maxillae form the front of the hard palate through their palatine processes. The back part is the palatine bones.
The sphenoid is the central wedge of the cranial base and does not form the roof of the mouth.
The vomer forms the lower part of the nasal septum, not the hard palate.
questions.answerText: A palatine bone, a facial bone.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Moving backward along the medial wall of the orbit, a probe slides from a small bone grooved for the tear duct onto a deeper bone between the orbits that holds air cells. Which bones are these, and which sinus does the second one hold?
options: The lacrimal bone, then the sphenoid with its sphenoidal sinus.
The nasal bone, then the ethmoid with its ethmoidal sinuses.
The lacrimal bone, then the maxilla with its maxillary sinus.
The lacrimal bone, then the ethmoid with its ethmoidal sinuses.
questions.why: Identify each bone, then its sinus. The small bone of the medial orbital wall grooved for the tear duct is the lacrimal bone. The deeper bone between the orbits is the ethmoid, the deepest cranial bone, and its air cells are the ethmoidal sinuses.
notes: The sphenoid helps form the orbit, but its sinus is in its body in the cranial base. The bone between the orbits with air cells is the ethmoid.
The nasal bones form the bridge of the nose. The orbital bone grooved for the tear duct is the lacrimal bone.
The maxillary sinus lies in the cheek region, below the orbit. The bone between the orbits with air cells is the ethmoid.
Correct. The lacrimal bone is grooved for the tear duct, and the ethmoid between the orbits holds the ethmoidal sinuses.
questions.answerText: The lacrimal bone, then the ethmoid with its ethmoidal sinuses.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Which openings in the ethmoid bone pass the olfactory nerve filaments, cranial nerve I?
questions.why: The cribriform plate is the perforated horizontal plate of the ethmoid, and its many small openings are the cribriform foramina. The filaments of the olfactory nerve, cranial nerve I, pass through them.
notes: The optic canal is in the sphenoid and passes the optic nerve, cranial nerve II.
The foramen ovale is in the sphenoid and passes a branch of the trigeminal nerve to the lower jaw.
Correct. The olfactory filaments pass through the cribriform foramina of the ethmoid.
The superior orbital fissure is in the sphenoid and passes nerves that supply the eye, including those that move it.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: Inside the skull, a student finds two openings in the same bone: a canal carrying cranial nerve II and, beside it, a slit carrying the nerves that move the eye. Which bone holds them, and what are the openings?
options: The ethmoid, with the cribriform foramina and optic canal.
The sphenoid, with the foramen ovale and jugular foramen.
The temporal, with the internal acoustic meatus and carotid canal.
The sphenoid, with the optic canal and superior orbital fissure.
questions.why: Name each opening from what it carries, then find the bone. Cranial nerve II is the optic nerve, which runs through the optic canal. The nerves that move the eye pass through the superior orbital fissure, and both openings are in the sphenoid.
notes: The cribriform foramina in the ethmoid carry the olfactory filaments, cranial nerve I. The optic canal is in the sphenoid.
The foramen ovale is in the sphenoid but carries a trigeminal branch, and the jugular foramen lies between the temporal and occipital bones.
These temporal bone openings carry the hearing and facial nerves and the internal carotid artery, not the nerves of the eye.
Correct. The optic canal and the superior orbital fissure are both in the sphenoid.
questions.answerText: The sphenoid, with the optic canal and superior orbital fissure.
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: A skull fracture runs through the temporal bone. Which two openings of that bone could be damaged, and what passes through each?
options: Internal acoustic meatus (hearing, facial nerves); carotid canal (internal carotid).
Foramen ovale (trigeminal branch); optic canal (optic nerve).
Internal acoustic meatus (internal carotid); carotid canal (hearing nerves).
Foramen magnum (spinal cord); hypoglossal canal (nerve XII).
questions.why: First list the openings that pierce the temporal bone, then recall their contents. The internal acoustic meatus carries the nerves for hearing and for facial movement, and the carotid canal carries the internal carotid artery. A fracture through the temporal bone puts both at risk.
notes: Correct. The temporal bone holds the internal acoustic meatus and the carotid canal.
Both of these openings are in the sphenoid, not the temporal bone.
The openings are right but the contents are swapped. The carotid canal carries the internal carotid artery.
Both of these are in the occipital bone. The foramen magnum passes the spinal cord, and the hypoglossal canal passes cranial nerve XII.
questions.answerText: Internal acoustic meatus (hearing, facial nerves); carotid canal (internal carotid).
review: territory set from the card's topic

questions.q: How many vertebrae are in the cervical region of the vertebral column?
questions.why: The cervical region is the neck, and it has seven vertebrae, numbered C1 through C7 from the skull downward. These are the smallest vertebrae in the column because they carry only the weight of the head. A quick way to keep the counts straight is to think of the day pattern: breakfast at 7, lunch at 12, dinner at 5, for cervical, thoracic, and lumbar.
notes: Twelve is the number of thoracic vertebrae, one for each pair of ribs. Pick twelve if the question asks about the chest region of the spine.

Twenty-four is the total number of separate, unfused vertebrae in the cervical, thoracic, and lumbar regions together. It would be right for a question about all the movable vertebrae, not just the neck.
Five is the number of lumbar vertebrae in the lower back, L1 to L5. Choose five if the question asks about the lumbar region or the number of fused sacral vertebrae.
Correct. The neck holds seven cervical vertebrae, C1 through C7.

questions.q: How many vertebrae are in the thoracic region of the vertebral column?
questions.why: The thoracic region is the chest portion of the spine, and it has twelve vertebrae, T1 through T12. The count matches the twelve pairs of ribs, because each thoracic vertebra articulates with a pair of ribs. Linking the vertebrae to the ribs makes the number easy to recall.
notes: Four is the usual number of small vertebrae that fuse to form the coccyx, the tailbone. Pick four if the question were about the coccyx.
Seven is the number of cervical vertebrae in the neck. It would be the answer if the question asked about the cervical region.
Five is the number of lumbar vertebrae and also the number of vertebrae that fuse to form the sacrum. Choose five for either of those questions.
Correct. There are twelve thoracic vertebrae, matching the twelve pairs of ribs.

questions.q: How many vertebrae are in the lumbar region of the vertebral column?
questions.why: The lumbar region is the lower back, and it has five vertebrae, L1 through L5. These are the largest separate vertebrae because they carry the weight of everything above them. Below L5 the column continues as the sacrum.
notes: Seven is the cervical count, the vertebrae of the neck. It would be right for a question about the cervical region.
Correct. The lower back has five lumbar vertebrae, L1 through L5.
Three does not match any region of the vertebral column. Students sometimes pick it by mixing up the vertebra count with the three bones of the sternum or the three phalanges in a finger.
Twelve is the thoracic count, one vertebra for each pair of ribs. Choose twelve if the question asked about the chest region of the spine.

questions.q: How many separate, unfused vertebrae are in the adult vertebral column, not counting the sacrum and coccyx?
questions.why: The separate vertebrae are the ones in the three movable regions: seven cervical, twelve thoracic, and five lumbar, which adds up to twenty-four. The sacrum and coccyx are each made of several vertebrae fused into a single bone, so they are counted separately. Adding those two fused bones gives the adult total of twenty-six bones.
notes: Twenty-six is the total number of bones in the adult column when the sacrum and coccyx are each counted as one bone. Pick it if the question asks how many bones make up the whole adult column.
Thirty-three is the number of vertebrae present early in development, before the sacral and coccygeal vertebrae fuse. Choose it for a question about the developing column.
Twelve is only the thoracic count. Students pick it when they count one region instead of adding all three movable regions together.
Correct. Seven cervical plus twelve thoracic plus five lumbar gives twenty-four separate vertebrae.

questions.q: Which bone is formed by five fused vertebrae and is wedged between the two hip bones?
questions.why: The sacrum is a single triangular bone made of five vertebrae that fuse in the adult. It sits wedged between the two hip bones, forming the back wall of the pelvis. Its job is to pass the weight of the upper body into the pelvic girdle and down to the legs.
notes: The axis is C2, the second cervical vertebra, which carries the dens. It would be right for a question about the vertebra the head rotates on.
The atlas is C1, the first cervical vertebra, a ring that holds up the skull. Pick it for a question about the vertebra that supports the head.
The coccyx is the tailbone, a small bone of usually four fused vertebrae just below the sacrum. Choose it if the question describes the tailbone or the lowest part of the column.
Correct. The sacrum is five fused vertebrae wedged between the hip bones.

questions.q: What is the anatomical name for the tailbone?
questions.why: The coccyx is the tailbone, a small bone formed by several tiny vertebrae (usually four) fused together at the very bottom of the vertebral column. It sits just below the sacrum. It serves as an attachment point for pelvic ligaments and muscles.
notes: Correct. The coccyx is the fused tailbone at the bottom of the column.
The vertebra prominens is C7, the vertebra with the long spinous process you can feel at the base of the neck. It belongs at the top of the column, not the bottom.
The sacral promontory is the anterior ridge of the first sacral vertebra. Choose it if the question asks about a landmark on the front of the sacrum.
The sacrum is the larger triangular bone just above the coccyx, wedged between the hip bones. Pick it if the question asks about five fused vertebrae or the back wall of the pelvis.

questions.q: What is the thick, weight-bearing anterior portion of a vertebra called?
questions.why: The body, also called the centrum, is the thick, drum-shaped part at the front of a vertebra. Stacked bodies carry the weight of the trunk, and intervertebral discs sit between them as cushions. Everything else on a vertebra, the arch and its processes, projects from the back of the body.
notes: The spinous process is the single projection pointing backward from the arch, the bump you feel along your back. It is posterior, not the weight-bearing front.
Correct. The body is the thick anterior portion that bears weight.
The pedicles are the two short bars that connect the arch to the body. Pick them for a question about what joins the arch to the body.
The vertebral arch is the bony ring behind the body that surrounds the spinal cord. Choose it if the question asks what encloses the vertebral foramen from behind.

questions.q: Which single projection points backward from the vertebral arch?
questions.why: The spinous process is the one projection that extends straight back from the vertebral arch in the midline. The row of spinous processes forms the bumps you can feel down the middle of your back. Muscles and ligaments attach to them.
notes: The transverse processes are a pair that point laterally, to the left and right, from the arch. Choose them if the question asks about the side projections.
The pedicles are short bars connecting the arch to the body, not projections that stick out backward. Choose them for a question about what links the arch to the body.
Correct. The spinous process is the single backward-pointing projection.
The articular processes are the superior and inferior pairs that join one vertebra to the next. Pick them for a question about how neighboring vertebrae connect.

questions.q: What is the opening enclosed by the body and arch of a single vertebra called?
questions.why: The vertebral foramen is the large hole in each vertebra, bounded by the body in front and the arch behind. The spinal cord passes through it. The word foramen simply means a hole for something to pass through.
notes: The vertebral canal is the long channel made when many vertebral foramina line up. Choose it if the question describes the whole stacked channel rather than one opening.
Correct. The vertebral foramen is the hole in one vertebra that the spinal cord passes through.
The intervertebral foramen is a gap between two stacked vertebrae, not a hole in a single bone. Pick it if the question asks where spinal nerves exit the column.
The transverse foramen is a small hole in each transverse process of a cervical vertebra. It would be the answer for a question about where the vertebral arteries pass.

questions.q: Which vertebra is the atlas?
questions.why: The atlas is C1, the first cervical vertebra, sitting directly under the skull. It is named after the figure from Greek myth who held up the world, because it holds up the head. It is a ring with no body and no spinous process.
notes: C7 is the vertebra prominens, with the long spinous process at the base of the neck. Pick it for a question about that palpable landmark.
C2 is the axis, the vertebra with the upward peg called the dens. Choose C2 if the question asks about the axis.
Correct. The atlas is C1, the first cervical vertebra.
T1 is the first thoracic vertebra, the first one to carry a pair of ribs. It would be right for a question about where the thoracic region begins.

questions.q: Which vertebra is the axis?
questions.why: The axis is C2, the second cervical vertebra. Its defining feature is the dens, a peg that projects upward into the ring of the atlas. The atlas and skull turn around this peg when you shake your head no, which is why C2 is called the axis.
notes: C5 is an ordinary, typical cervical vertebra with no special name. Students pick it when they guess a middle number rather than recalling that the named vertebrae are C1, C2, and C7.
Correct. The axis is C2, the vertebra that bears the dens.
C7 is the vertebra prominens, with its long spinous process felt at the base of the neck. Pick it for a question about that landmark.
C1 is the atlas, the ring with no body that holds up the skull. Choose C1 if the question asks about the atlas.

questions.q: What is the upward bony peg on the axis called?
questions.why: The dens, also called the odontoid process, is a tooth-like peg that rises from the body of the axis (C2). It fits into the front of the atlas ring and is held there by a ligament. The atlas pivots around the dens when the head turns side to side.
notes: The spinous process points backward from the vertebral arch, not upward. Choose it if the question asks about the midline projection you feel along the back.
Correct. The dens is the upward peg of the axis.
The sacral promontory is a ridge on the front of the first sacral vertebra, far from the neck. It would be right for a question about the anterior edge of the sacrum.
The transverse processes point out to the sides of a vertebra. Pick them for a question about the lateral projections.

questions.q: Which type of cartilage forms an intervertebral disc?
questions.why: Intervertebral discs are made of fibrocartilage, the toughest cartilage, packed with thick collagen fibers. Fibrocartilage resists being squeezed and pulled, which suits a pad that cushions the weight of the trunk between vertebral bodies. The same tissue forms the pubic symphysis and the knee menisci.
notes: Elastic cartilage is the flexible cartilage of the external ear and epiglottis. Pick it for a question about a structure that bends and springs back into shape.
Articular cartilage is hyaline cartilage covering the ends of bones in synovial joints. It would be right for a question about the smooth cap on a joint surface.
Hyaline cartilage is the smooth, glassy cartilage of costal cartilages, the airways, and joint surfaces. Choose it if the question asks what connects the ribs to the sternum.
Correct. The discs are fibrocartilage, built to withstand compression.

questions.q: What is the tough outer ring of an intervertebral disc called?
questions.why: The anulus fibrosus is the tough ring of fibrocartilage that forms the outer part of each disc. Anulus means ring and fibrosus means fibrous. It holds the soft center in place and resists tearing when the disc is loaded.
notes: The vertebral arch is the bony ring behind the vertebral body. Students confuse it with the disc ring because both are described as rings, but the arch is bone that surrounds the spinal cord.
A lamina is one of the two flat bony plates that complete the vertebral arch behind. It is part of the vertebra, not the disc, so pick it only for a question about the arch.
The nucleus pulposus is the soft, gel-like core inside the ring. Choose it if the question asks about the center of the disc.
Correct. The anulus fibrosus is the fibrous outer ring of the disc.

questions.q: What is the soft, gel-like core of an intervertebral disc called?
questions.why: The nucleus pulposus is the soft, gel-like center of each intervertebral disc. Pulposus means pulpy. When the spine is loaded, this core spreads the pressure out evenly, and if the outer ring tears, it is the part that bulges out in a herniated disc.
notes: The dens is the upward peg of the axis (C2). It would be right for a question about the pivot for turning the head.
Correct. The nucleus pulposus is the gel-like core of the disc.
The anulus fibrosus is the tough outer ring that surrounds the core. Pick it if the question asks about the fibrous ring of the disc.
The centrum is another name for the vertebral body, the bone the disc sits between. Choose it for a question about the weight-bearing part of a vertebra.

questions.q: Which part of the sternum is the superior portion that articulates with the clavicles?
questions.why: The sternum has three fused parts, and the manubrium is the top one. It articulates with the clavicles at the sternoclavicular joints and with the first pair of ribs. Its shape is often compared to the handle of a sword, with the body as the blade.
notes: Correct. The manubrium is the superior part and joins the clavicles.
The body is the long middle part of the sternum, where most of the true ribs attach. Choose it if the question asks about the largest, central section.
The jugular notch is a dip at the top of the manubrium, a landmark rather than a separate part. Choose it if the question asks about the notch you can feel at the base of the neck.
The xiphoid process is the small inferior tip of the sternum. Pick it for a question about the bottom of the breastbone.

questions.q: Which two spinal curvatures are primary curvatures, present from birth?
questions.why: A newborn's spine is curved in one long C shape, like its position in the uterus. The thoracic and sacral curvatures keep that original direction, so they are the primary curvatures. The cervical and lumbar curvatures form later as the baby lifts its head and then stands, so they are secondary.
notes: This pair mixes a secondary curve (cervical) with a primary curve (thoracic). It would only fit if both curves had the same origin, which they do not.
This pair mixes the secondary lumbar curve with the primary sacral curve. Students pick it because both are low in the back, but location does not decide primary or secondary.
Correct. The thoracic and sacral curvatures are present at birth.
The cervical and lumbar curvatures are the two secondary curves that develop after birth. Choose this pair if the question asks which curves develop with infant milestones.

questions.q: Which spinal curvature develops as an infant begins to hold up its head?
questions.why: The cervical curvature is a secondary curve that forms in the neck when an infant starts lifting and holding up its head. Holding the head up against gravity bends the neck region the opposite way from the fetal C shape. The other secondary curve, the lumbar, comes later with standing and walking.
notes: Correct. The cervical curvature forms as the infant holds up its head.
The sacral curvature is a primary curve present from birth. It would be right for a question about the original curve in the pelvic region.
The thoracic curvature is a primary curve, present at birth. Choose it if the question asks about a curve the baby is born with in the chest region.
The lumbar curvature is also secondary, but it develops later, when a child begins to stand and walk. Pick it for a question about that milestone.

questions.q: Which spinal curvature is secondary and develops as a child stands and walks?
questions.why: The lumbar curvature forms in the lower back once a child begins standing and walking. Standing upright bends the lumbar spine opposite to the fetal C shape, which makes it a secondary curvature. It balances the trunk over the hips and legs.
notes: The sacral curvature is primary and present at birth. Pick it for a question about the curve in the pelvic region that the baby already has.
Correct. The lumbar curvature develops with standing and walking.
The thoracic curvature is primary and present at birth. Choose it if the question asks about the original curve in the chest region.
The cervical curvature is also secondary, but it develops earlier, when the infant holds up its head. Choose it if the question names that earlier milestone.

questions.q: Which two parts of a vertebra connect the vertebral arch to the body?
questions.why: The pedicles are two short, thick bars that project backward from the vertebral body and form the sides of the arch. Pedicle means little foot, since they are the feet the arch stands on. Notches above and below each pedicle help form the intervertebral foramina where spinal nerves exit.
notes: The transverse processes project to the sides from where the pedicles and laminae meet. Pick them for a question about the lateral projections.
Correct. The pedicles link the arch to the body.
The articular processes are the superior and inferior pairs that join one vertebra to the next. Choose them for a question about connections between neighboring vertebrae.
The laminae are the two flat plates that complete the arch behind, meeting in the midline at the spinous process. Choose them if the question asks what closes the back of the arch.

questions.q: Which two flat plates complete the vertebral arch behind?
questions.why: The laminae are two flat plates of bone that extend from the pedicles toward the midline, where they meet to close the back of the vertebral arch. The spinous process projects from the spot where they join. A laminectomy, removal of the laminae, is a surgery that opens the arch to relieve pressure on the spinal cord.
notes: The pedicles are the short bars that connect the arch to the body at the front of the arch. Choose them if the question asks what links the arch to the body.
The body is the thick weight-bearing part in front of the arch. Choose it for a question about the anterior part of a vertebra.
Correct. The laminae are the flat plates that close the arch behind.
The spinous process is a single projection, not a pair of plates, and it sticks out from where the laminae meet. Pick it for a question about the backward-pointing projection.

questions.q: Through which openings do the spinal nerves exit the vertebral column?
questions.why: The intervertebral foramina are openings on each side between two stacked vertebrae, formed by notches above and below the pedicles. A spinal nerve leaves the vertebral canal through each one. That is why a bulging disc or bone spur near this opening can press on a nerve and send pain down a limb.
notes: Correct. Spinal nerves exit through the intervertebral foramina between vertebrae.
The transverse foramina are small holes in the transverse processes of cervical vertebrae. Pick them for a question about where the vertebral arteries pass.
The sacral hiatus is one opening at the lower end of the sacral canal on the back of the sacrum. It would be right for a question about where the sacral canal ends.
The vertebral foramina are the large central holes that stack to form the vertebral canal, which holds the spinal cord itself. Choose them if the question asks where the cord runs.

questions.q: Which vertebral region has transverse foramina in its transverse processes?
questions.why: Only cervical vertebrae have transverse foramina, small holes through each transverse process. The vertebral arteries travel up through these holes on their way to the brain. Because no other region has them, a transverse foramen is enough by itself to identify a cervical vertebra.
notes: Thoracic vertebrae are identified by costal facets where the ribs articulate, not transverse foramina. Choose the thoracic region if the question names costal facets.
Correct. Transverse foramina are found only in cervical vertebrae.
Lumbar vertebrae have neither transverse foramina nor costal facets. Pick the lumbar region for a question about massive, kidney-shaped bodies built for weight bearing.
The sacrum is a fused bone with sacral foramina that pass the sacral nerves. Students confuse these with transverse foramina, but sacral foramina are a different feature on a different bone.

questions.q: Which vertebral region has costal facets where the ribs articulate?
questions.why: Costal facets are small smooth joint surfaces on thoracic vertebrae, on the bodies and on the transverse processes, where the ribs meet the spine. Costal means rib. Since ribs attach only in the chest, costal facets identify a thoracic vertebra.
notes: The coccyx is the small fused tailbone and does not articulate with ribs. It would be right for a question about the lowest fused segment of the column.
Cervical vertebrae have transverse foramina for the vertebral arteries but no rib joints. Choose the cervical region if the question names transverse foramina or a bifid spinous process.
Correct. Costal facets for the ribs are found on thoracic vertebrae.
Lumbar vertebrae have no costal facets and no transverse foramina. Pick the lumbar region for a question about the largest, kidney-shaped bodies.

questions.q: Which vertebrae are the largest, with thick, kidney-shaped bodies built for weight bearing?
questions.why: The lumbar vertebrae in the lower back are the largest separate vertebrae, with massive, kidney-shaped bodies. They support the weight of the head, arms, and trunk above them, so they need the biggest weight-bearing surfaces. Body size increases steadily from the neck down to the lumbar region.
notes: Correct. Lumbar vertebrae are the largest, with kidney-shaped bodies.
The coccygeal vertebrae are tiny and fused into the tailbone. They would fit a question about the smallest, lowest segments of the column.
Cervical vertebrae are the smallest, with small oval bodies, because they carry only the head. Choose them for a question about the smallest vertebrae or transverse foramina.
Thoracic vertebrae have medium, heart-shaped bodies and costal facets for the ribs. Pick them for a question that names a heart-shaped body.

questions.q: The atlas is unlike a typical vertebra. Which two features does the atlas lack?
options: A body and a spinous process
A vertebral foramen and articular facets
questions.why: The atlas (C1) is a ring of bone made of an anterior arch and a posterior arch, with no body and no true spinous process. The missing body leaves room for the dens of the axis to sit in the front of the ring. Like other cervical vertebrae, the atlas still has transverse processes with transverse foramina.
notes: The atlas does have transverse processes, and each has a transverse foramen like every cervical vertebra. Thoracic and lumbar vertebrae are the ones that lack transverse foramina, though they still have transverse processes.
The anterior and posterior arches are exactly what the atlas is made of. They replace the body and form its ring shape, so the atlas clearly has them.
Correct. The atlas has no body and no spinous process.
The atlas has a large vertebral foramen for the spinal cord and articular facets for the skull and the axis. Students pick this when they assume an unusual vertebra lacks everything.
questions.answerText: A body and a spinous process

questions.q: Which vertebra is the vertebra prominens, with a long spinous process you can feel at the base of the neck?
questions.why: C7 is the last cervical vertebra, and its spinous process is long and not forked, so it sticks out at the base of the neck. Prominens means prominent. Because it is easy to feel, clinicians use it as a starting point for counting vertebrae.
notes: C5 is a typical cervical vertebra with a short, often forked spinous process that is hard to feel. Students pick it when they guess a middle neck vertebra instead of the lowest one.
C2 is the axis, which carries the dens. Pick C2 for a question about the peg the head turns on.
C1 is the atlas, which has no spinous process at all. Choose C1 for a question about the ring that holds up the skull.
Correct. C7 is the vertebra prominens.

questions.q: Which ridge marks where the manubrium meets the body of the sternum?
