questions.why: The sternal angle is a slight horizontal ridge where the manubrium joins the body of the sternum. It lies at the level of the second rib, so it is a reliable landmark you can feel through the skin. Clinicians find it first and then count ribs downward from there.
notes: The xiphoid process is the small tip at the bottom of the sternum. Pick it for a question about the inferior end of the breastbone.
Correct. The sternal angle is the ridge at the manubrium and body junction.
Costal cartilage is the hyaline cartilage that connects a rib toward the sternum. It would be right for a question about what links the ribs to the sternum, not a sternal ridge.
The jugular notch is the central dip at the top of the manubrium, at the base of the neck. Choose it if the question asks about the notch above the sternum.

questions.q: Which rib pairs are the true ribs?
questions.why: The true ribs are pairs 1 through 7, and each one attaches directly to the sternum by its own costal cartilage. They are called true because they have a direct line to the sternum. The ribs below them are false ribs, which do not reach the sternum on their own.
notes: Pairs 8 to 10 are the false ribs that join the costal cartilage of the rib above. They would be the answer for a question about ribs that reach the sternum only indirectly.
Correct. Pairs 1 to 7 attach directly to the sternum.
Pairs 11 and 12 are the floating ribs, with no anterior attachment at all. Pick them for a question about the ribs that end freely in the abdominal wall.
Pairs 8 to 12 are the false ribs, which do not reach the sternum directly. Choose them if the question asks about the false ribs.

questions.q: Which rib pairs are the floating ribs, with no anterior attachment at all?
questions.why: Pairs 11 and 12 are the floating ribs. They attach to the vertebrae in back but end freely in the muscles of the abdominal wall, with no cartilage connection to the sternum. They are counted as a subset of the false ribs, pairs 8 to 12.
notes: Pairs 8 to 10 are false ribs that do have an anterior connection, through the costal cartilage of the rib above. Pick them for a question about indirect attachment.
Pairs 1 and 2 are true ribs at the top of the cage. Students pick them by confusing floating with the shortest or highest ribs, but the floating ribs are the lowest.
Correct. Pairs 11 and 12 have no anterior attachment.
Pairs 1 to 7 are the true ribs, which attach directly to the sternum. Choose them if the question asks about direct sternal attachment.

questions.q: What is the small inferior tip of the sternum called?
questions.why: The xiphoid process is the small, pointed tip at the bottom of the sternum. It starts out as cartilage and slowly turns to bone with age. Several abdominal muscles attach to it, and its name comes from the Greek word for sword.
notes: The jugular notch is the dip at the top of the manubrium, at the base of the neck. It would be right for a question about the notch at the superior edge of the sternum.
The sternal angle is the ridge where the manubrium meets the body, level with the second rib. Pick it for a question about the landmark used to count ribs.
The manubrium is the superior part of the sternum, the part that meets the clavicles. Choose it if the question asks about the top of the breastbone.
Correct. The xiphoid process is the inferior tip of the sternum.

questions.q: Which part of a rib is the posterior end that articulates with the vertebral bodies?
questions.why: The head is the posterior end of a rib, and it fits against the bodies of the thoracic vertebrae at the costal facets. Just beyond the head is a short neck, and then the tubercle, which meets the transverse process. Together these two joints anchor each rib to the spine.
notes: The neck is the short narrow section between the head and the tubercle. It does not form a joint itself, so pick it only for a question about the segment that connects those two parts.
Costal cartilage is the hyaline cartilage at the anterior end of a rib that connects it toward the sternum. Choose it for a question about the front end of the rib.
Correct. The head is the posterior end that meets the vertebral bodies.

The tubercle is the knob just past the neck of the rib, and it articulates with the transverse process of a vertebra, not the body. Choose it if the question asks about the rib's joint with the transverse process.

questions.q: The tubercle of a rib articulates with which part of a thoracic vertebra?
questions.why: Each rib makes two joints with the spine. The head of the rib meets the vertebral bodies, and the tubercle, a knob a little farther along the rib, meets the transverse process. The transverse processes of thoracic vertebrae carry costal facets for this purpose.
notes: The spinous process points backward in the midline and does not form a joint with any rib. Students pick it because it is the most familiar bump of a vertebra, but ribs attach to the sides.
Correct. The rib tubercle articulates with a transverse process.
The vertebral body receives the head of the rib, not the tubercle. Choose the body if the question asks where the rib head articulates.
The pedicles connect the arch to the body and do not carry a facet for the rib. Pick a pedicle for a question about what links the arch to the body.

questions.q: In lab, a student picks up a loose vertebra with a small oval body, a short forked spinous process, and a hole in each transverse process. Which region is it from?
questions.why: Each clue points to the neck. Cervical vertebrae are the smallest, with small oval bodies, and their spinous processes are short and often bifid, meaning forked. Most decisive of all, only cervical vertebrae have transverse foramina, the holes in the transverse processes that pass the vertebral arteries.
notes: Correct. A forked spinous process and transverse foramina identify a cervical vertebra.
Lumbar vertebrae have thick, kidney-shaped bodies and short, blunt spinous processes, with no transverse foramina. Pick the lumbar region for the largest, heaviest vertebra.
The sacrum is a single triangular bone of fused vertebrae, so a loose single vertebra cannot come from it. Choose the sacral region for a question about the fused bone between the hip bones.
Thoracic vertebrae have heart-shaped bodies, long downward-angled spinous processes, and costal facets for ribs. Choose the thoracic region if the vertebra shows rib facets.

questions.q: A vertebra has a heart-shaped body, a long spinous process angled sharply downward, and smooth facets on its body for ribs. Which region is it from?
questions.why: These features describe a thoracic vertebra. The bodies are heart-shaped, the spinous processes are long and point steeply downward, overlapping like shingles, and the costal facets on the body and transverse processes are where the ribs articulate. The rib facets alone are enough to place it in the thoracic region.
notes: Lumbar vertebrae have massive, kidney-shaped bodies and short, blunt spinous processes, with no rib facets. Pick the lumbar region for the largest vertebra in the column.
Correct. Costal facets and a heart-shaped body identify a thoracic vertebra.
Cervical vertebrae have small oval bodies, short forked spinous processes, and transverse foramina. Choose the cervical region if the vertebra has holes in its transverse processes.
The coccyx is a small fused tailbone with no rib facets and no long spinous processes. It fits a question about the lowest fused segment of the column.

questions.q: A vertebra has a thick, kidney-shaped body and a short, blunt spinous process, with no rib facets and no transverse foramina. Which region is it from?
questions.why: A lumbar vertebra is identified as much by what it lacks as by what it has. It has the largest, kidney-shaped body for bearing weight and a short, blunt spinous process, but no costal facets (so it is not thoracic) and no transverse foramina (so it is not cervical). That combination leaves only the lumbar region.
notes: The sacrum is a single fused bone, not a separate vertebra with its own spinous process. It would be right for a question about the fused bone between the hip bones.
Thoracic vertebrae have costal facets for the ribs and heart-shaped bodies. Pick the thoracic region if rib facets are present.
Cervical vertebrae always have transverse foramina, so a vertebra without them cannot be cervical. Choose the cervical region when you see those holes in the transverse processes.
Correct. A massive kidney-shaped body without rib facets or transverse foramina is lumbar.

questions.q: A clinician runs a finger down the back of a patient's neck and feels one spinous process sticking out more than the others at the base of the neck. Which vertebra is it?
questions.why: C7, the vertebra prominens, has a long spinous process that is not forked, so it projects clearly at the base of the neck. Most other cervical spinous processes are short and lie deep under the neck muscles. Clinicians use C7 as a starting landmark for counting vertebrae down the back.
notes: Correct. The prominent spinous process at the base of the neck belongs to C7.
The axis, C2, does have a spinous process, but it sits high in the neck just below the skull. Pick C2 for a question about the vertebra bearing the dens.
The atlas, C1, has no spinous process at all, so it cannot be felt as a projecting bump. Choose it for a question about the ring that holds up the skull.

C5 is a typical cervical vertebra in the middle of the neck with a short, often forked spinous process that is hard to feel. Students pick it when they guess a mid-neck vertebra instead of the lowest one.

questions.q: Before listening to a patient's heart, a nurse feels for a bony ridge on the sternum level with the second rib, then counts ribs down from it. Which landmark is the nurse using?
questions.why: The sternal angle is the ridge where the manubrium meets the body of the sternum, and it sits at the level of the second rib. Because the first rib is hidden behind the clavicle, the sternal angle is the most reliable starting point for counting ribs and the spaces between them.
notes: The xiphoid process is the small tip at the bottom of the sternum, far below the second rib. Pick it for a question about the inferior end of the sternum.

The costal margin is the lower edge of the rib cage, formed by the joined costal cartilages of the lower ribs. It would fit a question about the lower border of the thoracic cage, not a ridge level with rib 2.
Correct. The sternal angle marks the second rib and starts the rib count.
The jugular notch is the dip at the top of the manubrium, above the level of the first rib. Choose it if the question asks about the notch at the base of the neck.

questions.q: On the lateral side of the sacrum, a student finds an ear-shaped surface that joins the hip bone. What is this surface called?
questions.why: The auricular surface is the ear-shaped joint surface on each side of the sacrum. Auricular means ear-like. It meets a matching surface on the ilium of the hip bone to form the sacroiliac joint, which carries body weight from the spine into the pelvis.
notes: The median sacral crest is the ridge of fused spinous processes along the posterior midline. Pick it for a question about the bumpy ridge down the back of the sacrum.
Correct. The auricular surface joins the hip bone at the sacroiliac joint.
The sacral hiatus is the opening at the lower end of the sacral canal. It would be right for a question about where the sacral canal ends.
The sacral promontory is the anterior ridge of the first sacral vertebra, at the top front of the sacrum. Choose it for a question about the front edge of the sacrum.

questions.q: On the posterior surface of the sacrum, a ridge runs down the midline. It formed from fused spinous processes. Which marking is it?
questions.why: The median sacral crest is a bumpy ridge running down the middle of the back of the sacrum. Each bump is what remains of the spinous process of one of the five sacral vertebrae, now fused together. Median means in the midline, and crest means a ridge.
notes: The sacral promontory is a ridge on the front of the first sacral vertebra, not the back. Choose it for a question about the anterior edge of the sacrum.
The auricular surface is the ear-shaped joint surface on the side of the sacrum. Pick it for a question about where the sacrum meets the hip bone.
Correct. The median sacral crest is the ridge of fused spinous processes.
The sacral canal is the channel running through the sacrum, the continuation of the vertebral canal. It is a passage inside the bone, not a ridge on its surface.

questions.q: Which list gives the five regions of the vertebral column in order from superior to inferior?
questions.why: Moving down the body, the column begins in the neck (cervical), continues through the chest where the ribs attach (thoracic), then the lower back (lumbar). Below the lumbar region come the two fused bones, the sacrum between the hip bones and finally the coccyx, the tailbone. Matching each region to a body area makes the order easy to rebuild.
notes: This order starts with the thoracic region, but the neck vertebrae sit above the chest. The cervical region is always first, directly under the skull.
This order swaps the thoracic and lumbar regions. The thoracic region is in the chest, above the lower back, so it must come before the lumbar region.
This order puts the coccyx above the sacrum. The coccyx is the tailbone at the very bottom, so it always comes last.
Correct. Cervical, thoracic, lumbar, sacrum, and coccyx is the superior to inferior order.

questions.q: Which list gives the four spinal curvatures from superior to inferior with the correct type for each?
questions.why: The curves alternate down the spine. The cervical curve is secondary (formed when the infant holds up its head), the thoracic is primary (present at birth), the lumbar is secondary (formed with standing and walking), and the sacral is primary. The two primary curves are the ones that keep the original fetal C shape.
notes: This list has the types right but places the lumbar curve above the thoracic. The lower back lies below the chest, so the thoracic curve comes second.
This list has the order right but reverses every type. The thoracic and sacral curves are the primary ones present at birth, not the cervical and lumbar.
Correct. The curves run cervical, thoracic, lumbar, sacral, alternating secondary and primary.
This list has the types right but puts the thoracic curve above the cervical. The neck is above the chest, so the cervical curve comes first.

questions.q: A probe passes from the front of a vertebra straight back to the tip of its spinous process, staying on one side of the vertebral foramen. Which list gives the parts it crosses in order?
options: The spinous process, the lamina, the pedicle, then the body
The body, the pedicle, the lamina, then the spinous process
The body, the lamina, the pedicle, then the spinous process
The pedicle, the body, the spinous process, then the lamina
questions.why: The body is in front. The pedicles project backward from the body to form the sides of the arch, and the laminae continue from the pedicles toward the midline to close the arch behind. The spinous process projects backward from the point where the two laminae meet, so it is the last part reached.
notes: This is the correct sequence run backward, from the spinous process to the body. It would be right only if the probe started at the back and moved forward.
Correct. Body, pedicle, lamina, and spinous process is the front to back path.
This order swaps the pedicle and lamina. The pedicle attaches directly to the body, so it must come before the lamina.
This order starts at the pedicle and ends at the lamina. The body is the front of the vertebra, and the spinous process is at the very back, so neither can be in the middle.
questions.answerText: The body, the pedicle, the lamina, then the spinous process

questions.q: Which set correctly names the joint used to nod yes, the peg the atlas pivots around to shake no, and the vertebra that carries that peg?
options: The atlanto-occipital joint, the dens, and the atlas
The atlanto-occipital joint, the spinous process, and the axis
The atlanto-axial joint, the dens, and the axis
The atlanto-occipital joint, the dens, and the axis
questions.why: Nodding yes happens at the atlanto-occipital joint, where the atlas meets the occipital condyles of the skull. Shaking the head no happens when the atlas, carrying the skull, rotates around the dens. The dens is the upward peg of the axis, C2, not of the atlas.
notes: This set gives the dens to the atlas. The atlas is a ring with no body or peg, and it is the axis that carries the dens.
The spinous process points backward from the arch and is not a pivot. Students pick it when they forget the special name of the upward peg on the axis.
The atlanto-axial joint is where the atlas pivots on the dens, the joint for shaking no. It would be the answer for the no motion, but the question asks for the joint used to nod yes.
Correct. The yes nod is at the atlanto-occipital joint, and the atlas turns on the dens of the axis.
questions.answerText: The atlanto-occipital joint, the dens, and the axis

questions.q: A patient has pain shooting down one leg from a herniated lumbar disc. Which description correctly traces how the disc presses on a spinal nerve?
options: The nucleus pulposus pushes through the anulus fibrosus and presses a nerve at an intervertebral foramen
The nucleus pulposus pushes through the anulus fibrosus and presses a nerve at a transverse foramen
The anulus fibrosus pushes through the nucleus pulposus and presses a nerve at an intervertebral foramen
The nucleus pulposus pushes through a lamina and presses a nerve at an intervertebral foramen
questions.why: In a herniated disc, the tough outer ring (anulus fibrosus) tears and the soft gel core (nucleus pulposus) bulges out through the tear. The bulge often presses on a spinal nerve where it leaves the column through an intervertebral foramen. Because that nerve serves the leg, the pain travels down the limb.
notes: Correct. The core pushes through the torn ring and presses a nerve at an intervertebral foramen.

Transverse foramina are holes in cervical transverse processes that carry the vertebral arteries, not exits for spinal nerves, and lumbar vertebrae do not have them. Choose transverse foramen only for a question about the vertebral arteries.
This reverses the two parts of the disc. The anulus is the outer ring and stays in place, while the soft core is what escapes through it.
A lamina is a bony plate of the vertebral arch, not part of the disc, so the core does not push through it. Pick the lamina for a question about what closes the arch behind.
questions.answerText: The nucleus pulposus pushes through the anulus fibrosus and presses a nerve at an intervertebral foramen

questions.q: Which statement correctly describes the bones that form the walls of the thoracic cage?
options: The clavicles in front, the ribs on the sides, and the thoracic vertebrae behind
The ribs in front, the sternum on the sides, and the thoracic vertebrae behind
The sternum in front, the ribs on the sides, and the thoracic vertebrae behind
The sternum in front, the thoracic vertebrae on the sides, and the ribs behind
questions.why: The thoracic cage is a bony basket that shields the heart and lungs. The sternum forms the front wall in the midline, the twelve pairs of ribs curve around to form the sides, and the twelve thoracic vertebrae form the back wall where the ribs attach. All three are part of the axial skeleton.
notes: The clavicles belong to the pectoral girdle, which attaches the arm to the trunk. They sit on top of the cage but are not part of its walls, so choose them only for a question about the shoulder girdle.
This swaps the sternum and the ribs. The sternum is a single midline bone in front, so it cannot form the sides.
Correct. Sternum in front, ribs at the sides, and thoracic vertebrae behind.
This swaps the vertebrae and the ribs. The vertebral column runs down the back midline, and the ribs are what wrap around the sides.
questions.answerText: The sternum in front, the ribs on the sides, and the thoracic vertebrae behind

questions.q: Which statement correctly classifies the ribs by how they attach to the sternum?
options: True ribs (1 to 10) attach directly, false ribs (11 and 12) do not, and floating ribs are true ribs
True ribs (1 to 7) attach directly, false ribs (8 to 10) do not, and floating ribs are a third group
True ribs (8 to 12) attach directly, false ribs (1 to 7) do not, and floating ribs are true ribs
True ribs (1 to 7) attach directly, false ribs (8 to 12) do not, and floating ribs are false ribs
questions.why: True ribs, pairs 1 to 7, each reach the sternum by their own costal cartilage. False ribs, pairs 8 to 12, do not reach it directly: pairs 8 to 10 join the cartilage of the rib above, and pairs 11 and 12 have no front attachment at all. Those last two are the floating ribs, which are counted as part of the false ribs.
notes: Pairs 8 to 10 do not reach the sternum on their own, because each joins the costal cartilage of the rib above. Students choose this when they count any rib with cartilage toward the front as a true rib.
This leaves pairs 11 and 12 out of the false ribs. The false ribs are 8 to 12, so the floating ribs are a subset of them rather than a separate group.
This flips the numbering. The upper ribs, 1 to 7, are the ones with a direct attachment, and the lower ribs are false.
Correct. True ribs are 1 to 7, false ribs are 8 to 12, and the floating ribs belong to the false group.
questions.answerText: True ribs (1 to 7) attach directly, false ribs (8 to 12) do not, and floating ribs are false ribs

questions.q: Which set correctly names the channel through the movable vertebrae, its continuation through the sacrum, and the opening at the lower end of that sacral channel?
options: The vertebral canal, the sacral canal, and the sacral promontory
The sacral canal, the vertebral canal, and the sacral hiatus
The vertebral canal, the sacral hiatus, and the sacral foramina
The vertebral canal, the sacral canal, and the sacral hiatus
questions.why: The stacked vertebral foramina of the cervical, thoracic, and lumbar vertebrae form the vertebral canal. Inside the sacrum the same channel continues as the sacral canal. It ends at the sacral hiatus, an opening on the lower back of the sacrum where the laminae of the last sacral segment failed to meet in the midline.
notes: The sacral promontory is a ridge on the front of the first sacral vertebra, not an opening. Choose it for a question about the anterior edge of the sacrum.
This swaps the first two names. The vertebral canal runs through the movable vertebrae above, and the sacral canal is its lower continuation.
The sacral foramina are the paired openings that let sacral nerves out of the sacrum, not the opening at the end of the canal. Pick them for a question about where the sacral nerves exit.
Correct. Vertebral canal, sacral canal, then sacral hiatus.
questions.answerText: The vertebral canal, the sacral canal, and the sacral hiatus

questions.q: Which structure is the anterior ridge of the first sacral vertebra?
questions.why: The sacral promontory is the forward-bulging upper edge of the body of the first sacral vertebra. A promontory is a point of land that juts out, and this ridge juts into the pelvis. It marks part of the boundary between the upper (false) pelvis and the lower (true) pelvis.
notes: The auricular surface is the ear-shaped joint surface on the side of the sacrum. It would be right for a question about where the sacrum meets the hip bone.
The median sacral crest is the ridge of fused spinous processes on the posterior surface. Pick it for a question about the midline ridge on the back of the sacrum.
The sacral hiatus is the opening at the inferior end of the sacral canal on the back of the sacrum. Choose it for a question about where the sacral canal ends.
Correct. The sacral promontory is the anterior ridge of S1.

questions.q: Which joint, between the atlas and the occipital condyles of the skull, lets you nod your head yes?
questions.why: The atlanto-occipital joint is where the superior surfaces of the atlas cradle the occipital condyles, the two rounded knobs on the base of the skull. The name combines its two parts, atlas and occipital bone. Rocking the skull forward and back on the atlas produces the yes nod.
notes: The temporomandibular joint is the jaw joint between the mandible and the temporal bone. It would be right for a question about opening and closing the mouth.
Correct. The atlanto-occipital joint produces the yes nod.
The atlanto-axial joint is between the atlas and the axis, where the atlas pivots on the dens. Choose it if the question asks about shaking the head no.
The sacroiliac joint is where the sacrum meets the hip bone in the pelvis. Pick it for a question about the auricular surface of the sacrum.

questions.q: How many bones make up the adult vertebral column?
questions.why: The adult column has 24 separate vertebrae (7 cervical, 12 thoracic, 5 lumbar) plus two fused bones, the sacrum and the coccyx. Each fused bone counts as one, giving 26 bones in total. Early in development there are 33 vertebrae, but the sacral and coccygeal ones fuse.
notes: 12 is the number of thoracic vertebrae or of rib pairs. Students pick it by recalling one region's count instead of the whole column.
24 is only the separate vertebrae of the three movable regions. It would be right if the question excluded the sacrum and coccyx.
Correct. 24 separate vertebrae plus the sacrum and coccyx make 26 bones.
33 is the number of vertebrae early in development, before the sacral and coccygeal vertebrae fuse. Choose it for a question about the developing column.

questions.q: Which region of the vertebral column contains seven vertebrae?
questions.why: The cervical region, in the neck, contains seven vertebrae, C1 through C7. This includes the specialized atlas (C1), axis (C2), and vertebra prominens (C7). Remembering 7 for the neck, 12 for the chest, and 5 for the lower back covers all three movable regions.
notes: The thoracic region has twelve vertebrae, one for each pair of ribs. Choose it if the question asks about twelve vertebrae.
Correct. The cervical region has seven vertebrae.
The sacrum is a single bone made of five fused vertebrae. It would be right for a question about five vertebrae fused into one bone.
The lumbar region has five vertebrae in the lower back. Pick it for a question about five separate, weight-bearing vertebrae.

questions.q: Which region of the vertebral column contains twelve vertebrae?
questions.why: The thoracic region contains twelve vertebrae, T1 through T12, in the chest. There are also twelve pairs of ribs, and each thoracic vertebra articulates with a pair. Linking the number of thoracic vertebrae to the number of rib pairs makes both easy to remember.
notes: The cervical region has seven vertebrae in the neck. Choose it for a question about seven vertebrae.
The coccyx is a small fused tailbone, usually of four tiny vertebrae. It would be right for a question about the lowest fused bone of the column.
The lumbar region has five vertebrae in the lower back. Pick it for a question about five separate vertebrae.
Correct. The thoracic region has twelve vertebrae.

questions.q: What makes a spinal curvature a primary curvature?
options: It develops as a child stands and walks
It is an exaggerated, abnormal curve
It develops as an infant holds up its head
questions.why: Primary curvatures are the ones a baby is born with, left over from the curled C shape of the fetus. In the adult these are the thoracic and sacral curvatures. Curvatures that appear later with infant milestones are called secondary.
notes: Correct. A primary curvature is present at birth.
Developing with standing and walking describes the lumbar curvature, which is secondary. Pick this for a question about how the lower back curve forms.
An exaggerated curve is a disorder such as kyphosis or lordosis, not a normal primary curve. Choose this for a question about abnormal curvatures.
Developing as the infant holds up its head describes the cervical curvature, which is secondary. Choose this for a question about how the neck curve forms.

questions.q: What is another name for the body of a vertebra?
questions.why: The body of a vertebra is also called the centrum, because it forms the central, weight-bearing core of each vertebra. The bodies stack into a column separated by intervertebral discs. Both names appear in lab and on exams, so it helps to know they mean the same part.
notes: Correct. The centrum is another name for the vertebral body.
A lamina is one of the two flat plates that close the vertebral arch behind. Choose it for a question about the back of the arch.
A pedicle is one of the two short bars connecting the arch to the body. Pick it for a question about what links the arch to the body.
The dens is the upward peg of the axis, sometimes called the odontoid process. Students mix up these alternate names, but the dens is a peg on C2, not the body of every vertebra.

questions.q: When the vertebral foramina of many vertebrae line up, what channel do they form?
questions.why: Each vertebra has a vertebral foramen, and when the vertebrae are stacked those holes line up into one long bony tunnel called the vertebral canal. The spinal cord runs inside it, protected on all sides by bone. A single opening is a foramen, and the whole stacked channel is the canal.
notes: Correct. Stacked vertebral foramina form the vertebral canal.
The carpal tunnel is a passage at the wrist under the flexor retinaculum. It would be right for a question about where flexor tendons and the median nerve enter the hand.
The central canal is the tiny fluid-filled channel inside the spinal cord itself, not a bony tunnel. Pick it for a question about the canal in the middle of the cord's gray matter.
The sacral canal is the lower continuation of the vertebral canal inside the fused sacrum. Choose it if the question asks about the channel through the sacrum specifically.

questions.q: What is the first cervical vertebra called?
questions.why: The first cervical vertebra, C1, is the atlas. It sits directly under the skull and holds up the head, like the figure from myth who held up the world. It is a ring with no body and no spinous process.
notes: The dens is a peg on the axis, not a whole vertebra. It would be right for a question about the pivot the atlas turns around.
The vertebra prominens is C7, the last cervical vertebra, with the long spinous process at the base of the neck. Pick it for a question about C7.
The axis is C2, the second cervical vertebra, which carries the dens. Choose it if the question asks about the second cervical vertebra.
Correct. C1 is the atlas.

questions.q: What is the second cervical vertebra called?
questions.why: The second cervical vertebra, C2, is the axis. It is named for its dens, an upward peg that acts as the axis of rotation when the atlas and skull turn side to side. That rotation is the motion of shaking your head no.
notes: The atlas is C1, the ring directly under the skull. Choose it if the question asks about the first cervical vertebra.
The vertebra prominens is C7, with the long spinous process felt at the base of the neck. Pick it for a question about the seventh cervical vertebra.
Correct. C2 is the axis.
The sacrum is the fused triangular bone between the hip bones, not a cervical vertebra. It would be right for a question about five fused vertebrae.

questions.q: The sternum is made of how many fused parts?
questions.why: The sternum, or breastbone, is a flat bone made of three parts fused together. From top to bottom they are the manubrium, the body, and the xiphoid process. The sternal angle marks the junction between the first two parts.
notes: Five is the number of fused vertebrae in the sacrum, not the number of sternal parts. Students pick it when they mix up the sternum with the sacrum, another bone built from fused parts.
Four is too many. Students may count a landmark such as the jugular notch or sternal angle as a separate part, but those are features, not parts.
Correct. The manubrium, body, and xiphoid process make three parts.
Two would leave out one of the parts. Students choose it when they think of the manubrium and body but forget the small xiphoid process at the bottom.

questions.q: How many pairs of ribs does the thoracic cage have?
questions.why: There are twelve pairs of ribs, twenty-four ribs in all, matching the twelve thoracic vertebrae they attach to in back. They are grouped by how they reach the sternum in front: seven pairs of true ribs and five pairs of false ribs, two of which are floating ribs.
notes: Ten counts the ribs that have any anterior cartilage connection, pairs 1 to 10. Students pick it by forgetting the two floating pairs below.
Correct. There are twelve pairs of ribs.
Seven is the number of true rib pairs, the ones that attach directly to the sternum. Choose it for a question about the true ribs only.
Five is the number of false rib pairs, pairs 8 to 12. It would be right for a question about how many pairs are false ribs.

questions.q: Which rib pairs are classified as false ribs?
questions.why: False ribs are pairs 8 through 12, the ribs that do not reach the sternum by their own costal cartilage. Pairs 8 to 10 connect indirectly by joining the cartilage of the rib above, and pairs 11 and 12 have no front attachment at all. So every rib below the seventh pair is a false rib.
notes: Pairs 1 to 7 are the true ribs, which each attach directly to the sternum. Choose them for a question about direct sternal attachment.
Pairs 11 and 12 are the floating ribs, which are only part of the false rib group. Pick them for a question about ribs with no anterior attachment at all.
Pairs 1 to 10 mixes the seven true ribs with three false ribs. Students choose it when they count every rib with a cartilage link to the front as the same group.
Correct. Pairs 8 to 12 are the false ribs.

questions.q: How do rib pairs 8, 9, and 10 connect to the front of the thoracic cage?
options: Each joins the costal cartilage of the rib above
Each attaches to the xiphoid process by a ligament
Each attaches directly to the sternum by its own cartilage
Each ends freely in the abdominal wall
questions.why: Ribs 8 to 10 are false ribs that reach the sternum only indirectly. The costal cartilage of each one merges with the cartilage of the rib above it, and that shared cartilage eventually reaches the sternum through rib 7. Together these joined cartilages form the lower edge of the rib cage, the costal margin.
notes: Correct. Ribs 8 to 10 join the costal cartilage of the rib above.
The xiphoid process is the small tip of the sternum and serves as a muscle attachment, not the anchor for ribs 8 to 10. Students pick it because those ribs sit near the bottom of the sternum.
Attaching directly by its own cartilage describes the true ribs, pairs 1 to 7. Choose this for a question about the true ribs.
Ending freely in the abdominal wall describes the floating ribs, pairs 11 and 12. Pick this for a question about the floating ribs.
questions.answerText: Each joins the costal cartilage of the rib above

questions.q: What is the central dip at the top of the manubrium, easily felt at the base of the neck, called?
questions.why: The jugular notch is the shallow dip in the middle of the superior border of the manubrium, between the two clavicles. You can feel it at the base of the front of the neck. It is also called the suprasternal notch and is a common surface landmark.
notes: The xiphoid process is the small tip at the bottom of the sternum. Pick it for a question about the inferior end of the breastbone.
Costal notches are the small notches along the sides of the sternum where the costal cartilages of the ribs attach. Choose them for a question about where ribs meet the sternum.
Correct. The jugular notch is the dip at the top of the manubrium.
The sternal angle is the ridge where the manubrium meets the body of the sternum, lower down at the level of the second rib. Choose it for a question about the landmark used to count ribs.

questions.q: A vertebra has a short spinous process that splits into two tips (a bifid spinous process). Which region does it most likely come from?
questions.why: A bifid, or forked, spinous process is typical of cervical vertebrae, especially C2 through C6. Thoracic and lumbar spinous processes end in a single tip. A forked spinous process and transverse foramina are the two quick features that identify a vertebra from the neck.
notes: Lumbar spinous processes are short, blunt, and point straight back as a single tip. Pick the lumbar region for a vertebra with a massive kidney-shaped body.
The sacrum is a fused bone whose spinous processes merge into the median sacral crest. It would be right for a question about that ridge on the back of the sacrum.
Correct. A forked spinous process points to the cervical region.
Thoracic spinous processes are long, single, and angled sharply downward. Choose the thoracic region for a vertebra with a long, downward-pointing spinous process or costal facets.

questions.q: A vertebra has a heart-shaped body. Which region does it come from?
questions.why: Thoracic vertebrae have medium-sized bodies shaped like a heart when viewed from above. Body shape changes along the column: small and oval in the neck, heart-shaped in the chest, and large and kidney-shaped in the lower back. Thoracic vertebrae also carry costal facets for the ribs, which confirms the region.
notes: Correct. A heart-shaped body identifies a thoracic vertebra.
Lumbar vertebrae have thick, kidney-shaped bodies, the largest in the column. Pick the lumbar region for a massive weight-bearing body.
The coccygeal vertebrae are tiny fused remnants without a distinct heart-shaped body. They would fit a question about the tailbone.
Cervical vertebrae have small, oval bodies, the smallest in the column. Choose the cervical region for a small oval body or transverse foramina.

questions.q: A vertebra has a short, blunt spinous process that points straight back instead of angling downward. Which region does it come from?
questions.why: Lumbar vertebrae have short, thick, blunt spinous processes that project straight backward, often compared to a hatchet blade. This contrasts with the long, downward-angled thoracic spinous processes and the short, forked cervical ones. The straight-back direction leaves gaps between lumbar spinous processes, which is why a needle can be placed there for a lumbar puncture.
notes: Thoracic spinous processes are long and angled sharply downward, overlapping the vertebra below. Pick the thoracic region for that shingled pattern.
The sacrum has no separate spinous processes; they are fused into the median sacral crest. It would fit a question about that fused ridge.
Correct. A short, blunt spinous process pointing straight back identifies a lumbar vertebra.
Cervical spinous processes are short but usually forked at the tip, not blunt and broad. Choose the cervical region for a bifid spinous process.

questions.q: The atlanto-occipital joint allows the head to nod yes. Which two structures meet at this joint?
options: The axis and the occipital condyles
The atlas and the occipital condyles
questions.why: The name of the joint tells you its parts: atlanto refers to the atlas (C1) and occipital refers to the occipital bone of the skull. The rounded occipital condyles on the base of the skull rest in the superior facets of the atlas. Rocking the condyles forward and back on the atlas produces the yes nod.
notes: The axis is C2 and does not touch the skull. Students pick it by mixing up the two named cervical vertebrae, but the atlas is the one directly under the skull.
Correct. The atlas meets the occipital condyles.
The axis and atlas together form the atlanto-axial joint, not the atlanto-occipital joint. Pick this pair for a question about the rotation joint between C1 and C2.
The atlas and the dens meet at the atlanto-axial joint, which turns the head side to side. Choose this pair for a question about shaking the head no.
questions.answerText: The atlas and the occipital condyles

questions.q: The sternal angle sits level with which rib?
questions.why: The costal cartilage of the second rib attaches at the sternal angle, the ridge where the manubrium meets the body of the sternum. Because the sternal angle is easy to feel and the first rib is hard to reach under the clavicle, clinicians start counting ribs at the second rib beside the angle.
notes: Correct. The sternal angle is level with the second rib.
The fourth rib attaches lower on the body of the sternum. Students pick a middle rib when they picture the angle near the middle of the sternum, but it sits near the top.

The first rib attaches to the manubrium, above the sternal angle, and is mostly hidden behind the clavicle. Choose it for a question about the rib that articulates with the manubrium below the clavicle.
The seventh rib is the last true rib, attaching near the bottom of the sternal body by the xiphoid process. Pick it for a question about the lowest true rib.

questions.q: In cervical vertebrae, which structures travel through the transverse foramina?
questions.why: The transverse foramina are small holes in the transverse processes of cervical vertebrae. Stacked one above another, they form a protected bony channel for the vertebral arteries as they climb the neck to supply the brain. This is why transverse foramina are found only in the cervical region.
notes: The spinal cord runs through the large central vertebral foramen of each vertebra. Pick the spinal cord for a question about the vertebral foramen or vertebral canal.
Spinal nerves leave the column through the intervertebral foramina between vertebrae, not through the transverse processes. Choose spinal nerves for a question about the intervertebral foramina.
The sacral nerves exit through the sacral foramina of the sacrum, far below the neck. It would be right for a question about the openings in the sacrum.
Correct. The vertebral arteries pass through the transverse foramina.

questions.q: Which two bones meet at the sacroiliac joint?
options: The sacrum and the fifth lumbar vertebra
The sacrum and the ilium of the hip bone
questions.why: The sacroiliac joint is named for its two bones, the sacrum and the ilium, the upper wing of the hip bone. The auricular surface on each side of the sacrum meets a matching auricular surface on the ilium. This joint transfers the weight of the upper body from the spine into the pelvis.
notes: The sacrum meets L5 at the lumbosacral joint at the top of the sacrum. Pick this pair for a question about where the lumbar spine joins the sacrum.
The femur meets the hip bone at the hip joint, in the acetabulum, not at the ilium's joint with the spine. This pair fits a question about the hip joint.
Correct. The sacroiliac joint joins the sacrum and the ilium.
The sacrum and coccyx meet at the sacrococcygeal joint at the bottom of the sacrum. Choose this pair for a question about where the tailbone attaches.
questions.answerText: The sacrum and the ilium of the hip bone

questions.q: The seventh cervical vertebra is called the vertebra prominens. What feature earns it that name?
options: Its long spinous process felt at the base of the neck
Its ring shape with no body
Its upward peg that the atlas turns around
questions.why: Prominens means prominent. C7 has a long spinous process that is not forked, and it sticks out under the skin at the base of the back of the neck. Because it is easy to find, it serves as a landmark for counting vertebrae.
notes: Correct. C7 is named for its prominent, palpable spinous process.
A large, kidney-shaped body belongs to lumbar vertebrae, which carry the most weight. Choose this feature for a question about the lumbar region.
A ring with no body describes the atlas, C1. It would be right for a question about the vertebra that holds up the skull.
The upward peg is the dens of the axis, C2. Pick this feature for a question about the axis.
questions.answerText: Its long spinous process felt at the base of the neck

questions.q: What is the fibrocartilage pad between two adjacent vertebral bodies called?
questions.why: An intervertebral disc is a pad of fibrocartilage that sits between the bodies of two neighboring vertebrae. Each disc has a tough outer ring (anulus fibrosus) and a soft gel core (nucleus pulposus). The discs absorb shock and allow small movements between vertebrae.
notes: Correct. The intervertebral disc is the fibrocartilage pad between vertebral bodies.
The articular processes are bony projections that join one vertebra to the next at small joints behind the bodies. Choose them for a question about the bony connections between vertebral arches.
The vertebral arch is the bony ring behind the body that surrounds the spinal cord. Pick it for a question about what encloses the vertebral foramen.
Costal cartilage is hyaline cartilage that connects the ribs toward the sternum. It would be right for a question about the cartilage at the front of the rib cage.

questions.q: Which paired processes of a vertebra join it to the vertebrae directly above and below?
options: The superior and inferior articular processes
questions.why: Each vertebra has a pair of superior articular processes that point up and a pair of inferior articular processes that point down. The inferior processes of one vertebra meet the superior processes of the vertebra below at small joints. These joints guide and limit how the spine bends and twists.
notes: The transverse processes point out to the sides and serve as muscle attachments, and in the thorax they meet the ribs. Choose them for a question about the lateral projections.
Correct. The articular processes link one vertebra to the next.

Each vertebra has a single spinous process pointing back, and it does not form a joint with the next vertebra. Students pick it because spinous processes line up down the back, but they only anchor muscles and ligaments.
The pedicles connect the arch to the body of the same vertebra, not to neighboring vertebrae. Pick them for a question about what joins the arch to the body.
questions.answerText: The superior and inferior articular processes

questions.q: A patient has pain that travels down one leg after the soft core of a lumbar disc pushes through its torn outer ring. What is this condition called?
questions.why: A herniated disc happens when the nucleus pulposus bulges through a tear in the anulus fibrosus. The bulge can press on a spinal nerve as it exits through an intervertebral foramen. Because that nerve carries signals from the leg, the pain is felt along the limb rather than only in the back.
notes: Scoliosis is an abnormal sideways curve of the spine. Choose it if the question describes a spine that curves to one side.
Correct. A disc core pushing through a torn ring is a herniated disc.
Kyphosis is an exaggerated thoracic curve that rounds the upper back. Pick it for a question about a hunched upper back.
A fractured dens is a break of the peg on the axis, high in the neck. It would be right for a question about a serious injury near the brainstem.

questions.q: During a school screening, a student bends forward and the nurse sees that the spine curves to one side. Which abnormal curvature is this?
questions.why: Scoliosis is an abnormal sideways curve of the spine. The normal curvatures all bend forward or backward, so any curve to the left or right is abnormal. The other named abnormal curvatures, kyphosis and lordosis, are exaggerations of the normal front-to-back curves.
notes: Kyphosis is an exaggerated thoracic curve that rounds the upper back forward, a front-to-back problem. Choose it for a hunched upper back.
Lordosis is an exaggerated lumbar curve that makes the lower back sway inward. Pick it for a question about an excessive curve in the lower back.
A herniated disc is a bulging disc core pressing on a nerve, not a curvature. It would be right for a question about pain traveling down a limb.
Correct. A sideways curve is scoliosis.

questions.q: During CPR, a rescuer locates the small bony tip at the lower end of the sternum so that the hands press on the sternum just above it rather than on the tip. Which structure is the rescuer finding?
questions.why: The xiphoid process is the small inferior tip of the sternum. Rescuers use it as a landmark so they press on the lower half of the sternum body above it. Pressing directly on the xiphoid could break it and push it toward the liver, so finding it keeps the hands in the right spot.
notes: The jugular notch is the dip at the top of the manubrium at the base of the neck. Pick it for a question about the superior border of the sternum.
The manubrium is the superior part of the sternum near the clavicles, far from where compressions are given. Choose it for a question about the top of the sternum.
Correct. The xiphoid process is the inferior tip that guides hand placement.
The sternal angle is the ridge between the manubrium and body, level with the second rib. It would be right for a question about where to start counting ribs.

questions.q: A diver strikes the top of the head on the pool floor and fractures a bony peg that is held against the atlas by a ligament. Which structure is fractured?
options: The anterior arch of the atlas
questions.why: The dens is the upward peg of the axis (C2). It sits inside the front of the atlas ring, held there by a strong ligament, so the atlas can pivot around it. A fracture of the dens is very serious because the fragment lies right next to the brainstem and upper spinal cord.
notes: The anterior arch of the atlas is the front part of the C1 ring that the dens presses against. It is part of the ring, not a peg, so choose it for a question about the front of the atlas.
The transverse process of C1 projects to the side and contains a transverse foramen for the vertebral artery. It would fit a question about the lateral parts of the atlas.
The spinous process of C7 is the long projection felt at the base of the neck. Pick it for a question about the vertebra prominens.
Correct. The peg held against the atlas is the dens of the axis.

questions.q: A broken vertebra is treated as an emergency mainly because of a delicate structure that runs through the column. Which structure is at risk?
questions.why: The stacked vertebral foramina form the vertebral canal, which carries the spinal cord. A fractured vertebra can shift or splinter into the canal and injure the cord, which can cause paralysis below the level of injury. That is why a vertebral fracture is dangerous for what runs inside the column, not only for the bone.
notes: The esophagus runs in front of the vertebral column, not through it. It would be right for a question about the tube carrying food to the stomach.
Correct. The spinal cord runs through the vertebral canal and can be injured by a fracture.

Red bone marrow does fill the spongy bone of the vertebral bodies, but damage to it is not what makes a spinal fracture an emergency. Students pick it by reading inside the bone literally rather than thinking about the canal.
The nucleus pulposus is the gel core of an intervertebral disc. Choose it for a question about a herniated disc, not a fractured vertebra.

questions.q: The adult vertebral column has four curves instead of being a straight rod. What do these curves do for the spine?
options: They hold the vertebrae rigidly in line so the column cannot bend
They create the openings where spinal nerves leave the column
They act like a spring, absorbing shock and helping balance the body's weight
They give every vertebra a place for a rib to attach
questions.why: A column with alternating curves can flex and rebound under a load, much like a spring, so the jolts of walking and running are cushioned instead of traveling straight up to the skull. The curves also keep the weight of the head and trunk balanced over the hips. This gives the spine strength, flexibility, and balance at the same time.
notes: The curves do the opposite of making the spine rigid; they add flexibility. Students who picture the spine as a support pole pick this, but a rigid column would pass every jolt to the head.
The openings for spinal nerves are the intervertebral foramina, formed by notches between neighboring vertebrae, not by the curves. Choose this idea for a question about where spinal nerves exit.
Correct. The curves work like a spring for shock absorption and balance.
Ribs attach only to the twelve thoracic vertebrae, and that has nothing to do with the curves. Pick rib attachment for a question about costal facets on thoracic vertebrae.
questions.answerText: They act like a spring, absorbing shock and helping balance the body's weight

questions.q: Lumbar vertebrae have much larger bodies than cervical vertebrae. What best explains this size difference?
options: Lower vertebrae carry more of the body's weight above them
Lumbar vertebrae must anchor the twelve pairs of ribs
Lumbar vertebrae need room for transverse foramina
Lumbar vertebrae surround a much thicker spinal cord
questions.why: Weight adds up as you move down the spine. Cervical vertebrae carry only the head, but lumbar vertebrae carry the head, arms, and entire trunk. Larger, thicker bodies spread that heavier load, so vertebral body size increases steadily from the neck to the lower back.
notes: Correct. Lumbar bodies are larger because they bear more weight.
Ribs attach to the thoracic vertebrae, not the lumbar ones, and lumbar vertebrae have no costal facets. Choose rib attachment for a question about thoracic features.
Transverse foramina are found only in cervical vertebrae, and lumbar vertebrae lack them. Pick transverse foramina for a question about identifying a cervical vertebra.
The spinal cord does not get thicker in the lower back; in adults it ends near the first or second lumbar vertebra. Students assume big vertebrae must hold a big cord, but the size is about weight.
questions.answerText: Lower vertebrae carry more of the body's weight above them

questions.q: Each intervertebral disc has a soft gel core inside a tough outer ring. How does this two-part design suit the disc's job?
options: The gel core spreads pressure while the tough ring holds the core in place
The two layers enclose a joint cavity filled with synovial fluid
The tough core bears the weight while the gel ring lets the vertebrae slide
The ring anchors the spinal nerves as they leave the column
questions.why: When the spine is loaded, the gel-like nucleus pulposus squashes slightly and spreads the force evenly across the vertebral bodies. The fibrous anulus fibrosus surrounds the core, keeps it contained, and resists the tension the spreading core creates. The pairing gives both cushioning and containment.
notes: Correct. The core spreads pressure and the ring contains it.
An intervertebral disc forms a cartilaginous joint with no synovial cavity. Choose a synovial cavity for a question about freely movable joints such as the shoulder or knee.
This reverses the layers. The core is the soft gel and the ring is the tough fibrous part, not the other way around.

Spinal nerves exit through the intervertebral foramina beside the disc, but the disc does not anchor them. Students pick this because a bulging disc can press a nerve, which is a problem, not the disc's purpose.
questions.answerText: The gel core spreads pressure while the tough ring holds the core in place

questions.q: The atlas is a ring of bone with no body, sitting directly under the skull. Which job does the atlas perform?
options: It carries the dens that the head rotates around
It carries costal facets for the first pair of ribs
It forms the long spinous process felt at the base of the neck
It holds up the skull and forms the joint for nodding yes with the occipital condyles
questions.why: The atlas supports the head. Its superior facets cradle the occipital condyles of the skull, forming the atlanto-occipital joint that rocks the head forward and back to nod yes. With no body in the way, the front of its ring holds the dens of the axis, and the large opening leaves room for the spinal cord.
notes: Carrying the dens is the job of the axis, C2. The atlas pivots around the dens but does not carry it, so choose this for a question about the axis.
The first pair of ribs articulates with T1, the first thoracic vertebra. Pick this for a question about where the thoracic region and the ribs begin.
The long palpable spinous process belongs to C7, the vertebra prominens. The atlas has no spinous process at all.
Correct. The atlas holds up the skull and forms the yes-nodding joint.
questions.answerText: It holds up the skull and forms the joint for nodding yes with the occipital condyles

questions.q: The axis has an upward peg, the dens, that fits into the ring of the atlas. Which head movement does this arrangement make possible?
options: Turning the head side to side, as in shaking no
Tilting the ear toward the shoulder
questions.why: The dens acts as a pivot. The atlas, carrying the skull on top of it, rotates around the dens at the atlanto-axial joint, which turns the head left and right. That is the motion of shaking your head no, and it is why C2 is called the axis.
notes: Correct. The atlas pivots on the dens to turn the head side to side.
Nodding yes happens at the atlanto-occipital joint between the atlas and the skull. Choose it for a question about the joint above the atlas.
Tilting the ear toward the shoulder is side bending shared across many cervical vertebrae, not rotation on a single peg. Students pick it because it is also a sideways movement of the head.
Opening and closing the jaw happens at the temporomandibular joint between the mandible and temporal bone. It would be right for a question about chewing or talking.
questions.answerText: Turning the head side to side, as in shaking no

questions.q: Thoracic vertebrae have costal facets that cervical and lumbar vertebrae lack. Why are these facets found only in the thoracic region?
options: They pass the vertebral arteries up to the brain
Ribs articulate with the spine only in the thoracic region
They hold the intervertebral discs in place
They anchor the clavicles to the spine
questions.why: Costal means rib, and costal facets are the smooth joint surfaces where ribs meet the spine. The head of each rib meets facets on the vertebral bodies, and the tubercle meets a facet on the transverse process. Since ribs attach only to the twelve thoracic vertebrae, only they need these facets.
notes: Passing the vertebral arteries is the job of the transverse foramina, found only in cervical vertebrae. Choose this for a question about a feature unique to the neck.
Correct. Costal facets exist where the ribs articulate, which is only in the thoracic region.
Intervertebral discs sit between the vertebral bodies and are held by their attachment to the bodies, not by facets. Students pick this because the facets and discs are both near the body.
The clavicles articulate with the manubrium of the sternum and the acromion of the scapula, never with the spine. Pick the clavicle for a question about the pectoral girdle.
questions.answerText: Ribs articulate with the spine only in the thoracic region

questions.q: The sacrum forms from five vertebrae that fuse into one solid bone. Why is a fused bone an advantage at this location?
options: It lets the lower back twist more freely
It protects the spinal cord, which ends inside the sacrum
It forms a stable base that passes body weight into the pelvis and legs
It gives the floating ribs a place to attach
questions.why: The sacrum sits between the hip bones and transfers the weight of the entire upper body into the pelvic girdle at the sacroiliac joints. Movement here would make the base unstable, so five separate vertebrae fusing into one rigid bone gives the strength and stability this load transfer needs. Mobility is provided higher up in the column instead.
notes: Fusion reduces movement rather than adding it. Choose free movement for a question about the separate vertebrae of the cervical or lumbar regions.

In adults the spinal cord ends near the first or second lumbar vertebra, so it does not reach the sacrum. The sacral canal carries nerve roots instead, and students pick this by assuming the cord runs the full length of the column.
Correct. Fusion creates a strong, stable base for weight transfer.
The floating ribs attach to the thoracic vertebrae T11 and T12 in back and to nothing in front. Pick them for a question about ribs with no anterior attachment.
questions.answerText: It forms a stable base that passes body weight into the pelvis and legs

questions.q: Why is it important that the vertebral foramina of stacked vertebrae line up with one another?
options: Together they form a continuous bony tunnel that protects the spinal cord
Together they hold the intervertebral discs between the bodies
Together they form the openings where spinal nerves leave the column
Together they carry the vertebral arteries up to the brain
questions.why: Each vertebra contributes one ring around the spinal cord. When the rings line up, they form the vertebral canal, a continuous tunnel that shields the cord along its whole length, much as the skull guards the brain. If the openings were out of line, parts of the cord would be exposed or pinched.
notes: Correct. The aligned foramina form the vertebral canal that protects the cord.
The discs sit between the vertebral bodies in front of the foramina and are not held by them. Students pick this because the discs also line up down the column.
Spinal nerves leave through the intervertebral foramina, the side gaps between vertebrae, not through the central foramina. Choose this for a question about intervertebral foramina.
The vertebral arteries climb through the transverse foramina of cervical vertebrae. Pick this for a question about transverse foramina.
questions.answerText: Together they form a continuous bony tunnel that protects the spinal cord

questions.q: An older patient has a rounded, hunched upper back from an exaggerated thoracic curve. Which abnormal curvature is this?
questions.why: Kyphosis is an exaggerated thoracic curvature that rounds the upper back forward into a hunch. The thoracic curve is normal, but in kyphosis it is bent much more than usual. It is especially common in older adults whose vertebral bodies have weakened and compressed.
notes: Scoliosis is a sideways curve of the spine to the left or right. Pick it for a question about a spine that bends to one side.
Correct. An exaggerated thoracic curve is kyphosis.
Lordosis is an exaggerated lumbar curve that makes the lower back sway inward. Choose it for a question about the lower back.
A herniated disc is a disc core pushing through its outer ring and pressing a nerve, not a curvature. It would be right for a question about pain shooting down a limb.

questions.q: A patient's lower back sways inward much more than normal because of an exaggerated lumbar curve. Which abnormal curvature is this?
questions.why: Lordosis is an exaggerated lumbar curvature, which deepens the normal inward curve of the lower back into a swayback. It can show up temporarily in late pregnancy, when the weight in front pulls the lower spine forward. The lumbar curve is normal; lordosis means it is curved too far.
notes: Kyphosis is an exaggerated thoracic curve, a hunch in the upper back. Choose it for a question about the upper back.
A primary curvature is a normal curve present at birth, the thoracic or sacral curve, not an abnormality. The lumbar curve is actually secondary, so this does not fit either way.
Scoliosis is a sideways curve, not a front-to-back exaggeration. Pick it for a question about a spine that curves to one side.
Correct. An exaggerated lumbar curve is lordosis.

questions.q: Which joint lets you shake your head no?
questions.why: The atlanto-axial joint lies between the atlas (C1) and the axis (C2). The atlas, carrying the skull, pivots around the dens of the axis, turning the head left and right. Its name combines the two vertebrae that meet there.
notes: The temporomandibular joint is the jaw joint between the mandible and the temporal bone. Pick it for a question about chewing or opening the mouth.
Correct. The atlanto-axial joint turns the head side to side.
The sternoclavicular joint joins the clavicle to the manubrium of the sternum. It would be right for a question about the joint linking the upper limb to the axial skeleton.
The atlanto-occipital joint is between the atlas and the skull, and it rocks the head forward and back. Choose it for a question about nodding yes.

questions.q: An infant can now hold up its head but has not yet stood or walked. Which curvatures does its spine have, and which one is still missing?
options: Only thoracic and sacral; cervical and lumbar are missing.
Cervical and lumbar; thoracic and sacral are missing.
Thoracic, sacral, and lumbar; the cervical curve is missing.
Thoracic, sacral, and cervical; the lumbar curve is still missing.
questions.why: Sort the curves by when they appear. The thoracic and sacral curvatures are primary and present from birth. The cervical curvature develops as the infant holds up its head, and the lumbar curvature develops only once the child stands and walks, so it has not formed yet.
notes: This would be true at birth. Holding up the head is the milestone that produces the cervical curvature.
The thoracic and sacral curves are primary, present from birth, so they cannot be missing.
This reverses the two secondary curves. The cervical curve comes with head control, and the lumbar curve comes with walking.
Correct. The thoracic and sacral curves are present from birth, the cervical forms with head control, and the lumbar waits for walking.
questions.answerText: Thoracic, sacral, and cervical; the lumbar curve is still missing.

questions.q: In lab, one loose bone is five fused vertebrae wedged between the hip bones, and another is four fused vertebrae. Which regions are they, and how do they explain 26 adult bones instead of 33 vertebrae?
options: Lumbar region and coccyx; 9 vertebrae fuse into 2 bones.
Sacrum and coccyx; 9 vertebrae fuse into 2 bones.
Sacrum and coccyx; 7 vertebrae fuse into 1 bone.
Sacrum and lumbar region; 5 lumbar vertebrae fuse.
questions.why: Identify the bones first. Five fused vertebrae between the hip bones form the sacrum, and four fused vertebrae form the coccyx. Those nine vertebrae become just two bones, so 33 vertebrae become 24 separate vertebrae plus the sacrum and coccyx, which is 26.
notes: The lumbar region has 5 separate vertebrae that do not fuse. The fused bone between the hip bones is the sacrum.
Correct. Five sacral and four coccygeal vertebrae fuse into 2 bones, so 33 becomes 26.
The bones are right but the count is off. Five sacral plus four coccygeal is 9 vertebrae, forming 2 bones.
The lumbar vertebrae stay separate in the adult. The second fused bone is the coccyx, the tailbone.
questions.answerText: Sacrum and coccyx; 9 vertebrae fuse into 2 bones.

questions.q: In lab, a student is handed a vertebra with a hole in each transverse process and a bony peg rising from its body. Which vertebra is it, and which joint does the peg form?
options: The atlas (C1); its dens forms the atlanto-occipital joint.
The axis (C2); its dens forms the atlanto-occipital joint.
The vertebra prominens (C7); its peg forms the atlanto-axial joint.
The axis (C2); its dens forms the atlanto-axial joint.
questions.why: Use one feature at a time. A hole in each transverse process is a transverse foramen, which places the bone in the cervical region. The upward peg is the dens, which only the axis has, and the atlas pivots around it at the atlanto-axial joint to turn the head side to side.
notes: The atlas is a ring with no body, so it has no peg. The atlanto-occipital joint is where the atlas meets the occipital condyles for the yes nod.
The bone is right, but the dens pivots in the atlas at the atlanto-axial joint. The atlanto-occipital joint is between the atlas and the skull.
C7 is cervical, but it is known for a long spinous process at the base of the neck. Only the axis carries the dens.
Correct. Transverse foramina make it cervical, and the upward peg, the dens, makes it the axis.
questions.answerText: The axis (C2); its dens forms the atlanto-axial joint.

questions.q: Starting at the rib that sits level with the sternal angle, a clinician counts down five more ribs. Which rib is reached, and how does it attach in front?
options: Rib 7, a false rib joined to the costal cartilage of the rib above.
Rib 8, a false rib joined to the costal cartilage of the rib above.
Rib 6, a floating rib with no anterior attachment at all.
Rib 7, a true rib with its own costal cartilage to the sternum.
questions.why: First locate the start. The sternal angle sits level with the second rib, so counting five more ribs down reaches rib 7. Ribs 1 to 7 are true ribs, each attached directly to the sternum by its own costal cartilage.
notes: The count is right, but rib 7 is the last true rib. Only ribs 8 to 10 join the costal cartilage of the rib above.
The sternal angle is level with rib 2, not rib 3, so five more ribs ends at rib 7.
Only ribs 11 and 12 are floating ribs. Rib 6 is a true rib, and the count reaches rib 7 anyway.
Correct. The sternal angle is level with rib 2, five more ribs down is rib 7, and ribs 1 to 7 are true ribs.
questions.answerText: Rib 7, a true rib with its own costal cartilage to the sternum.

questions.q: A patient fractures rib 11. A student worries the broken rib will pull on the sternum. Why is that not a concern?
options: Rib 11 is a true rib whose own cartilage absorbs the pull.
Rib 11 is a floating rib with no anterior attachment.
Rib 11 joins the costal cartilage of rib 10 instead.
Rib 11 attaches to the xiphoid process, which is cartilage.
questions.why: Place the rib in its group, then recall that group's attachment. Ribs 11 and 12 are the floating ribs, a subset of the false ribs, and they have no anterior attachment at all. With no link to the sternum, a break in rib 11 cannot pull on it.
notes: True ribs are pairs 1 to 7. Rib 11 is a floating rib with no costal link to the sternum.
Correct. Ribs 11 and 12 are floating ribs and do not attach to anything in front.
Only ribs 8 to 10 join the cartilage of the rib above. Rib 11 has no anterior attachment.
The xiphoid is the inferior tip of the sternum and a muscle attachment. Rib 11 has no anterior attachment at all, to the xiphoid or anywhere else.
questions.answerText: Rib 11 is a floating rib with no anterior attachment.

questions.q: A clinician feels the central dip at the top of the breastbone, then slides a finger down to the first ridge. Which part of the sternum was crossed, and which rib lies level with the ridge?
options: The manubrium; rib 2 lies level with the ridge.
The body; rib 2 lies level with the ridge.
The manubrium; rib 1 lies level with the ridge.
The xiphoid process; rib 7 lies level with the ridge.
questions.why: Start with the landmarks. The central dip is the jugular notch on top of the manubrium, and the first ridge below it is the sternal angle, where the manubrium meets the body. The sternal angle sits level with the second rib, the starting point for counting ribs.
notes: Correct. The dip is the jugular notch at the top of the manubrium, and the ridge is the sternal angle, level with rib 2.
The body is the long middle part below the sternal angle. The part between the jugular notch and the ridge is the manubrium.
The manubrium does articulate with the first ribs, but the sternal angle sits level with the second rib.
The xiphoid process is the small inferior tip of the sternum, at the opposite end from the jugular notch.
questions.answerText: The manubrium; rib 2 lies level with the ridge.

questions.topic: Pectoral girdle and upper limb bones
questions.q: Which two bones make up the pectoral girdle?
questions.why: The pectoral girdle, also called the shoulder girdle, is the clavicle in front and the scapula in back. Together they attach the upper limb to the trunk. The clavicle connects to the sternum, and the scapula holds the socket for the humerus.
notes: The sternum belongs to the axial skeleton, not the girdle, although the clavicle articulates with it. Choose this pair for a question about the sternoclavicular joint.
The humerus is the bone of the arm, which hangs from the girdle rather than forming part of it. This pair would describe the bones that meet at the shoulder joint.
The radius and ulna are the two bones of the forearm. Pick them for a question about the bones between the elbow and the wrist.
Correct. The clavicle and scapula form the pectoral girdle.

questions.topic: Pectoral girdle and upper limb bones
questions.q: What is the common name for the clavicle?
questions.why: The clavicle is the collarbone, an S-shaped bone that runs horizontally across the top of the thorax from the sternum to the shoulder. It lies just under the skin, so you can feel its whole length. It acts as a strut that holds the shoulder out from the body.
notes: The breastbone is the sternum, the flat midline bone at the front of the chest. Pick it for a question about the bone the clavicle attaches to medially.
The funny bone is not a bone at all but the spot behind the medial epicondyle of the humerus where the ulnar nerve runs. It would fit a question about the jolt felt in the little finger.
Correct. The clavicle is the collarbone.
The shoulder blade is the scapula, the flat triangular bone on the upper back. Choose it for a question about the posterior bone of the pectoral girdle.

questions.topic: Pectoral girdle and upper limb bones
questions.q: Which bone is the single bone of the arm, from shoulder to elbow?
questions.why: In anatomy, the arm (brachium) is only the part between the shoulder and the elbow, and it has a single bone, the humerus. The forearm, between the elbow and the wrist, has two bones. Keeping arm and forearm separate is important for naming muscles and bones correctly.
notes: The ulna is the medial bone of the forearm, on the little-finger side. Pick it for a question about the bone that forms the point of the elbow.
Correct. The humerus is the one bone of the arm.
The radius is the lateral bone of the forearm, between the elbow and the wrist. Choose it for a question about the thumb side of the forearm.
The scapula is the shoulder blade, part of the pectoral girdle rather than the arm. It would be right for a question about the bone holding the shoulder socket.

questions.topic: Pectoral girdle and upper limb bones
questions.q: How many carpal bones form the wrist?
questions.why: The wrist, or carpus, is made of eight small carpal bones arranged in two rows of four. The proximal row meets the radius, and the distal row meets the metacarpals of the palm. Many small bones gliding against each other let the wrist move smoothly in several directions.
notes: Fourteen is the number of phalanges in one hand. Pick it for a question about the finger bones.
Correct. There are eight carpal bones.
Seven is the number of tarsal bones in the ankle and foot. Students mix up the carpals and tarsals because both are short bones of the wrist and ankle.
Five is the number of metacarpals, the bones of the palm. Choose five for a question about the palm.

questions.topic: Pectoral girdle and upper limb bones
questions.q: What is the shallow socket on the scapula that receives the head of the humerus?
questions.why: The glenoid cavity is a shallow, oval socket on the lateral angle of the scapula. The rounded head of the humerus fits into it to form the glenohumeral joint, the shoulder joint. Because the socket is so shallow, the shoulder moves freely but dislocates more easily than deeper joints.
notes: The coracoid process is a hook-like projection on the front of the scapula used for muscle attachment. It would be right for a question about that anterior hook.
Correct. The glenoid cavity is the shoulder socket for the humeral head.
The olecranon fossa is a deep pit on the back of the distal humerus that receives the olecranon of the ulna. Choose it for a question about the elbow.
The acromion is the flat process at the tip of the scapular spine, the point of the shoulder. Pick it for a question about where the clavicle meets the scapula.

questions.topic: Pectoral girdle and upper limb bones
questions.q: Which bony marking is the ridge running across the posterior surface of the scapula?
questions.why: The spine of the scapula is a prominent ridge that crosses the back of the shoulder blade at an angle. It divides the posterior surface into a smaller hollow above (supraspinous fossa) and a larger hollow below (infraspinous fossa). It ends laterally as the flattened acromion.
notes: The coracoid process is a hook-like projection on the front of the scapula. Pick it for a question about the anterior hook used as a muscle attachment.
Correct. The spine is the ridge across the posterior scapula.
The medial border is the edge of the scapula closest to the vertebral column. It would be right for a question about the vertebral edge of the triangle.
The acromion is the flattened lateral end of the spine, forming the point of the shoulder. Choose it for a question about the tip of the spine.

questions.topic: Pectoral girdle and upper limb bones
questions.q: What is the rounded proximal end of the humerus called?
questions.why: The head of the humerus is the smooth, rounded ball at its proximal end. It faces medially into the glenoid cavity of the scapula, forming the ball of the ball-and-socket shoulder joint. In bone-marking vocabulary, a head is a bony expansion carried on a neck.
notes: The trochlea is the spool-shaped surface at the distal end that meets the ulna. Pick it for a question about the hinge surface of the elbow.
The capitulum is a small rounded knob at the distal end of the humerus that meets the radius. Choose it for a question about the elbow end of the humerus.
The deltoid tuberosity is a roughened area on the shaft where the deltoid muscle attaches. It would be right for a question about a muscle attachment on the middle of the bone.
Correct. The head is the rounded proximal end.

questions.topic: Pectoral girdle and upper limb bones
questions.q: How many phalanges are in one human hand?
questions.why: The thumb has two phalanges (proximal and distal), and each of the other four fingers has three (proximal, middle, and distal). That gives 2 plus 12, or fourteen phalanges per hand. The thumb is the one digit missing a middle phalanx.
notes: Ten would be right only if every digit had two phalanges. Students reach it by giving all the fingers the thumb's count.
Correct. Two in the thumb and three in each finger make fourteen.
Fifteen would be right only if the thumb had three phalanges like the other fingers. Students pick it by forgetting that the thumb lacks a middle phalanx.
Eight is the number of carpal bones in the wrist. Choose it for a question about the wrist.

questions.topic: Pectoral girdle and upper limb bones
questions.q: What is the deep posterior pit on the distal humerus that receives the ulna when the elbow straightens?
