questions.why: The olecranon fossa is a deep hollow on the back of the distal humerus. When the elbow straightens, the olecranon, the hook-shaped tip of the ulna, swings into this pit. The bone-on-bone fit stops the elbow from extending too far.
notes: Correct. The olecranon fossa receives the olecranon when the elbow extends.
The coronoid fossa is a smaller pit on the front of the distal humerus that receives the coronoid process of the ulna when the elbow bends. Choose it for a question about elbow flexion.
The intertubercular sulcus is a groove near the top of the humerus between the two tubercles. It would be right for a question about where a biceps tendon runs.
The supraspinous fossa is a hollow on the scapula above its spine. Pick it for a question about the posterior shoulder blade.

questions.topic: Pectoral girdle and upper limb bones
questions.q: Which bones form the palm of the hand?
questions.why: The five metacarpals are the long bones inside the palm, one leading to each digit. Meta means beyond, so the metacarpals are the bones beyond the carpus (wrist). Their rounded distal heads form the knuckles when you make a fist.
notes: Correct. The metacarpals form the palm.
The phalanges are the bones of the fingers and thumb, distal to the palm. Pick them for a question about the digits.
The tarsals are the bones of the ankle and back of the foot. Students mix them up with carpals, but tarsals belong to the lower limb.
The carpals are the eight small bones of the wrist, proximal to the palm. Choose them for a question about the wrist.

questions.topic: Pectoral girdle and upper limb bones
questions.q: What is the anatomical name for the thumb?
questions.why: The pollex is the anatomical name for the thumb, digit 1 of the hand. It has only two phalanges, a proximal and a distal. Its metacarpal meets the trapezium at a saddle joint, which lets the thumb swing across the palm to touch the fingertips.
notes: The hallux is the great toe, digit 1 of the foot. Choose it for a question about the big toe.
Correct. The pollex is the thumb.
The carpus is the wrist as a whole, the region made by the eight carpal bones. It would be right for a question about the wrist.
The pisiform is a small pea-shaped carpal bone on the little-finger side of the wrist. Pick it for a question about the proximal row of carpals.

questions.topic: Pectoral girdle and upper limb bones
questions.q: Which carpal bones make up the proximal row of the wrist?
questions.why: The proximal row, the row closer to the forearm, is the scaphoid, lunate, triquetrum, and pisiform, listed from the thumb side to the little-finger side. The mnemonic So Long To Pinky covers this row. The scaphoid and lunate are the two that meet the radius.
notes: Correct. Scaphoid, lunate, triquetrum, and pisiform form the proximal row.
Trapezium, trapezoid, capitate, and hamate are the distal row, the row next to the metacarpals. Choose this set for a question about the distal row.
This set also mixes rows, pairing the trapezium and hamate from the distal row with the lunate and pisiform from the proximal row. It does not match either row.
This set mixes two proximal bones (scaphoid and lunate) with two distal bones (capitate and hamate). Students make this mistake when they remember the names but not which row each belongs to.

questions.topic: Pectoral girdle and upper limb bones
questions.q: What is the roughened area on the humeral shaft where the deltoid muscle attaches?
questions.why: The deltoid tuberosity is a rough, raised area on the lateral side of the middle of the humeral shaft. The deltoid, the muscle that caps the shoulder, inserts there. In bone-marking vocabulary, a tuberosity is a large, rough projection where a muscle attaches.
notes: Correct. The deltoid tuberosity is on the humeral shaft.
The greater tubercle is a bump on the lateral side of the proximal humerus, near the head. Choose it for a question about the lateral bump near the shoulder.
The radial tuberosity is on the radius just below its neck, not on the humerus. It would be right for a question about a muscle attachment on the proximal radius.
The lateral epicondyle is a projection at the distal end of the humerus, above the capitulum. Pick it for a question about the outer elbow.

questions.topic: Pectoral girdle and upper limb bones
questions.q: The clavicle is the only bony link in which connection?
options: The first rib to the sternum
The upper limb to the axial skeleton
questions.why: The clavicle is the sole bony strut connecting the upper limb to the axial skeleton. Its medial end joins the manubrium of the sternum, and its lateral end joins the acromion of the scapula. The scapula itself is held to the trunk only by muscles, which is why the shoulder is so mobile.
notes: The radius and ulna connect to each other at the radioulnar joints and by the interosseous membrane. Pick this pair for a question about the forearm.
The first rib connects to the manubrium by its own costal cartilage, not through the clavicle. This would fit a question about how the first rib attaches to the sternum.
The scapula and humerus connect directly at the glenohumeral (shoulder) joint without the clavicle. Choose this pair for a question about the shoulder joint.
Correct. The clavicle is the only bony link between the upper limb and the axial skeleton.
questions.answerText: The upper limb to the axial skeleton

questions.topic: Pectoral girdle and upper limb bones
questions.q: The sternal end of the clavicle articulates with which structure?
options: The coracoid process of the scapula
questions.why: The sternal end is the medial end of the clavicle. It meets the manubrium, the top part of the sternum, at the sternoclavicular joint. This is the only joint that connects the upper limb to the axial skeleton.
notes: The body of the sternum is the long middle part, below the manubrium, where ribs 2 to 7 attach. Students pick it because it is also part of the sternum, but the clavicle meets only the manubrium.
Correct. The sternal end meets the manubrium at the sternoclavicular joint.

The coracoid process is a hook on the front of the scapula that anchors ligaments and muscles but does not form a joint with the clavicle. Pick it for a question about the anterior hook of the scapula.
The acromion meets the acromial end, the lateral end of the clavicle, at the acromioclavicular joint. Choose it for a question about the lateral end.

questions.topic: Pectoral girdle and upper limb bones
questions.q: Which marking on the distal humerus articulates with the radius?
questions.why: The capitulum is a small rounded knob on the lateral side of the distal humerus. Capitulum means little head, and the disc-shaped head of the radius rests against it. In anatomical position the radius is lateral, so it pairs with the lateral articular surface.
notes: The olecranon fossa is a pit on the back of the humerus that receives the olecranon of the ulna. It would be right for a question about elbow extension.
The medial epicondyle is a projection above the trochlea for muscle attachment, not a joint surface. Pick it for a question about the funny bone or the medial elbow bump.
The trochlea is the spool-shaped surface on the medial side that articulates with the ulna. Choose it for a question about the ulna's partner at the elbow.
Correct. The capitulum articulates with the radius.

questions.topic: Pectoral girdle and upper limb bones
questions.q: Which marking on the distal humerus articulates with the ulna?
questions.why: The trochlea is a spool-shaped surface on the medial side of the distal humerus. Trochlea means pulley. The trochlear notch of the ulna wraps around it to form the hinge of the elbow, which bends and straightens in one plane.
notes: The capitulum is the rounded lateral knob that articulates with the radius. Choose it for a question about the radius at the elbow.
The greater tubercle is at the proximal end of the humerus near the shoulder. It would be right for a question about a lateral muscle attachment near the head.
The lateral epicondyle is a projection above the capitulum for muscle attachment, not an articular surface. Pick it for a question about the outer elbow bump.
Correct. The trochlea articulates with the ulna.

questions.topic: Pectoral girdle and upper limb bones
questions.q: In anatomical position, on which side of the forearm does the radius lie?
options: The medial side, the little-finger side
The anterior side, in front of the ulna
The lateral side, the thumb side
The posterior side, behind the ulna
questions.why: In anatomical position, with the palms facing forward, the radius lies on the lateral side of the forearm, in line with the thumb. The ulna lies on the medial side, in line with the little finger. The two bones sit side by side, so they are described as lateral and medial rather than front and back.
notes: The medial, little-finger side is where the ulna lies. Choose this side for a question about the ulna.
The radius is not anterior to the ulna in anatomical position; the two bones are parallel and side by side. Front and back positions would only describe the pronated forearm.
Correct. The radius is lateral, on the thumb side.

In anatomical position the radius and ulna lie side by side, not one behind the other. Students pick a front or back position when they picture the forearm turned palm down, where the radius crosses over the ulna.
questions.answerText: The lateral side, the thumb side

questions.topic: Pectoral girdle and upper limb bones
questions.q: The trochlear notch of the ulna grips which marking of the humerus?
questions.why: The trochlear notch is a deep C-shaped curve on the proximal ulna, between the olecranon and the coronoid process. It wraps around the spool-shaped trochlea of the humerus like a wrench around a bolt. This tight fit forms the hinge of the elbow.
notes: The medial epicondyle is a projection for muscle attachment and does not form a joint surface. Pick it for a question about the medial elbow bump.
The olecranon fossa receives the olecranon when the elbow straightens, but it is a pit for the tip of the ulna, not the surface the notch wraps around. Choose it for a question about elbow extension.
The capitulum meets the head of the radius, not the ulna. Choose it for a question about the radius at the elbow.
Correct. The trochlear notch grips the trochlea.

questions.topic: Pectoral girdle and upper limb bones
questions.q: Which scapular process forms the point of the shoulder at the lateral tip of the spine?
questions.why: The acromion is the flattened lateral end of the scapular spine. It forms the bony point at the top of the shoulder that you can feel, and it articulates with the lateral end of the clavicle at the acromioclavicular joint. Acromion means the highest point of the shoulder.
notes: Correct. The acromion is the point of the shoulder.
The superior angle is the upper medial corner of the scapular triangle, near the neck. It would be right for a question about the corners of the scapula.
The coracoid process is a hook that projects forward from the front of the scapula, below the clavicle. Choose it for a question about the anterior hook used for muscle attachment.
The glenoid cavity is the shallow socket for the head of the humerus, not a process. Pick it for a question about the shoulder joint socket.

questions.topic: Pectoral girdle and upper limb bones
questions.q: The head of the radius articulates with which two structures at the elbow?
options: The olecranon fossa and the coronoid process
The trochlea of the humerus and the trochlear notch of the ulna
The capitulum of the humerus and the ulnar notch of the radius
The capitulum of the humerus and the radial notch of the ulna
questions.why: The disc-shaped head of the radius touches two bones. Its top surface rests against the capitulum of the humerus, and its rim spins against the radial notch on the side of the ulna. The joint with the radial notch is the proximal radioulnar joint, which lets the radius rotate when the palm turns.
notes: The olecranon fossa and coronoid process are humerus and ulna features that take part in extension and flexion, not radial head joints. Pick them for a question about the ulna's movement at the elbow.
The trochlea and trochlear notch are the surfaces where the humerus and ulna meet, forming the elbow hinge. Choose this pair for a question about the ulna's joint with the humerus.
The ulnar notch is on the radius itself, at the wrist, and it receives the head of the ulna. Students pick it because the names mirror each other, but the radial head meets the radial notch.
Correct. The radial head meets the capitulum and the radial notch of the ulna.
questions.answerText: The capitulum of the humerus and the radial notch of the ulna

questions.topic: Pectoral girdle and upper limb bones
questions.q: Which carpal bone articulates with the first metacarpal at the base of the thumb?
questions.why: The trapezium is the distal-row carpal on the thumb side. It meets the base of the first metacarpal at the carpometacarpal joint of the thumb, a saddle joint that lets the thumb swing across the palm. A helpful memory link is that the trapeziUM sits under the thUMb.
notes: The trapezoid sits next to the trapezium but articulates with the second metacarpal, the index finger's. Pick it for a question about the base of the index finger.
The scaphoid is in the proximal row on the thumb side and meets the radius, not a metacarpal. Choose it for a question about the most commonly fractured carpal.
Correct. The trapezium meets the first metacarpal.
The capitate is the largest carpal, in the center of the distal row, and it meets the third metacarpal. It would be right for a question about the largest carpal bone.

questions.topic: Pectoral girdle and upper limb bones
questions.q: Which forearm bone has a styloid process on the medial side of the wrist?
questions.why: Both forearm bones end in a pointed styloid process at the wrist. The ulna is the medial bone, so its styloid process is on the medial, little-finger side, where you can feel a bump. The radius has its styloid process on the lateral, thumb side.
notes: The humerus is the bone of the arm and ends at the elbow, not the wrist. Pick it for a question about the epicondyles or capitulum.
Correct. The ulna has the medial styloid process.
The radius also has a styloid process, but on the lateral, thumb side of the wrist. Choose the radius for a question about the lateral styloid process.
The scaphoid is a carpal bone of the wrist, not a forearm bone, and it has no styloid process. It would be right for a question about the most frequently fractured carpal.

questions.topic: Pectoral girdle and upper limb bones
questions.q: Which list names the phalanges of the index finger in order from the palm to the fingertip?
questions.why: Each finger other than the thumb has three phalanges named by their position. The proximal phalanx is closest to the palm, the middle phalanx is next, and the distal phalanx forms the fingertip. Proximal means nearer to the trunk and distal means farther from it.
notes: This order places the distal phalanx in the middle. Distal means farthest from the trunk, so the distal phalanx must be at the tip.
Correct. Proximal, middle, then distal from palm to fingertip.
This is the correct list run in reverse, from fingertip to palm. It would be right if the question asked for the order starting at the fingertip.
Only proximal and distal describes the thumb, which lacks a middle phalanx. Choose this for a question about the phalanges of the thumb.

questions.topic: Pectoral girdle and upper limb bones
questions.q: The intertubercular sulcus of the humerus lies between which two markings?
options: The greater tubercle and the lesser tubercle
The head and the anatomical neck
questions.why: The intertubercular sulcus is a groove on the front of the proximal humerus. Its name tells you where it is: inter means between and tubercular refers to the tubercles, so it runs between the greater and lesser tubercles. A tendon of the biceps brachii slides in this groove, which is also called the bicipital groove.
notes: Correct. The sulcus runs between the greater and lesser tubercles.
The anatomical neck is a narrow groove just below the head, not a groove between two bumps. It would be right for a question about where the head meets the rest of the proximal humerus.
The epicondyles are projections at the distal end of the humerus, with no groove named for lying between them. Pick them for a question about muscle attachments at the elbow.
The capitulum and trochlea are the two articular surfaces at the distal end of the humerus. Choose them for a question about where the radius and ulna meet the humerus.
questions.answerText: The greater tubercle and the lesser tubercle

questions.topic: Pectoral girdle and upper limb bones
questions.q: Which hollow of the scapula lies on its anterior surface, facing the ribs?
questions.why: The subscapular fossa is the broad, shallow hollow covering most of the anterior surface of the scapula, the side that faces the ribs. Sub means under, and this surface lies underneath the scapula against the thoracic wall. The subscapularis muscle fills it.
notes: Correct. The subscapular fossa is on the anterior surface.
The supraspinous fossa is on the posterior surface, above the scapular spine. Choose it for a question about the hollow above the spine.
The glenoid cavity is the shallow socket at the lateral angle that holds the head of the humerus. It would be right for a question about the shoulder joint.
The infraspinous fossa is on the posterior surface, below the scapular spine. Pick it for a question about the larger hollow below the spine.

questions.topic: Pectoral girdle and upper limb bones
questions.q: The ulnar notch of the radius receives which structure to form the distal radioulnar joint?
options: The styloid process of the ulna
questions.why: The ulnar notch is a small concave surface on the medial side of the distal radius. It is named for the bone that fits into it: the head of the ulna, which is at the ulna's distal (wrist) end. This distal radioulnar joint lets the radius swing around the ulna when the palm turns over.
notes: The ulnar styloid process is a pointed projection beside the ulnar head, not the part that sits in the notch. Pick it for a question about the medial bump at the wrist.
The head of the radius is at the elbow end and fits into the radial notch of the ulna, forming the proximal radioulnar joint. Choose it for a question about the elbow end.
Correct. The head of the ulna fits into the ulnar notch at the wrist.
The olecranon is at the proximal end of the ulna, forming the point of the elbow. It would be right for a question about the elbow.

questions.topic: Pectoral girdle and upper limb bones
questions.q: The metacarpals are numbered 1 to 5. Where does the numbering begin?
questions.why: Metacarpals are numbered from lateral to medial in anatomical position, starting with the thumb as number 1 and ending with the little finger as number 5. The digits follow the same numbering, so the thumb is digit 1. This matches the lab list, which numbers metacarpals lateral to medial.
notes: The little finger is metacarpal 5, the last in the series, not the first. Students start there when they forget that numbering runs from lateral to medial in anatomical position.
Correct. Numbering starts at the thumb, which is metacarpal 1.
The index finger is metacarpal 2, the one that meets the trapezoid. Students pick it because they think of the thumb as separate from the fingers.
The middle finger is metacarpal 3, in the center of the hand. Choose it for a question about which metacarpal meets the capitate.

questions.topic: Pectoral girdle and upper limb bones
questions.q: Which marking is the narrow groove just below the head of the humerus?
questions.why: The anatomical neck is a slight groove right at the edge of the humeral head, marking where the smooth joint surface ends. It sits above the greater and lesser tubercles. The surgical neck, by contrast, is a narrowing below the tubercles where the shaft begins.
notes: Correct. The anatomical neck is the groove just below the head.
The intertubercular sulcus is a groove between the two tubercles, running down the shaft rather than around the head. It would be right for a question about where a biceps tendon runs.
The deltoid tuberosity is a rough area on the middle of the shaft. Pick it for a question about the deltoid muscle attachment.
The surgical neck is lower, the narrowing below the tubercles, and it is a common fracture site. Choose it for a question about where the humerus most often breaks near the shoulder.

questions.topic: Pectoral girdle and upper limb bones
questions.q: In lab, a student points to a rounded knob on the lateral side of the distal humerus where a forearm bone meets it. Which marking is the student pointing to?
questions.why: The capitulum is the rounded knob on the lateral half of the distal humerus. The head of the radius meets it at the elbow. Fixing the humerus in anatomical position first makes the pairing easy: the capitulum and radius are both lateral, and the trochlea and ulna are both medial.
notes: The greater tubercle is at the proximal end of the humerus near the shoulder. It would be right for a question about a lateral bump near the head.
The lateral epicondyle is a roughened projection just above the capitulum, used for muscle attachment rather than as a joint surface. Pick it for a question about the outer elbow bump.
The trochlea is the spool-shaped surface on the medial side that meets the ulna. Choose it for a medial articular surface.
Correct. The lateral rounded knob that meets the radius is the capitulum.

questions.topic: Pectoral girdle and upper limb bones
questions.q: Starting at the elbow and moving toward the wrist along the thumb side of the forearm, which bone are you following?
questions.why: The radius is the lateral forearm bone, which means it lies on the thumb side in anatomical position. It is narrow at the elbow, where its disc-shaped head sits, and wide at the wrist, where it forms most of the joint with the carpals. Tracing the thumb side from elbow to wrist follows the radius the whole way.
notes: The first metacarpal is in the hand, beyond the wrist, in line with the thumb. It would be right for a path from the wrist to the base of the thumb.
The ulna runs along the medial, little-finger side of the forearm. Choose it for a path along the little-finger side.
The humerus is the arm bone, proximal to the elbow, so it does not run between the elbow and the wrist. Pick it for a path from the shoulder to the elbow.
Correct. The thumb side of the forearm is the radius.

questions.topic: Pectoral girdle and upper limb bones
questions.q: A student feels the bony point at the very tip of the elbow when the arm is straight. Which marking is this?
options: The coronoid process of the ulna
The medial epicondyle of the humerus
questions.why: The olecranon is the large, hook-shaped proximal end of the ulna, and it forms the point of the elbow you lean on. When the elbow straightens, the olecranon fits into the olecranon fossa on the back of the humerus. It lies just under the skin, so it is easy to feel.
notes: The radial tuberosity is a roughened bump on the front of the proximal radius, buried under muscle. It would be right for a question about a muscle attachment just below the radial neck.
Correct. The olecranon forms the point of the elbow.

The coronoid process is on the front of the proximal ulna, so it cannot be felt at the back tip of the elbow. Choose it for a question about the anterior lip that fits into the coronoid fossa during flexion.
The medial epicondyle is a bump on the inner side of the elbow, off to the side of the point. Pick it for a question about the funny bone or the medial elbow bump.

questions.topic: Pectoral girdle and upper limb bones
questions.q: Which hollow lies above the spine on the posterior surface of the scapula?
questions.why: The spine of the scapula divides its back surface into two hollows. Supra means above, so the supraspinous fossa is the smaller hollow above the spine. The supraspinatus muscle, one of the rotator cuff muscles, fills it.
notes: The infraspinous fossa is the larger hollow below the spine. Choose it for a question using infra, meaning below.
The glenoid cavity is the socket for the head of the humerus, not a hollow on the back of the blade. It would be right for a question about the shoulder joint.
Correct. The supraspinous fossa is above the spine.
The subscapular fossa is on the anterior surface facing the ribs. Pick it for a question about the front of the scapula.

questions.topic: Pectoral girdle and upper limb bones
questions.q: A hook-like process projects forward from the upper scapula, below the clavicle, and serves as a muscle attachment. Which marking is it?
questions.why: The coracoid process is a curved, finger-like hook that juts forward from the top of the scapula, just below the lateral clavicle. Its name means shaped like a crow's beak. Several muscles and ligaments of the shoulder and chest attach to it.
notes: The spine of the scapula is a ridge across the posterior surface, not a hook that points forward. Pick it for a question about the ridge dividing the back of the blade.
Correct. The coracoid process is the forward-pointing hook.
The lateral border is the edge of the scapula nearest the armpit, also called the axillary border. It would be right for a question about the edges of the scapular triangle.
The acromion is the flat process at the lateral tip of the spine, forming the point of the shoulder. Choose it for a question about where the scapula meets the lateral clavicle.

questions.topic: Pectoral girdle and upper limb bones
questions.q: An X-ray shows a fracture across the humerus at the narrowing just below the greater and lesser tubercles. Which marking is the fracture site?
questions.why: The surgical neck is the narrowing of the humerus just below the tubercles, where the wider proximal end tapers into the shaft. It is named surgical because it fractures so often, especially in falls. The anatomical neck is higher, directly at the edge of the head.
notes: The anatomical neck is the groove right below the head, above the tubercles. Choose it for a question about the groove marking the edge of the head.
The intertubercular sulcus is the groove running between the tubercles, not a narrowing below them. It would be right for a question about the biceps tendon groove.
The deltoid tuberosity is a rough area farther down the shaft, on the lateral side. Pick it for a question about the deltoid attachment.
Correct. The narrowing below the tubercles is the surgical neck.

questions.topic: Pectoral girdle and upper limb bones
questions.q: After a fall on an outstretched hand, an X-ray shows a broken carpal bone in the proximal row on the thumb side. Which bone is it?
questions.why: The scaphoid is the proximal-row carpal on the thumb side, and it is the carpal fractured most often. In a fall on an outstretched hand, force passes from the palm through the scaphoid to the radius, so it takes the brunt. Its name means boat-shaped.
notes: The pisiform is in the proximal row on the little-finger side, the opposite side from the thumb. It would be right for a question about the small pea-shaped carpal.
The trapezium is on the thumb side but in the distal row, where it meets the first metacarpal. Pick it for a question about the base of the thumb.
The lunate is also in the proximal row but sits in the middle, next to the scaphoid. Choose it for a question about the carpal most often dislocated.
Correct. The scaphoid is the proximal-row carpal on the thumb side and the most often fractured.

questions.topic: Pectoral girdle and upper limb bones
questions.q: Which forearm marking is the disc-shaped proximal end that articulates with the capitulum?
options: The coronoid process of the ulna
questions.why: The head of the radius is a flat, disc-shaped end at the top of the radius. Its upper surface rests against the capitulum of the humerus, and its rim turns inside the radial notch of the ulna. That disc shape lets the radius spin in place when the forearm turns the palm up or down.
notes: The olecranon is the hook-shaped proximal end of the ulna at the back of the elbow, which fits the olecranon fossa. Choose it for a question about the point of the elbow.
The coronoid process is the front lip of the proximal ulna that helps grip the trochlea. It would be right for a question about the anterior ulna at the elbow.
The radial tuberosity is a rough bump just below the radial neck where a muscle attaches, not a joint surface. Pick it for a question about a muscle attachment on the radius.
Correct. The disc-shaped head of the radius meets the capitulum.

questions.topic: Pectoral girdle and upper limb bones
questions.q: Which marking is the medial projection of the distal humerus, just above the trochlea?
questions.why: The medial epicondyle is a large bump on the inner side of the distal humerus, above the spool-shaped trochlea. Epicondyle means above a condyle, a raised area beside a joint surface. It serves as a muscle attachment, and the ulnar nerve passes just behind it.
notes: Correct. The medial epicondyle sits above the trochlea.
The lesser tubercle is at the proximal end of the humerus near the head, not near the elbow. Pick it for a question about the anterior bump near the shoulder.
The lateral epicondyle is the projection on the outer side, above the capitulum. Choose it for a question about the lateral bump of the distal humerus.
The coronoid process belongs to the ulna, not the humerus. It would be right for a question about the front lip of the proximal ulna.

questions.topic: Pectoral girdle and upper limb bones
questions.q: On the proximal ulna, a lip projects forward and fits into a small pit on the humerus when the elbow bends. Which marking is it?
questions.why: The coronoid process is the anterior lip of the proximal ulna, forming the lower edge of the trochlear notch. When the elbow bends fully, it fits into the coronoid fossa on the front of the humerus. The olecranon does the matching job at the back when the elbow straightens.
notes: Correct. The coronoid process fits the coronoid fossa during flexion.
The ulnar styloid process is at the distal end, at the wrist, not the elbow. Pick it for a question about the medial bump of the wrist.
The radial notch is a smooth surface on the lateral side of the proximal ulna that holds the head of the radius. It would be right for a question about the proximal radioulnar joint.
The olecranon is the posterior hook of the proximal ulna, which fits the olecranon fossa when the elbow straightens. Choose it for a question about elbow extension.

questions.topic: Pectoral girdle and upper limb bones
questions.q: Following the medial side of the forearm from elbow to wrist, which bone are you tracking, and which marking forms its elbow end?
options: The ulna, with the olecranon at its elbow end
The radius, with its head at the elbow end
The ulna, with its styloid process at its elbow end
The humerus, with the lateral epicondyle at its elbow end
questions.why: The ulna is the medial forearm bone, on the little-finger side. Its proximal end is large and hook-shaped, with the olecranon forming the point of the elbow. The ulna is wide at the elbow and narrow at the wrist, the opposite of the radius.
notes: Correct. The medial forearm bone is the ulna, and the olecranon forms its elbow end.
The radius and its disc-shaped head are on the lateral, thumb side. Choose this pairing for a path along the thumb side of the forearm.
The ulna is the right bone, but its styloid process is at the wrist end, not the elbow end. Students mix up the two ends when they remember the markings but not where each sits.
The humerus is the arm bone, above the elbow, and the lateral epicondyle is on its outer side. Pick it for a question about the outer bump of the distal humerus.
questions.answerText: The ulna, with the olecranon at its elbow end

questions.topic: Pectoral girdle and upper limb bones
questions.q: Which joint is formed where the acromion of the scapula meets the lateral end of the clavicle?
questions.why: Joints are often named for the two parts that meet, and the acromioclavicular joint joins the acromion with the clavicle. It sits at the top of the shoulder, where you can feel a small bump. A hard fall onto the point of the shoulder can injure this joint, often called a separated shoulder.
notes: The glenohumeral joint is the shoulder joint proper, where the humeral head sits in the glenoid cavity. Pick it for a question about the ball-and-socket joint of the shoulder.
The sternoclavicular joint is at the medial end of the clavicle, where it meets the manubrium. Choose it for a question about the only joint linking the upper limb to the axial skeleton.
Correct. The acromion and clavicle meet at the acromioclavicular joint.
The sacroiliac joint joins the sacrum and the ilium in the pelvis. It would be right for a question about the auricular surface of the sacrum.

questions.topic: Pectoral girdle and upper limb bones
questions.q: Which marking is the smaller anterior bump near the head of the humerus, serving as a muscle attachment?
questions.why: The proximal humerus has two tubercles, small rounded bumps for muscle attachment. The lesser tubercle is the smaller one, facing forward (anteriorly), and the greater tubercle is the larger one on the lateral side. The intertubercular sulcus runs between them.
notes: The greater tubercle is the larger bump on the lateral side of the proximal humerus. Choose it for a question about the lateral bump near the head.
The medial epicondyle is at the distal end of the humerus near the elbow. It would be right for a question about the inner elbow bump.
The deltoid tuberosity is on the middle of the shaft, well below the head. Pick it for a question about where the deltoid attaches.
Correct. The lesser tubercle is the anterior bump near the head.

questions.topic: Pectoral girdle and upper limb bones
questions.q: Which carpal bone in the distal row lies between the trapezium and the capitate and meets the second metacarpal?
questions.why: The distal row runs trapezium, trapezoid, capitate, and hamate from the thumb side. The trapezoid is the small second bone in that row, wedged between the trapezium and the capitate. It meets the base of the second metacarpal, the one for the index finger.
notes: The hamate is at the little-finger end of the distal row and has a hook. Choose it for a question about the medial-most distal carpal.
The scaphoid is in the proximal row, next to the radius. Pick it for a question about the carpal most often fractured.
Correct. The trapezoid lies between the trapezium and capitate.
The lunate is also in the proximal row, in the middle, and it is the carpal most often dislocated. It would be right for a question about that injury.

questions.topic: Pectoral girdle and upper limb bones
questions.q: Which three bones meet at the elbow?
questions.why: The elbow is where the arm meets the forearm. The distal humerus meets the ulna at the trochlea and the radius at the capitulum, and the radius and ulna also meet each other at the proximal radioulnar joint. All three bones share one joint capsule.
notes: The femur, tibia, and patella form the knee, the lower limb joint that matches the elbow's position. Students pick it because the knee and elbow are both hinge joints in the middle of a limb.
The radius, ulna, and carpals meet in the wrist region. Pick this set for a question about the wrist.
Correct. The humerus, radius, and ulna meet at the elbow.
The humerus, scapula, and clavicle meet in the shoulder region. Choose this set for a question about the bones around the shoulder.

questions.topic: Pectoral girdle and upper limb bones
questions.q: Which list traces the bones of the upper limb in order from the shoulder joint to a fingertip, not counting the girdle?
options: Humerus, carpal, radius and ulna, metacarpal, phalanges
Humerus, radius and ulna, metacarpal, carpal, phalanges
Humerus, radius and ulna, carpal, metacarpal, phalanges
questions.why: The limb runs arm, forearm, wrist, palm, then fingers. That means the humerus first, then the radius and ulna, then a carpal bone of the wrist, then a metacarpal in the palm, and finally the phalanges of a finger. Meta means beyond, so the metacarpals come right after the carpals.
notes: This list places the carpals before the forearm bones. The wrist lies between the forearm and the palm, so the carpals must come after the radius and ulna.
This list swaps the carpal and metacarpal. The carpals form the wrist and the metacarpals form the palm beyond them.
The clavicle belongs to the pectoral girdle, which the question excludes, and this list also skips the carpals. Choose a clavicle-first list only for a path that starts at the sternum.
Correct. Humerus, radius and ulna, carpal, metacarpal, then phalanges.
questions.answerText: Humerus, radius and ulna, carpal, metacarpal, phalanges

questions.topic: Pectoral girdle and upper limb bones
questions.q: Which list names the distal row of carpal bones in order from the thumb side to the little-finger side?
questions.why: The distal row starts at the thumb with the trapezium, which meets the first metacarpal, then the trapezoid, then the large capitate, and ends with the hooked hamate on the little-finger side. The mnemonic Here Comes The Thumb gives the row in reverse, starting from the little-finger side: hamate, capitate, trapezoid, trapezium.
notes: Scaphoid, lunate, triquetrum, and pisiform make up the proximal row, not the distal row. Choose this list for the proximal row.
This order swaps the trapezoid and trapezium. The trapezium is the one next to the thumb, so it comes first from the thumb side.
This is the correct row listed in the opposite direction, from the little-finger side to the thumb. It would be right if the question asked for that direction.
Correct. Trapezium, trapezoid, capitate, and hamate run from the thumb side.

questions.topic: Pectoral girdle and upper limb bones
questions.q: Which set correctly names the girdle bone that forms the shoulder joint, the bone of the arm, and the socket where they meet?
options: The clavicle, the humerus, and the acromion
The scapula, the ulna, and the olecranon fossa
The clavicle, the radius, and the trochlear notch
The scapula, the humerus, and the glenoid cavity
questions.why: The shoulder joint, or glenohumeral joint, is where the head of the humerus sits in the glenoid cavity of the scapula. The scapula is the girdle bone that carries the socket, and the humerus is the single bone of the arm. The clavicle braces the shoulder but does not form part of this joint.
notes: The clavicle meets the acromion at the acromioclavicular joint, but it does not hold the humeral head. Choose this set for a question about the joint at the top of the shoulder.
The ulna is a forearm bone, and the olecranon fossa is a pit on the humerus at the elbow. Pick this combination for a question about elbow extension.
The clavicle and radius never articulate, and the trochlear notch is on the ulna at the elbow. This set mixes bones from different regions, so it fits no single joint.
Correct. The scapula and humerus meet at the glenoid cavity.
questions.answerText: The scapula, the humerus, and the glenoid cavity

questions.topic: Pectoral girdle and upper limb bones
questions.q: Which statement correctly matches each forearm bone to the markings at its wrist end?
options: Radius: lateral styloid process and ulnar notch. Ulna: medial styloid process
Radius: lateral styloid process and ulnar notch. Ulna: trochlear notch
Radius: lateral styloid process and radial notch. Ulna: medial styloid process
Radius: medial styloid process and radial notch. Ulna: lateral styloid process
questions.why: At the wrist, each forearm bone ends in a styloid process on its own side: lateral for the radius and medial for the ulna. The radius also has an ulnar notch on its medial side, which receives the head of the ulna at the distal radioulnar joint. Notches are named for the bone that fits into them.
notes: Correct. The radius carries the lateral styloid process and the ulnar notch, and the ulna carries the medial styloid process.
The trochlear notch is at the elbow end of the ulna, where it grips the trochlea of the humerus. Pick it for a question about the elbow hinge.
The radial notch is a feature of the proximal ulna that holds the head of the radius at the elbow. Choose it for a question about the proximal radioulnar joint.
This reverses the sides of the styloid processes and puts the radial notch on the radius. The radial notch is on the ulna at the elbow, and the radius is the lateral bone.
questions.answerText: Radius: lateral styloid process and ulnar notch. Ulna: medial styloid process

questions.topic: Pectoral girdle and upper limb bones
questions.q: Which path correctly traces the bony connections from the manubrium of the sternum out to the shoulder socket?
options: Manubrium to the acromial end of the clavicle, sternal end to the acromion, then the glenoid cavity
Manubrium to the sternal end of the clavicle, acromial end to the acromion, then the glenoid cavity
Manubrium to the sternal end of the clavicle, acromial end to the coracoid process, then the glenoid cavity
Manubrium to the scapula, scapula to the clavicle, then the clavicle's glenoid cavity
questions.why: The clavicle is the bridge. Its medial (sternal) end meets the manubrium at the sternoclavicular joint, and its lateral (acromial) end meets the acromion of the scapula at the acromioclavicular joint. The scapula then carries the glenoid cavity, the socket for the head of the humerus.
notes: This swaps the two ends of the clavicle. The sternal end is medial and meets the sternum, while the acromial end is lateral and meets the acromion.
Correct. Manubrium, clavicle, acromion, then the glenoid cavity of the scapula.

The coracoid process is a hook on the front of the scapula. Ligaments tie it to the clavicle, but the clavicle forms its joint with the acromion, so choose the coracoid for a question about the anterior hook.
The scapula does not touch the manubrium; it reaches the trunk only through the clavicle and muscles. The glenoid cavity is also a scapular feature, not part of the clavicle.
questions.answerText: Manubrium to the sternal end of the clavicle, acromial end to the acromion, then the glenoid cavity

questions.topic: Pectoral girdle and upper limb bones
questions.q: Which statement correctly compares how the radius and ulna meet the humerus at the elbow?
options: Both bones grip the trochlea, and neither meets the capitulum
The ulna grips the trochlea, and the radius meets the capitulum
The radius grips the trochlea, and the ulna meets the capitulum
The ulna grips the capitulum, and the radius meets the olecranon fossa
questions.why: At the elbow the medial ulna wraps its trochlear notch around the spool-shaped trochlea, forming the hinge. The lateral radius rests its disc-shaped head against the rounded capitulum. In anatomical position the medial bone pairs with the medial surface and the lateral bone with the lateral surface.
notes: Only the ulna grips the trochlea; the radius has its own partner, the capitulum. Students pick this when they remember the hinge but forget the radius also touches the humerus.
Correct. The ulna grips the trochlea, and the radius meets the capitulum.
This swaps the partners. The radius is lateral and meets the lateral capitulum, while the ulna is medial and grips the medial trochlea.
The ulna does not touch the capitulum, and the olecranon fossa receives the ulna's olecranon, not the radius. This mixes up both bones' partners.
questions.answerText: The ulna grips the trochlea, and the radius meets the capitulum

questions.topic: Pectoral girdle and upper limb bones
questions.q: In anatomical terms, which region of the upper limb spans from the elbow to the wrist?
questions.why: Anatomy divides the upper limb into four parts: the pectoral girdle, the arm (shoulder to elbow), the forearm (elbow to wrist), and the hand. The forearm, or antebrachium, contains the radius and ulna. In everyday speech arm can mean the whole limb, but in anatomy it means only the part with the humerus.
notes: Correct. The forearm spans the elbow to the wrist.
The pectoral girdle is the clavicle and scapula, which attach the limb to the trunk. It would be right for a question about the shoulder girdle.
The hand spans the wrist to the fingertips and contains the carpals, metacarpals, and phalanges. Pick it for a question about the region beyond the wrist.
The arm, or brachium, spans the shoulder to the elbow and contains only the humerus. Choose it for a question about the region above the elbow.

questions.topic: Pectoral girdle and upper limb bones
questions.q: What is the fibrous sheet that spans the shafts of the radius and ulna, binding them together?
questions.why: The interosseous membrane is a sheet of dense connective tissue stretched between the shafts of the radius and ulna. Interosseous means between bones. It holds the two forearm bones together as a fibrous joint, a syndesmosis, and gives forearm muscles a broad surface for attachment.
notes: The periosteum is the membrane covering the outer surface of each bone. It wraps a single bone rather than connecting two, so choose it for a question about the bone's outer covering.
Correct. The interosseous membrane joins the radius and ulna along their shafts.
The flexor retinaculum is a fibrous band across the front of the wrist that roofs the carpal tunnel. Choose it for a question about the carpal tunnel.
Articular cartilage is the smooth hyaline cartilage on joint surfaces at the ends of bones, not a sheet between shafts. Pick it for a question about the lining of a synovial joint.

questions.topic: Pectoral girdle and upper limb bones
questions.q: Which forearm bone lies on the medial, little-finger side?
questions.why: In anatomical position, the ulna lies on the medial side of the forearm, in line with the little finger. The radius lies on the lateral, thumb side. The ulna is the bone that forms the point of the elbow with its olecranon.
notes: The radius is the lateral forearm bone on the thumb side. Choose it for a question about the thumb side.
The humerus is the bone of the arm, above the elbow, not a forearm bone. Pick it for a question about the region from the shoulder to the elbow.
The fibula is the lateral bone of the leg, in the lower limb. Students mix it up with the ulna because both are the thinner partner in a two-bone limb segment.
Correct. The ulna is on the medial, little-finger side.

questions.topic: Pectoral girdle and upper limb bones
questions.q: Which border of the scapula runs closest and parallel to the vertebral column?
questions.why: The scapula is a triangle with three borders. The medial border faces the spine, which is why it is also called the vertebral border. The lateral border faces the armpit (axilla) and is called the axillary border, and the short superior border runs along the top.
notes: The superior border is the short top edge of the scapula, near the suprascapular notch. Pick it for a question about the upper edge of the triangle.
Correct. The medial border is the vertebral border closest to the spine.
The inferior angle is the lowest point of the triangle, where the medial and lateral borders meet, not a border itself. It would be right for a question about the bottom tip of the scapula.
The lateral border faces the armpit and runs down from the glenoid cavity. Choose it for a question about the axillary border.

questions.topic: Pectoral girdle and upper limb bones
questions.q: How are the eight carpal bones arranged in the wrist?
options: In a proximal row of five and a distal row of three
questions.why: The carpals form two rows of four. The proximal row (scaphoid, lunate, triquetrum, pisiform) meets the forearm, and the distal row (trapezium, trapezoid, capitate, hamate) meets the metacarpals. The mnemonic So Long To Pinky, Here Comes The Thumb lists the proximal row and then the distal row.
notes: One row of eight would leave no separation between the bones meeting the forearm and those meeting the palm. The carpals are always described in two rows.
Four rows of two does not match the wrist; there are only a proximal and a distal row. Students pick it when they remember the numbers two and four but swap them.
A split of five and three mixes up the rows. Each row has exactly four bones, so a five and three split comes from misplacing one bone.
Correct. The carpals sit in two rows of four.

questions.topic: Pectoral girdle and upper limb bones
questions.q: How many metacarpal bones form the palm of one hand?
questions.why: There are five metacarpals, one leading to each digit, numbered 1 to 5 starting at the thumb. They lie inside the palm between the carpals and the phalanges. Their rounded heads form the knuckles of a closed fist.
notes: Eight is the number of carpal bones in the wrist. Pick it for a question about the wrist.
Fourteen is the number of phalanges in one hand. It would be right for a question about the finger bones.
Three is the number of phalanges in each finger other than the thumb. Choose it for a question about the bones in one finger.
Correct. Five metacarpals form the palm.

questions.topic: Pectoral girdle and upper limb bones
questions.q: Which carpal bone, in the middle of the proximal row, is the one most frequently dislocated?
questions.why: The lunate is a moon-shaped carpal in the center of the proximal row, between the scaphoid and the triquetrum. It is the carpal most frequently dislocated, usually pushed toward the palm, where it can crowd the carpal tunnel. Lunate means moon-shaped.
notes: Correct. The lunate is the carpal most frequently dislocated.
The capitate is the largest carpal, in the middle of the distal row. Pick it for a question about the largest carpal bone.
The hamate is at the little-finger end of the distal row and has a hook-shaped process. It would be right for a question about the hooked carpal.
The scaphoid is the proximal-row carpal on the thumb side, and it is the one most often fractured rather than dislocated. Choose it for a question about the most common carpal fracture.

questions.topic: Pectoral girdle and upper limb bones
questions.q: Which marking is the larger lateral bump near the head of the humerus, a muscle attachment?
questions.why: The greater tubercle is the larger of the two bumps at the proximal humerus, sitting on the lateral side just beyond the head. Several rotator cuff muscles attach to it. It forms the rounded outer contour of the shoulder below the acromion.
notes: The lateral epicondyle is on the lateral side but at the distal end, near the elbow. Pick it for a question about the outer bump of the elbow.
The lesser tubercle is the smaller bump on the anterior side near the head. Choose it for a question about the anterior tubercle.
Correct. The greater tubercle is the larger lateral bump near the head.
The capitulum is the rounded joint surface at the distal end that meets the radius. It would be right for a question about the elbow joint surfaces.

questions.topic: Pectoral girdle and upper limb bones
questions.q: Which roughened bump on the radius, just below its neck, serves as a muscle attachment?
questions.why: The radial tuberosity is a rough, oval bump on the medial front of the proximal radius, just below the neck. The tendon of the biceps brachii attaches there. As with all tuberosities, its rough surface marks where a strong tendon pulls on the bone.
notes: Correct. The radial tuberosity lies just below the neck of the radius.
The radial styloid process is at the distal end of the radius, on the lateral side of the wrist. Pick it for a question about the lateral wrist bump.
The ulnar notch is a joint surface at the distal radius that receives the head of the ulna. It would be right for a question about the distal radioulnar joint.
The deltoid tuberosity is on the shaft of the humerus, not the radius. Choose it for a question about the deltoid's attachment.

questions.topic: Pectoral girdle and upper limb bones
questions.q: Which carpal bone is the largest?
questions.why: The capitate is the largest carpal bone. It sits in the center of the distal row, between the trapezoid and the hamate, and its rounded head fits into a hollow formed by the scaphoid and lunate. It lines up with the third metacarpal, the long bone of the middle finger.
notes: Correct. The capitate is the largest carpal.
The scaphoid is the carpal most often fractured, not the largest. Pick it for a question about a fall on an outstretched hand.
The pisiform is the smallest carpal, a pea-shaped bone on the little-finger side of the proximal row. Choose it for a question about the smallest carpal.
The lunate is the carpal most frequently dislocated. It would be right for a question about that injury.

questions.topic: Pectoral girdle and upper limb bones
questions.q: Which small bump on the scapula sits just above the glenoid cavity?
questions.why: The supraglenoid tubercle is a small bump at the top edge of the glenoid cavity. Supra means above, so its name tells you its position relative to the socket. The tendon of the long head of the biceps brachii attaches there.
notes: The infraglenoid tubercle is the bump just below the glenoid cavity. Choose it for a question using infra, meaning below.
Correct. The supraglenoid tubercle is just above the glenoid cavity.
The coracoid process is a larger hook that projects forward from the scapula, medial to the glenoid cavity. Pick it for a question about the anterior hook below the clavicle.
The superior angle is the upper medial corner of the scapula, far from the glenoid cavity. It would be right for a question about the corners of the scapular triangle.

questions.topic: Pectoral girdle and upper limb bones
questions.q: The acromial end of the clavicle articulates with which structure?
options: The coracoid process of the scapula
questions.why: The acromial end is the flattened lateral end of the clavicle. As its name suggests, it meets the acromion of the scapula, forming the acromioclavicular joint at the top of the shoulder. The medial end does the opposite job, meeting the manubrium.
notes: The coracoid process lies just below the lateral clavicle and is tied to it by strong ligaments, but it does not form the joint. Pick it for a question about the anterior hook of the scapula.
The manubrium meets the sternal, or medial, end of the clavicle. Choose it for a question about the sternal end.
Correct. The acromial end meets the acromion.
The head of the humerus sits in the glenoid cavity of the scapula and never touches the clavicle. It would be right for a question about the shoulder joint.

questions.topic: Pectoral girdle and upper limb bones
questions.q: Which small pit on the anterior distal humerus, just above the capitulum, receives the head of the radius when the elbow bends fully?
questions.why: The radial fossa is a shallow pit on the front of the humerus above the capitulum. When the elbow is fully bent, the rim of the radial head moves up into it. It is the lateral partner of the coronoid fossa, which sits above the trochlea and receives the ulna.
notes: The coronoid fossa is the pit above the trochlea, on the medial side of the front of the humerus, and it receives the coronoid process of the ulna. Choose it for the ulna during elbow flexion.
The radial groove is a shallow groove on the posterior shaft of the humerus where the radial nerve runs. It would be right for a question about that nerve's path, not a pit at the elbow.
Correct. The radial fossa receives the radial head during full flexion.
The olecranon fossa is the deep pit on the back of the humerus that receives the olecranon when the elbow straightens. Pick it for a question about elbow extension.

questions.topic: Pectoral girdle and upper limb bones
questions.q: Which projection on the lateral side of the distal humerus sits just above the capitulum?
questions.why: The lateral epicondyle is a projection on the outer side of the distal humerus, just above the capitulum. It is smaller than the medial epicondyle and serves as an attachment for many forearm muscles. Each epicondyle sits above its matching articular surface: lateral above the capitulum, medial above the trochlea.
notes: The medial epicondyle is on the inner side, above the trochlea. Choose it for a question about the medial elbow bump.
The greater tubercle is also lateral, but it is at the proximal end of the humerus near the shoulder. Pick it for a question about the lateral bump near the head.
Correct. The lateral epicondyle lies above the capitulum.
The deltoid tuberosity is on the lateral middle of the shaft, well above the elbow. It would be right for a question about the deltoid attachment.

questions.topic: Pectoral girdle and upper limb bones
questions.q: When the elbow bends fully, the coronoid process of the ulna fits into which pit on the humerus?
questions.why: The coronoid fossa is a small pit on the anterior distal humerus, just above the trochlea. When the elbow flexes, the coronoid process on the front of the ulna slides up into it. Each process of the proximal ulna has a matching fossa on the humerus: coronoid in front for flexion and olecranon behind for extension.
notes: The olecranon fossa is on the back of the humerus and receives the olecranon when the elbow straightens. Choose it for a question about elbow extension.
The glenoid cavity is the shoulder socket on the scapula, not a pit at the elbow. It would be right for a question about where the humeral head sits.
Correct. The coronoid process fits the coronoid fossa during flexion.
The radial fossa is the lateral pit above the capitulum that receives the head of the radius during flexion. Pick it for a question about the radius.

questions.topic: Pectoral girdle and upper limb bones
questions.q: Which marking of the ulna wraps around the trochlea of the humerus to form the elbow hinge?
questions.why: The trochlear notch is a deep, C-shaped curve at the proximal end of the ulna, framed by the olecranon behind and the coronoid process in front. It hugs the spool-shaped trochlea, which lets the elbow bend and straighten in one plane. The notch is named for the structure that fits into it.
notes: Correct. The trochlear notch grips the trochlea.
The olecranon fossa is a pit on the humerus, not a marking of the ulna. Pick it for a question about where the olecranon rests when the elbow straightens.
The radial notch is a smaller surface on the lateral side of the proximal ulna that holds the head of the radius. Choose it for a question about the proximal radioulnar joint.
The ulnar notch is on the distal radius at the wrist, where it receives the head of the ulna. It would be right for a question about the distal radioulnar joint.

questions.topic: Pectoral girdle and upper limb bones
questions.q: Which marking of the radius projects on the lateral, thumb side of the wrist?
options: The styloid process of the radius
questions.why: The radial styloid process is a pointed projection at the distal end of the radius, on its lateral side. You can feel it on the thumb side of the wrist. The ulna has its own styloid process on the medial side, so each forearm bone has a styloid process on its own side.
notes: The head of the radius is at the elbow end, where it meets the capitulum. It would be right for a question about the proximal radius.
The radial tuberosity is at the proximal end of the radius, near the elbow. Pick it for a question about a muscle attachment just below the radial neck.
The ulnar notch is also at the distal radius, but on the medial side, where it receives the head of the ulna. Choose it for a question about the distal radioulnar joint.
Correct. The radial styloid process is on the lateral side of the wrist.
questions.answerText: The styloid process of the radius

questions.topic: Pectoral girdle and upper limb bones
questions.q: Which humeral marking is an oblique groove on the posterior shaft, along which the radial nerve runs?
questions.why: The radial groove is a shallow groove that spirals obliquely across the back of the humeral shaft. The radial nerve runs in it, close to the bone. Because the nerve lies right against the bone here, a fracture of the shaft can injure it.
notes: The anatomical neck is a groove just below the head, at the top of the bone, not along the shaft. Pick it for a question about the edge of the humeral head.
Correct. The radial nerve runs in the radial groove.
The olecranon fossa is a deep pit at the distal end of the posterior humerus. It would be right for a question about where the olecranon rests when the elbow straightens.
The intertubercular sulcus is a groove on the front of the proximal humerus, between the tubercles, holding a biceps tendon. Choose it for a question about that anterior groove.

questions.topic: Pectoral girdle and upper limb bones
questions.q: Which carpal bones make up the distal row of the wrist?
questions.why: The distal row is the row next to the metacarpals: trapezium, trapezoid, capitate, and hamate, from the thumb side. In the mnemonic So Long To Pinky, Here Comes The Thumb, the second half (Here Comes The Thumb) gives the distal row from the little-finger side. These bones meet the bases of the five metacarpals.
notes: Correct. The trapezium, trapezoid, capitate, and hamate form the distal row.
This set also mixes rows, pairing the scaphoid and triquetrum from the proximal row with two distal bones. It does not match either row.
Scaphoid, lunate, triquetrum, and pisiform make up the proximal row, next to the forearm. Choose this set for the proximal row.
This set mixes rows, adding the lunate and pisiform from the proximal row. Students make this mistake when they recall the names without their positions.

questions.topic: Pectoral girdle and upper limb bones
questions.q: How many phalanges does the thumb have, and how many does each of the other fingers have?
options: The thumb has three, and each finger has two
The thumb and each finger have two
The thumb has two, and each finger has three
The thumb and each finger have three
questions.why: The thumb, or pollex, has only two phalanges, a proximal and a distal, because it lacks a middle phalanx. Each of the other four fingers has three: proximal, middle, and distal. That is why the hand has fourteen phalanges in total.
notes: This reverses the counts. The thumb is the short digit with fewer phalanges, not more.
Giving every finger two would mean no finger has a middle phalanx. This count fits only the thumb.
Correct. Two in the thumb and three in each finger.
Giving the thumb three would mean it has a middle phalanx, which it does not. This would add up to fifteen phalanges per hand instead of fourteen.
questions.answerText: The thumb has two, and each finger has three

questions.topic: Pectoral girdle and upper limb bones
questions.q: Which hollow lies below the spine on the posterior surface of the scapula?
questions.why: The spine of the scapula divides the back of the bone into two hollows. Infra means below, so the infraspinous fossa is the larger hollow beneath the spine. The infraspinatus muscle, one of the rotator cuff muscles, fills it.
notes: The supraspinous fossa is the smaller hollow above the spine. Choose it for a question using supra, meaning above.
The subscapular fossa is on the anterior surface, facing the ribs. Pick it for a question about the front of the scapula.
The glenoid cavity is the shoulder socket at the lateral angle, not a hollow on the back of the blade. It would be right for a question about where the humeral head sits.
Correct. The infraspinous fossa lies below the spine.

questions.topic: Pectoral girdle and upper limb bones
questions.q: A cyclist falls onto an outstretched arm and breaks the slender S-shaped bone running across the top of the chest, most often in its middle third. Which bone is broken?
questions.why: The clavicle is a slender, S-shaped strut that runs from the sternum to the shoulder just under the skin. In a fall on the shoulder or an outstretched arm, force travels up the limb and into the clavicle, which often breaks in its middle third. It is one of the most commonly broken bones in the body.
notes: Correct. The S-shaped bone across the top of the chest is the clavicle.
The first rib is a short, flat rib tucked behind the clavicle, not an S-shaped bone across the top of the chest. Pick it for a question about the rib that articulates with the manubrium.
The humerus is the long bone of the arm, which runs vertically, not across the chest. It would be right for a question about a fracture at the surgical neck or shaft.
The scapula is a flat triangular bone on the upper back, padded by thick muscle, so it rarely breaks in a simple fall. Choose it for a question about the shoulder blade.

questions.topic: Pectoral girdle and upper limb bones
questions.q: An older adult breaks the humerus near the shoulder, and the doctor checks for nerve injury because the axillary nerve runs right beside the break. Which part of the humerus is fractured?
questions.why: The surgical neck is the narrowing below the greater and lesser tubercles, and it is a common fracture site in falls. The axillary nerve wraps around the back of the humerus at this level, so a break here can stretch or injure it. That is why a surgical neck fracture is checked for nerve damage.
notes: The capitulum is at the distal end of the humerus, at the elbow, not near the shoulder. It would be right for a question about where the radius meets the humerus.
The anatomical neck is the groove just below the head, above the tubercles, and it breaks much less often. Choose it for a question about the edge of the humeral head.
Correct. The axillary nerve runs beside the surgical neck.
The deltoid tuberosity is a muscle attachment on the middle of the shaft, below the level where the axillary nerve wraps the bone. Pick it for a question about where the deltoid inserts.

questions.topic: Pectoral girdle and upper limb bones
questions.q: A scaphoid fracture that is missed on the first X-ray may never heal properly. Which feature of the scaphoid explains this?
options: It is a sesamoid bone inside a tendon
It sits in the distal row, away from the radius
It is the largest carpal, so it heals slowly
questions.why: Bone heals by bringing in blood, cells, and nutrients to the break. The scaphoid has a poor blood supply, and in many people the vessels enter only at one end, so a break can cut off part of the bone. Without treatment, that part may not heal and can even die, which is why scaphoid injuries are taken seriously.
notes: The sesamoid carpal is the pisiform, a pea-shaped bone on the little-finger side. Pick it for a question about the smallest carpal.
The scaphoid is in the proximal row and meets the radius directly. Students pick this when they mix it up with the trapezium, the thumb-side bone of the distal row.
The largest carpal is the capitate, not the scaphoid, and size does not explain poor healing. Choose the capitate for a question about the largest carpal.
Correct. The scaphoid's poor blood supply limits healing.

questions.topic: Pectoral girdle and upper limb bones
questions.q: The pectoral girdle attaches to the axial skeleton only at the small sternoclavicular joint, and the scapula is held mainly by muscles. What does this loose attachment give the upper limb?
options: A wide range of motion at the shoulder
A weight-bearing base like the pelvic girdle
The most stable joint in the body
A scapula fixed tightly against the ribs
questions.why: With only one small joint linking it to the trunk, the pectoral girdle can glide and tilt freely over the back of the rib cage. The scapula moves along with the arm, adding to the reach of the shoulder joint. The trade-off is less stability, which suits a limb built for reaching and handling objects rather than bearing weight.
notes: Correct. The loose attachment gives the shoulder great mobility.
The pelvic girdle is the weight-bearing one, firmly joined to the sacrum at the sacroiliac joints. Choose a weight-bearing base for a question about the pelvic girdle.
The shoulder region is mobile, not highly stable; a loose girdle and a shallow socket make it prone to dislocation. Students pick this by assuming that important joints must be the most stable.
The scapula is not fixed; it slides over the ribs as the arm moves. A tightly fixed scapula would describe the opposite of how the pectoral girdle works.
questions.answerText: A wide range of motion at the shoulder

questions.topic: Pectoral girdle and upper limb bones
questions.q: Why is the clavicle so prone to fracture in a fall onto an outstretched arm?
options: It is a slender strut that carries force from the arm to the trunk
It is made mostly of cartilage, which snaps easily
It bears the full weight of the trunk when standing
It is buried deep under thick muscle that pins it in place
questions.why: The clavicle holds the shoulder out from the body and is the only bony link between the arm and the axial skeleton. When a person lands on an outstretched hand, the force travels up the arm and through the clavicle toward the sternum. Because the bone is slender and lies just under the skin, it often snaps, usually in its middle third.
notes: Correct. As the strut between arm and trunk, the clavicle takes the force of the fall.
The clavicle is bone, not cartilage. Students may confuse it with the costal cartilages nearby, which are hyaline cartilage connecting the ribs to the sternum.
The weight of the trunk is carried by the vertebral column and passed to the pelvis, not by the clavicle. Choose weight bearing for a question about the lumbar vertebrae or sacrum.
The clavicle lies just under the skin, which is why you can feel its whole length. Thick muscle padding describes bones like the scapula, which rarely break in a simple fall.
questions.answerText: It is a slender strut that carries force from the arm to the trunk

questions.topic: Pectoral girdle and upper limb bones
questions.q: The forearm has two parallel bones, the radius and ulna, instead of one. What movement does this two-bone design make possible?
options: Tilting the wrist toward the thumb or little finger
Bringing the thumb across the palm to the fingertips
Turning the palm up and down as the radius rotates around the ulna
questions.why: Turning the palm down (pronation) and up (supination) happens when the radius rotates around the ulna at the proximal and distal radioulnar joints. When the palm turns down, the radius crosses over the ulna. A single forearm bone could not cross over itself, so this rotation depends on having two bones.
notes: Tilting the wrist side to side happens at the wrist joint and between the carpal bones. It would be right for a question about how the carpals allow wrist motion.
Bending and straightening the elbow happens at the hinge between the humerus and ulna, which would work with one forearm bone. Choose this for a question about the humeroulnar joint.
Bringing the thumb to the fingertips is opposition, which depends on the saddle joint at the base of the thumb. Pick it for a question about the trapezium and first metacarpal.
Correct. Two bones allow the radius to rotate around the ulna.
questions.answerText: Turning the palm up and down as the radius rotates around the ulna

questions.topic: Pectoral girdle and upper limb bones
questions.q: The wrist contains eight small carpal bones instead of one solid block. How does this design help the hand?
options: The carpals produce the rotation that turns the palm up and down
Many small bones gliding on each other let the wrist bend and tilt smoothly while staying stable
Each carpal anchors one digit, so the hand needs eight
Many small bones lock together so the wrist cannot bend
questions.why: Each carpal glides a little against its neighbors, and those small movements add up across many joints. The result is a wrist that can bend forward and back and tilt side to side smoothly. Ligaments binding the bones keep the wrist stable under load at the same time.
notes: Turning the palm up and down is done by the radius rotating around the ulna, not by the carpals. Choose that for a question about pronation and supination.
Correct. Shared gliding among many bones gives smooth, stable wrist motion.
There are five digits, each served by one metacarpal, not one carpal per digit. Pick five for a question about the metacarpals.
The carpals do the opposite of locking; their many small joints allow movement. Students pick this by assuming more bones means more rigidity.
questions.answerText: Many small bones gliding on each other let the wrist bend and tilt smoothly while staying stable

questions.topic: Pectoral girdle and upper limb bones
questions.q: Which joint is the only joint that links the upper limb to the axial skeleton?
questions.why: The sternoclavicular joint is where the sternal end of the clavicle meets the manubrium of the sternum. The sternum is part of the axial skeleton, and the clavicle is part of the appendicular skeleton, so this is the single bony connection between the upper limb and the trunk. Everything else holding the shoulder in place is muscle.
notes: Costovertebral joints connect the ribs to the thoracic vertebrae, both parts of the axial skeleton. They would be right for a question about where the rib heads meet the spine.
Correct. The sternoclavicular joint is the only joint between the upper limb and the axial skeleton.
The acromioclavicular joint joins the clavicle to the acromion, two bones that are both part of the pectoral girdle. Choose it for a question about the joint at the top of the shoulder.
The glenohumeral joint joins the humerus to the scapula, both appendicular bones. Pick it for a question about the shoulder joint proper.

questions.topic: Pectoral girdle and upper limb bones
questions.q: Which bump on the scapula sits just below the glenoid cavity?
questions.why: The infraglenoid tubercle is a roughened bump at the lower edge of the glenoid cavity, on the lateral border of the scapula. Infra means below, so the name places it under the socket. The long head of the triceps brachii attaches there.
notes: The supraglenoid tubercle is the smaller bump just above the glenoid cavity. Choose it for a question using supra, meaning above.
The acromion is the flat process at the tip of the scapular spine, above and behind the glenoid cavity. It would be right for a question about the point of the shoulder.
The inferior angle is the lowest point of the whole scapula, far below the glenoid cavity. Pick it for a question about the bottom tip of the scapular triangle.
Correct. The infraglenoid tubercle lies just below the glenoid cavity.

questions.topic: Pectoral girdle and upper limb bones
questions.q: In bone-marking vocabulary, what is a tuberosity?
options: A hole for vessels or nerves
questions.why: Every bone marking is a projection, a depression, or an opening. A tuberosity is a projection: a large, rough area where a strong tendon attaches, such as the deltoid tuberosity of the humerus or the radial tuberosity. A tubercle is the smaller, rounded version.
notes: A shallow basin is a fossa, a type of depression, such as the olecranon fossa. Choose it for a question about a fossa.
A groove is a sulcus, a type of depression, such as the intertubercular sulcus. It would be right for a question about a sulcus.
A hole for vessels or nerves is a foramen, a type of opening, such as a nutrient foramen. Pick it for a question about a foramen.
Correct. A tuberosity is a large, rough projection.

questions.topic: Pectoral girdle and upper limb bones
questions.q: The olecranon fossa is an example of which kind of bone marking?
options: A tubercle, a small rounded bump
A foramen, a hole for vessels or nerves
An epicondyle, a raised area above a condyle
questions.why: A fossa is a depression, a basin-like hollow in a bone surface. The olecranon fossa on the back of the distal humerus is a deep one that holds the olecranon of the ulna when the elbow straightens. Other examples include the supraspinous and infraspinous fossae of the scapula.
notes: A tubercle is a small rounded bump, a projection, such as the greater tubercle of the humerus. Choose it for a question about a small bump near the humeral head.
A foramen is an opening that passes completely through bone, such as a nutrient foramen. Pick it for a question about a hole for vessels or nerves.
An epicondyle is a projection above a condyle, such as the medial epicondyle of the humerus. It would be right for a question about the bumps on either side of the distal humerus.
Correct. The olecranon fossa is a fossa, a depression.

questions.topic: Pectoral girdle and upper limb bones
questions.q: On an articulated skeleton, a student follows the S-shaped clavicle out to the point of the shoulder. Which end of the clavicle is there, which scapular marking does it meet, and which joint is formed?
options: The sternal end, at the acromion, forming the sternoclavicular joint.
The acromial end, at the acromion, forming the acromioclavicular joint.
The acromial end, at the coracoid process, forming the glenohumeral joint.
The acromial end, at the glenoid cavity, forming the shoulder joint.
questions.why: Work outward from the midline. The medial sternal end meets the manubrium, and the lateral acromial end reaches the shoulder. The point of the shoulder is the acromion, the flat process at the tip of the scapular spine, and the joint between them is the acromioclavicular joint.
notes: The sternal end is the medial end, which meets the manubrium at the sternoclavicular joint, not the shoulder.
Correct. The lateral, acromial end of the clavicle meets the acromion at the acromioclavicular joint.
The coracoid is the hook-like anterior process, and the glenohumeral joint is the shoulder joint between the humerus and glenoid cavity.
The glenoid cavity receives the head of the humerus, not the clavicle. The clavicle meets the acromion.
questions.answerText: The acromial end, at the acromion, forming the acromioclavicular joint.

questions.topic: Pectoral girdle and upper limb bones
questions.q: An X-ray shows a break through the projection just above the distal humeral surface that meets the ulna. Which marking is broken, and which nerve runs just behind it?
options: The lateral epicondyle, with the ulnar nerve behind it.
The medial epicondyle, with the radial nerve behind it.
The lateral epicondyle, with the radial nerve behind it.
The medial epicondyle, with the ulnar nerve behind it.
questions.why: Find the surface first. The distal humeral surface that meets the ulna is the trochlea, the medial spool. The projection just above the trochlea is the medial epicondyle, and the ulnar nerve passes just behind it, the spot called the funny bone.
notes: The lateral epicondyle sits above the capitulum, which meets the radius. The surface meeting the ulna is medial.
The marking is right, but the radial nerve runs in the radial groove on the posterior shaft. The ulnar nerve passes the medial epicondyle.
Both parts are off. The surface that meets the ulna is the medial trochlea, and the nerve behind the medial epicondyle is the ulnar nerve.
