questions.why: A labrum is a ring of fibrocartilage attached around the edge of a socket, which makes the socket deeper and slightly larger. The glenoid labrum surrounds the glenoid cavity of the shoulder, and the acetabular labrum surrounds the acetabulum of the hip. A deeper socket holds the ball more securely.
notes: A bursa is a small fluid-filled sac that reduces friction between tissues near a joint. It would be the answer for the subacromial sac at the shoulder.
Correct. A fibrocartilage rim that deepens a socket is a labrum.
An articular fat pad is a cushion of adipose tissue inside some joints. It is fat, not fibrocartilage, so it would fit a question about fatty cushioning.
A meniscus is also fibrocartilage, but it is a crescent-shaped pad lying between two bone surfaces, as in the knee, not a rim around a socket. Pick it for the C-shaped and O-shaped pads of the knee.

questions.q: An autoimmune disease attacks the cartilage and synovial membrane of the joints, usually starting in small joints and affecting both sides of the body. Which joint disorder is described?
questions.why: Rheumatoid arthritis is an autoimmune disease, meaning the immune system attacks the body's own tissue. It inflames the synovial membrane and destroys the articular cartilage, usually in the small joints first and symmetrically on both sides. That pattern separates it from the wear-and-tear damage of osteoarthritis.
notes: Correct. An autoimmune attack on cartilage and synovial membrane, on both sides, is rheumatoid arthritis.

Osteoarthritis is a progressive loss of joint cartilage from aging and wear, mainly in large weight-bearing joints like the knees and hips. Pick it if the question described wear rather than an immune attack.
Bursitis is inflammation of a bursa, a fluid sac near a joint, usually from overuse or infection. It would fit a question about a single inflamed sac rather than the joint lining.
Gouty arthritis comes from sodium urate crystals deposited in a joint, often at the base of the big toe. It would be the answer for crystal deposits causing sudden joint pain.

questions.q: A joint lets a limb move away from the midline, back toward it, forward and back, and trace a circle with its distal end, but it does not rotate. How many axes of motion are needed for these movements?
questions.why: Abduction and adduction happen around one axis, and flexion and extension happen around a second axis. Circumduction is not a separate axis; it is a blend of those four movements in sequence that makes the distal end trace a circle. Since the joint does not rotate, two axes are enough, which is the pattern of biaxial joints like the condyloid radiocarpal joint.
notes: One axis allows only one pair of movements, such as flexion and extension at a hinge. It cannot produce both side-to-side and forward-and-back motion.
Correct. These movements need two axes, as in a biaxial joint.
A third axis would be needed for rotation around the bone's long axis, which this joint does not do. Pick three if the joint also rotated, as at the shoulder.
No synovial joint moves around four axes. Students land here by counting circumduction as its own axis, when it is really a combination of the other movements.

questions.q: Put the structural classes of joints in this order: no cavity with dense fibrous tissue, then no cavity with cartilage, then a synovial cavity present.
options: Synovial joint, cartilaginous joint, fibrous joint
Cartilaginous joint, fibrous joint, synovial joint
Fibrous joint, cartilaginous joint, synovial joint
Fibrous joint, synovial joint, cartilaginous joint
questions.why: Fibrous joints have no cavity and are held by dense connective tissue rich in collagen. Cartilaginous joints also lack a cavity but are joined by hyaline cartilage or fibrocartilage. Synovial joints are the only class with a synovial cavity, enclosed by an articular capsule.
notes: This is the exact reverse order. The synovial joint is the one with a cavity, so it belongs last, not first.
This swaps the first two. Cartilaginous joints are joined by cartilage, so they match the second description, and fibrous joints match the first.
Correct. Fibrous, then cartilaginous, then synovial.
This puts the synovial joint second, but the second description has no cavity. Only the cartilaginous joint fits no cavity with cartilage.
questions.answerText: Fibrous joint, cartilaginous joint, synovial joint

questions.q: Which description correctly gives the structural class, the functional class, and the synovial joint type of the elbow?
options: A cartilaginous joint, an amphiarthrosis, and a symphysis
A fibrous joint, a synarthrosis, and a suture
A synovial joint, a diarthrosis, and a hinge joint
A synovial joint, an amphiarthrosis, and a ball-and-socket joint
questions.why: The elbow has a synovial cavity and capsule, so structurally it is a synovial joint, and like all synovial joints it is a diarthrosis, freely movable. Its convex and concave surfaces allow only flexion and extension, which makes it a hinge joint. Naming a joint all three ways is exactly what lab practicals ask for.
notes: This describes the pubic symphysis, a slightly movable cartilaginous joint. The elbow has a cavity and moves freely, so none of these labels fit.
This describes an adult skull suture, which is immovable. Pick it for the joints between cranial bones.
Correct. The elbow is a synovial joint, a diarthrosis, and a hinge joint.
The structural class is right, but synovial joints are diarthroses, not amphiarthroses, and the elbow moves in only one plane. The ball-and-socket type would fit the shoulder.
questions.answerText: A synovial joint, a diarthrosis, and a hinge joint

questions.q: Order these three synovial joint types from fewest axes of movement to most: hinge, ball-and-socket, and condyloid.
questions.why: A hinge joint is uniaxial, moving only in flexion and extension. A condyloid joint is biaxial, adding abduction and adduction. A ball-and-socket joint is triaxial, adding rotation as well, so the order from fewest to most axes is hinge, condyloid, ball-and-socket.
notes: This puts the biaxial condyloid joint ahead of the uniaxial hinge joint. The hinge has the fewest axes, so it comes first.
This places the triaxial ball-and-socket joint before the biaxial condyloid joint. Three axes is the most, so ball-and-socket belongs last.
Correct. One axis, then two, then three.
This is the order from most axes to fewest, the reverse of what was asked.

questions.q: The fibrous membrane of a synovial joint's articular capsule attaches to which covering of the bones?
questions.why: The fibrous membrane is the strong outer layer of the articular capsule, made of dense irregular connective tissue. It attaches to the periosteum, the connective tissue membrane covering the outer surface of each bone, so the capsule is continuous with the bones it unites. Thickened bundles of this membrane form the joint's ligaments.
notes: The articular cartilage covers the bone ends inside the joint cavity. The capsule attaches around it, not onto it. Pick it if the question asked what covers the articulating surfaces.
The synovial membrane is the inner layer of the capsule itself, lying against the fibrous membrane, not a bone covering. It would be the answer for the layer that secretes synovial fluid.
The endosteum lines the inner marrow cavity of a bone, not its outer surface. It would fit a question about the membrane inside the medullary cavity.
Correct. The fibrous membrane attaches to the periosteum.

questions.q: Which statement correctly compares extracapsular and intracapsular ligaments of the knee, with an example of each?
options: Extracapsular lies inside the capsule, like the fibular collateral, and intracapsular lies outside, like the anterior cruciate
Extracapsular lies outside the capsule, like the fibular collateral, and intracapsular lies inside, like the anterior cruciate
Extracapsular lies outside the capsule, like the anterior cruciate, and intracapsular lies inside, like the fibular collateral
Both lie inside the capsule and differ only in whether they cross each other
questions.why: Extra means outside and intra means inside, and the names refer to the articular capsule. The collateral ligaments run along the outer sides of the knee, outside the capsule, so they are extracapsular. The cruciate ligaments cross inside the capsule, though synovial folds keep them out of the synovial cavity, so they are intracapsular.
notes: The examples are right, but the definitions are reversed. Extra means outside, so extracapsular ligaments lie outside the capsule.
Correct. Collaterals are extracapsular, and cruciates are intracapsular.
The definitions are right, but the examples are swapped. The cruciate ligaments cross inside the knee, and the collateral ligaments run along its sides.
Only the cruciate ligaments lie inside the capsule. The collateral ligaments lie outside it, so the two groups differ in position, not just in whether they cross.
questions.answerText: Extracapsular lies outside the capsule, like the fibular collateral, and intracapsular lies inside, like the anterior cruciate

questions.q: The distal tibiofibular joint is united by a ligament. How is it classified structurally and functionally, and how does that compare with the knee?
options: A synovial joint and a diarthrosis, the same as the knee
A fibrous syndesmosis and an amphiarthrosis, while the knee is a synovial diarthrosis
A cartilaginous symphysis and an amphiarthrosis, while the knee is a synovial diarthrosis
A fibrous suture and a synarthrosis, while the knee is a synovial diarthrosis
questions.why: At the distal tibiofibular joint the tibia and fibula are bound by the anterior tibiofibular ligament, with no cavity, which makes it a fibrous joint of the syndesmosis type. It allows only slight movement, so it is an amphiarthrosis. The knee, by contrast, has a synovial cavity and capsule and moves freely, so it is a synovial joint and a diarthrosis.
notes: The distal tibiofibular joint has no synovial cavity and moves only slightly, so it is not synovial like the knee. This choice treats every joint in the leg as freely movable.
Correct. The distal tibiofibular joint is a fibrous syndesmosis and an amphiarthrosis, unlike the synovial knee.
The functional class is right, but the bones are joined by a ligament, not a fibrocartilage disc. A symphysis would describe the pubic symphysis.
Sutures are found only between skull bones and are immovable in adults. The distal tibiofibular joint is held by a ligament and gives slightly.
questions.answerText: A fibrous syndesmosis and an amphiarthrosis, while the knee is a synovial diarthrosis

questions.q: What single criterion does the functional classification of joints use?
options: The type of connective tissue present
The degree of movement the joint permits
Whether a synovial cavity is present
The shape of the articulating surfaces
questions.why: The functional classification sorts joints only by how much they move. Immovable joints are synarthroses, slightly movable joints are amphiarthroses, and freely movable joints are diarthroses. The structural classification, by contrast, looks at the cavity and the connecting tissue.
notes: The type of connective tissue is one of the two structural criteria, which separate fibrous, cartilaginous, and synovial joints. Pick it if the question asked about structural classification.
Correct. Functional classification uses the degree of movement.
Whether a synovial cavity is present is the other structural criterion. It would be part of the answer for how joints are classified by structure.
The shape of the articulating surfaces is used to sort synovial joints into six types, such as hinge and pivot. It would fit a question about naming synovial joint types.
questions.answerText: The degree of movement the joint permits

questions.q: Which type of fibrous joint is found only between the bones of the skull?
questions.why: Sutures are fibrous joints found only between skull bones. Thin layers of dense connective tissue join the bones, and their interlocking edges add strength and help absorb shock. Sutures are immovable in adults and slightly movable in infants.
notes: Correct. Sutures occur only between skull bones.
A symphysis is a cartilaginous joint joined by fibrocartilage, like the pubic symphysis. It is not a fibrous joint at all.
A gomphosis is a fibrous joint found in the skull region, but it holds a tooth in its socket rather than joining two skull bones. Pick it if the question asked about teeth.
A syndesmosis is a fibrous joint held by a ligament, like the distal tibiofibular joint in the leg. It would be the answer for a slightly movable fibrous joint outside the skull.

questions.q: Which two types of cartilaginous joint are distinguished by the kind of cartilage that joins the bones?
questions.why: Cartilaginous joints have no cavity and come in two types. A synchondrosis is joined by hyaline cartilage and is immovable, like the epiphyseal growth plate. A symphysis is joined by a broad disc of fibrocartilage and is slightly movable, like the pubic symphysis.
notes: Plane and hinge joints are two of the six types of synovial joint, sorted by surface shape. They would fit a question about synovial joints.
Sutures and gomphoses are both fibrous joints, held by dense connective tissue rather than cartilage. Pick this pair if the question asked for two immovable fibrous joints.
The symphysis is right, but a syndesmosis is a fibrous joint united by a ligament. Students mix them up because the names both start with syn.
Correct. A synchondrosis uses hyaline cartilage and a symphysis uses fibrocartilage.

questions.q: What is the inner layer of the articular capsule called?
questions.why: The articular capsule has two layers. The outer fibrous membrane is tough dense irregular connective tissue, and the inner synovial membrane is areolar connective tissue with elastic fibers that lines the cavity. The synovial membrane secretes synovial fluid.
notes: Correct. The synovial membrane is the inner layer of the capsule.
The articular cartilage covers the bone ends inside the joint. It lines the bone surfaces, not the capsule.
The periosteum covers the outer surface of bone, outside the joint. It is where the fibrous membrane attaches, not a layer of the capsule.
The fibrous membrane is the outer layer of the capsule, which gives it strength and attaches to the periosteum. Pick it if the question asked about the outer layer.

questions.q: What is the main lubricating component of synovial fluid?
questions.why: Synovial fluid is a clear, pale-yellow, viscous fluid made of hyaluronic acid and interstitial fluid. The hyaluronic acid gives the fluid its slippery, slightly thick texture, so it forms a thin film that reduces friction between the cartilage surfaces. The fluid also nourishes the cartilage and thins as the joint moves.
notes: Fibrin is the protein that forms the mesh of a blood clot. It would be the answer for what holds a clot together, not for joint lubrication.
Calcium salts harden the matrix of bone. Calcium deposits in a joint would increase friction, not reduce it.
Collagen is the strong protein fiber of ligaments, tendons, and the fibrous membrane. It gives tissues strength but does not lubricate.
Correct. Hyaluronic acid makes synovial fluid slippery.

questions.q: Which synovial joint type allows rotation, as at the joint between the atlas and the axis?
questions.why: The atlantoaxial joint is a pivot joint. The dens of the axis projects upward into a ring formed by the atlas and a ligament, and the atlas turns around it when you shake your head no. Pivot joints are uniaxial and allow only rotation.
notes: A hinge joint is uniaxial too, but it allows flexion and extension, not rotation. Pick it if the question asked about the elbow or the interphalangeal joints.
A saddle joint has surfaces that are each concave and convex and is biaxial, like the thumb's carpometacarpal joint. It would be the answer for the base of the thumb.
Correct. The atlantoaxial joint is a pivot joint.
A plane joint has flat surfaces that glide, like the intercarpal joints. It would be the answer for gliding, not turning.

questions.q: What is the chief source of stability for the shoulder joint?
questions.why: The shoulder's ligaments add little strength, and its bony socket is shallow. Most of its stability comes from the rotator cuff, the supraspinatus, infraspinatus, teres minor, and subscapularis, whose tendons wrap the joint and hold the humeral head in the glenoid cavity. This is why rotator cuff injuries so often leave the shoulder weak and unstable.
notes: Correct. The rotator cuff muscles are the shoulder's main stabilizers.
The deltoid is the large muscle that caps the shoulder and is the main abductor of the arm. It moves the shoulder powerfully but does not wrap the joint like the cuff tendons do.
The glenohumeral ligaments are three thickenings of the anterior capsule that help only near the limits of motion. Pick them if the question asked which ligaments reinforce the front of the capsule.
The coracohumeral ligament runs from the coracoid process to the greater tubercle and strengthens the top of the capsule. It would be the answer for the ligament reinforcing the superior capsule.

questions.q: Which type of joint best describes the knee (tibiofemoral) joint?
questions.why: The knee is classed as a modified hinge joint. Its main movements are flexion and extension, like a hinge, but the rounded femoral condyles also allow a little rotation when the knee is bent. It is the largest and most complex joint in the body and the one most often injured.
notes: A saddle joint has surfaces that are each concave and convex, like the thumb's carpometacarpal joint. It would be the answer for the base of the thumb.
A pivot joint allows only rotation around one axis, like the atlantoaxial joint. It would be the answer for a joint whose main job is turning.
A ball-and-socket joint has a round head in a cup and moves in all directions, like the hip just above the knee. Pick it if the question asked about the hip.
Correct. The knee is a modified hinge joint.

questions.q: Which form of arthritis is a progressive, degenerative loss of joint cartilage from aging and wear?
questions.why: Osteoarthritis is the gradual wearing away of articular cartilage that comes with age and use. It mainly affects the large weight-bearing joints such as the knees and hips. Unlike rheumatoid arthritis, it is not caused by the immune system.
notes: Correct. Osteoarthritis is degenerative wear of joint cartilage.

Rheumatoid arthritis is an autoimmune disease that inflames the synovial membrane and destroys cartilage, usually starting in small joints on both sides. Pick it if the question described an immune attack.
Gouty arthritis is caused by sodium urate crystals deposited in a joint, often at the base of the big toe. It would be the answer for crystal deposits.
Bursitis is inflammation of a bursa, a fluid sac near the joint, not loss of the cartilage itself. It would fit a question about an inflamed sac from overuse.

questions.q: In gouty arthritis, what deposits in the joints and erodes the cartilage?
questions.why: Gouty arthritis, or gout, happens when sodium urate crystals build up in a joint. The crystals irritate the tissue, causing inflammation and pain, and over time they erode the articular cartilage. A classic site is the joint at the base of the big toe.
notes: Correct. Sodium urate crystals deposit in the joints in gout.
Cholesterol plaques build up in artery walls in atherosclerosis. They would be the answer for a vessel disorder, not a joint disorder.
Fibrin clots form when blood clots, such as after an injury that bleeds into a joint. They are not crystals and do not cause gout.
Calcium phosphate is the mineral that hardens normal bone matrix. It is not the crystal of gout, so pick it if the question asked what makes bone hard.

questions.q: An athlete stretches and tears a ligament, the band of tissue that stabilizes a joint. What is this injury called?
questions.why: A sprain is a stretched or torn ligament. Because ligaments hold bones together and keep the joint stable, a sprained joint is painful, swollen, and often wobbly. Ankle and knee sprains are among the most common joint injuries.
notes: Correct. A stretched or torn ligament is a sprain.
Bursitis is inflammation of a bursa, a fluid-filled sac, usually from overuse. It would be the answer for a swollen sac rather than a torn band.
A strain is a stretched or torn muscle or tendon, not a ligament. Students confuse the two because the words sound alike, so pick strain if the injury were to a muscle.
A dislocation is the displacement of bones out of their normal alignment at a joint. Ligaments may be damaged too, but the defining feature is bones out of place.

questions.q: A synchondrosis at a growth plate is gradually replaced by bone, fusing two parts into one. What is the resulting joint called?
questions.why: A synostosis is a joint where two separate bones, or parts of a bone, have fused completely into one by bone. When growth ends, the hyaline cartilage of the epiphyseal plate is replaced by bone, and the synchondrosis becomes a synostosis. Skull sutures that ossify in adulthood also become synostoses.
notes: A symphysis is a slightly movable cartilaginous joint joined by fibrocartilage, like the pubic symphysis. It stays cartilage and does not fuse.
Correct. When bone replaces the cartilage, the joint becomes a synostosis.
A suture is a fibrous joint between skull bones. A suture can later ossify into a synostosis, but a growth plate never becomes a suture.
A syndesmosis is a fibrous joint held by a ligament, like the distal tibiofibular joint. It would be the answer for a slightly movable fibrous joint.

questions.q: A clinician sees a knee that swelled up immediately after an injury. What does immediate swelling most likely indicate?
questions.why: Swelling right after a knee injury means blood is leaking into the joint from torn vessels, often from a torn ligament such as the ACL. Swelling that appears later, over hours, is usually excess synovial fluid produced as the synovial membrane reacts. The timing of the swelling helps a clinician judge what was damaged.
notes: Correct. Immediate swelling is blood from torn vessels.
Worn articular cartilage is the slow damage of osteoarthritis over years. It would not swell a knee within minutes of an injury.
Excess synovial fluid causes swelling too, but it builds up gradually and is the delayed type. Pick it if the swelling appeared hours after the injury.
Urate crystals cause gouty arthritis, which flares without an injury, often at the big toe. They would be the answer for sudden joint pain with no trauma.

questions.q: The shoulder is the most mobile joint in the body but dislocates more easily than the hip. Which feature of its structure explains this trade-off?
options: Its ligaments are the strongest in the body, which loosens the joint
A shallow socket and loose capsule hold the humeral head loosely
A deep socket grips the humeral head tightly, which strains the capsule
The humeral head is smaller than its socket, so it slips out easily
questions.why: The glenoid cavity is shallow compared with the large humeral head, and the capsule is thin and loose. That design lets the arm move freely in every direction, but bone and ligaments do little to hold the head in place, so the rotator cuff muscles must do most of the work. The hip makes the opposite trade, with a deep socket that gives stability at the cost of range.
notes: The shoulder's ligaments add little strength, which is why the joint relies on muscles. Strong ligaments would tighten a joint, not loosen it.
Correct. A shallow socket and loose capsule give mobility at the cost of stability.
The shoulder's socket is shallow, not deep. A deep socket is a feature of the hip and makes a joint more stable, not less.
The humeral head is actually large relative to the small glenoid cavity. Instability comes from the shallow socket, not from a small head.
questions.answerText: A shallow socket and loose capsule hold the humeral head loosely

questions.q: Synovial joints have a fluid-filled cavity and move freely, while sutures of the adult skull do not move. Why does a joint cavity go along with movement?
options: Movement depends only on the muscles that cross a joint, not on its structure
The cavity holds a glue-like fluid that locks the bones together
Sutures contain more synovial fluid than synovial joints do
The cavity frees the bone ends to move, while fibrous tissue binds sutured bones
questions.why: In a synovial joint, the bone ends are not attached to each other directly. They are separated by a fluid-filled cavity and united only by the surrounding capsule, so they can slide and turn. In a suture, dense connective tissue binds the bone edges tightly with no space between them, which prevents movement.
notes: Muscles produce movement, but the joint's structure sets how much movement is possible. A muscle cannot move bones that are bound together at a suture.
Synovial fluid is a lubricant, not a glue. It reduces friction so the bones move more easily.
Sutures have no synovial cavity or synovial fluid at all. They are fibrous joints.
Correct. A cavity frees the bone ends to move, while fibrous tissue binds sutured bones directly.
questions.answerText: The cavity frees the bone ends to move, while fibrous tissue binds sutured bones

questions.q: Articular cartilage has no blood supply. Why does this cartilage depend on joint movement to stay healthy?
options: Movement wears the cartilage thin so nutrients can pass in from the bone
The cartilage has its own capillaries, so movement is not needed
Movement warms the cartilage so it can make its own nutrients
Movement circulates synovial fluid, which carries nutrients into the cartilage
questions.why: Articular cartilage is avascular, meaning it has no blood vessels. Its oxygen and nutrients come from synovial fluid, which also carries away its wastes. Movement and the pressing and releasing of the cartilage help move fluid in and out of it, so regular joint use supports cartilage health.
notes: Wearing cartilage thin is the damage seen in osteoarthritis, not a way it stays healthy. Thinning harms the joint rather than feeding it.
Articular cartilage has no blood vessels. That is exactly why it relies on synovial fluid for nourishment.
Movement does help synovial fluid thin out, but cartilage cells cannot make nutrients from warmth. They must receive them from the fluid.
Correct. Synovial fluid, moved by joint activity, nourishes the avascular cartilage.
questions.answerText: Movement circulates synovial fluid, which carries nutrients into the cartilage

questions.q: Ligaments connect bone to bone and are built mostly of collagen fibers. Why does this composition suit a ligament's job?
options: Collagen is soft and cushioning, so the ligament absorbs shock
Collagen stretches easily, so the ligament never limits motion
Collagen carries nerve signals that tell the joint when to stop
Collagen resists stretching, so the ligament limits excess motion
questions.why: Ligaments are dense connective tissue packed with collagen fibers, which are very strong when pulled. That strength lets a ligament hold two bones together, steer their movement, and stop the joint from moving past a safe range. Taut ligaments are one of the main factors that limit a joint's range of motion.
notes: Cushioning in a joint comes from articular cartilage and the fibrocartilage menisci. Ligaments resist pulling rather than absorbing compression.
Collagen does not stretch easily. Its strength against pulling is what allows ligaments to limit motion and prevent dislocation.
Nerve signals are carried by nerves, not by collagen. The joint does have nerves for pain and position, but collagen fibers do not conduct signals.
Correct. Strong collagen fibers let ligaments hold bones together and limit motion.
questions.answerText: Collagen resists stretching, so the ligament limits excess motion

questions.q: A hinge joint such as the elbow moves in only one plane, while a ball-and-socket joint moves in several. What explains the difference?
options: The surface shapes: a hinge bends in one plane, while a ball in a cup turns in many
Range of motion depends only on muscles, never on the shape of the joint
A ball-and-socket joint is limited to one plane, while a hinge moves in many
Both shapes allow the same motion, and ligaments alone make the difference
questions.why: The six synovial joint types are defined by the shape of their surfaces, and that shape sets the axes of movement. In a hinge, a convex surface fits a concave one so the bone can only swing back and forth in flexion and extension. A ball in a cup can turn in any direction, giving flexion, extension, abduction, adduction, and rotation.
notes: Correct. Surface shape sets the axes of motion.
Muscles produce movement, but bone shape is one of the main factors that limits range of motion. A muscle cannot rotate a hinge joint that has no surface to rotate on.
This reverses the two joints. The hinge is the uniaxial one, and the ball-and-socket is triaxial.
Ligament tension does affect range of motion, but the surface shapes of a hinge and a ball-and-socket are what give them different numbers of axes.
questions.answerText: The surface shapes: a hinge bends in one plane, while a ball in a cup turns in many

questions.q: Bursae are small fluid sacs placed where tendons and other tissues rub over bone near a joint. Why does inflammation of a bursa cause pain with movement?
options: The bursa normally locks the joint, and swelling releases it too far
A swollen bursa drains all synovial fluid out of the joint cavity
Pain in a joint always comes from bone, never from a fluid sac
The bursa normally cushions friction, so movement presses on the inflamed sac
questions.why: A bursa is a fluid-filled sac that sits between moving tissues, such as a tendon and a bone, to reduce friction. In bursitis, the sac becomes inflamed from overuse, infection, or rheumatoid arthritis. Every movement that slides the tissues over the swollen sac presses on it, causing pain, swelling, and limited movement.
notes: Bursae do not lock joints. Their job is to let tissues slide past each other with less friction.
Swelling of a bursa adds fluid to the sac itself. It does not drain fluid out of the joint cavity.
Bones are not the only source of joint pain. Inflamed soft tissues such as a bursa, tendon, or synovial membrane are common sources too.
Correct. Movement presses on the inflamed bursa that normally cushions friction.
questions.answerText: The bursa normally cushions friction, so movement presses on the inflamed sac

questions.q: The joints between vertebral bodies are cartilaginous joints that allow slight movement and absorb shock, unlike rigid sutures. Why does the fibrocartilage pad between vertebrae suit the spine?
options: The pad is a fluid-filled cavity, so the vertebrae move freely like a synovial joint
The pad binds the vertebrae rigidly, like a suture, so the spine cannot bend
The pad compresses to cushion loads and allows small movements
The pad is made of bone, so it passes shock straight through to the next vertebra
questions.why: The joints between vertebral bodies are symphyses, cartilaginous joints joined by a broad pad of fibrocartilage. The pad gives slightly under load, cushioning the vertebrae when you walk or jump, and allows a small amount of movement at each level. Added up along the column, those small movements let the spine bend and twist.
notes: The intervertebral symphyses have no synovial cavity. Freely movable synovial joints do exist in the vertebral column, but they are the small joints between the vertebral arches, not the pads between the bodies.
A suture is an immovable fibrous joint of the skull. The intervertebral joints are slightly movable, so they do not bind the vertebrae rigidly.
Correct. The fibrocartilage pad cushions loads and allows slight movement.
The pad is fibrocartilage, not bone. Bone would be rigid and would not absorb shock.
questions.answerText: The pad compresses to cushion loads and allows small movements

questions.q: When a joint is held still in a cast for weeks, it often becomes stiff. Which explanation fits this loss of range of motion?
options: Stiffness after a cast comes only from weak muscles, not from changes in the joint
Immobilization floods the capsule with extra synovial fluid
Unused connective tissue tightens, and the cartilage gets less nourishment
The cast causes the bones to fuse into a synostosis
questions.why: A joint needs movement to stay healthy. When it is held still, the capsule and ligaments shorten and tighten, and the articular cartilage gets less fresh synovial fluid, since movement helps move that fluid in and out of the cartilage. After the cast comes off, gentle movement gradually restores range of motion.
notes: Muscles do weaken in a cast, but that is not the only cause. The capsule, ligaments, and cartilage also change, which is why the joint itself feels stiff.
Swelling with extra synovial fluid follows injury or inflammation, not simple rest. Immobilization reduces the circulation of fluid rather than flooding the joint.
Correct. Tightened connective tissue and poorer cartilage nourishment reduce range of motion.
A synostosis forms when bones fuse, such as when a growth plate ossifies. A few weeks in a cast does not fuse a healthy synovial joint.
questions.answerText: Unused connective tissue tightens, and the cartilage gets less nourishment

questions.q: The knee is reinforced by ligaments inside and around it and by cartilage pads. Why does the knee need so much reinforcement?
options: Its bones interlock tightly, so the soft tissue is there only for cushioning
It carries heavy loads, and its bones fit loosely, so soft tissues add stability
The reinforcement stops the knee from bending under load
The knee bears little weight, so its supports mainly guide movement
questions.why: The rounded femoral condyles sit on the fairly flat tops of the tibial condyles, so the bones alone do not hold the knee together. The menisci improve that fit, and the cruciate and collateral ligaments keep the tibia from sliding or bending sideways. These supports are needed because the knee carries much of the body's weight while bending and straightening.
notes: The knee's bones do not interlock tightly. The poor bony fit is the reason ligaments and menisci are so important.
Correct. Heavy loads plus a loose bony fit make the knee depend on ligaments and menisci.
The supports let the knee bend safely rather than stopping it. They limit only abnormal motions such as forward or backward sliding of the tibia.
The knee carries a large share of the body's weight. Its supports are needed for stability, not just to guide motion.
questions.answerText: It carries heavy loads, and its bones fit loosely, so soft tissues add stability

questions.q: Which movement brings a limb toward the midline of the body?
questions.why: Adduction moves a body part toward the midline, as when you lower an outstretched arm back to your side. Its opposite, abduction, moves the part away from the midline. Both happen in the frontal plane.
notes: Abduction moves a limb away from the midline, as when you raise your arm out to the side. Pick it for movement away from the body.
Correct. Adduction brings a limb toward the midline.
Circumduction moves the distal end of a limb in a circle. It combines several movements rather than simply moving toward the midline.
Rotation turns a bone around its own long axis, as when you turn your arm so the palm faces in. It does not change the limb's distance from the midline.

questions.q: In which movement does the distal end of a limb trace a circle while the proximal end stays fixed?
questions.why: Circumduction is the movement of the distal end of a body part in a circle, while the proximal end stays in place. It is a combination of flexion, extension, abduction, and adduction done in sequence. Drawing a circle in the air with a straight arm is circumduction at the shoulder.
notes: Rotation turns a bone around its own long axis without moving its distal end in a circle. Pick it if the question described turning the arm in place.
Adduction moves a limb toward the midline in a straight path. It is one part of circumduction but not the whole circle.
Elevation lifts a body part upward, as in shrugging the shoulders. It would be the answer for a superior movement.
Correct. Tracing a circle with the distal end is circumduction.

questions.q: Rotating the forearm so the palm faces posteriorly is called what?
questions.why: Pronation turns the forearm so the palm faces posteriorly, or downward when the forearm is held out in front. During pronation the radius crosses over the ulna. Supination is the reverse and returns the palm to face anteriorly, as in anatomical position.
notes: Supination turns the palm to face anteriorly, the position of the hand in anatomical position. Pick it for turning the palm forward or up.
Eversion turns the sole of the foot outward. It is a foot movement, not a forearm movement.
Correct. Turning the palm to face posteriorly is pronation.
Opposition moves the thumb across the palm to touch the fingertips. It would be the answer for a thumb movement.

questions.q: Rotating the forearm so the palm faces anteriorly, as in anatomical position, is called what?
questions.why: Supination turns the forearm so the palm faces anteriorly, as it does in anatomical position. In supination the radius and ulna lie parallel. A memory aid is that you hold a bowl of soup with a supinated hand.
notes: Retraction moves a body part back, as when you pull the shoulders back. It would be the answer for squaring the shoulders.
Pronation turns the palm to face posteriorly, crossing the radius over the ulna. Pick it for turning the palm back or down.
Correct. Turning the palm to face anteriorly is supination.
Inversion turns the sole of the foot inward. It is a foot movement, not a forearm movement.

questions.q: Lifting the foot so the toes point upward, decreasing the angle at the ankle, is which movement?
questions.why: Dorsiflexion bends the foot upward at the ankle, bringing the top of the foot (the dorsum) toward the shin. It happens when you walk on your heels or lift your toes off the ground. The opposite movement, pointing the toes down, is plantar flexion.
notes: Correct. Lifting the toes toward the shin is dorsiflexion.
Plantar flexion points the toes downward, as when you stand on tiptoe. Pick it for the movement toward the sole.
Eversion turns the sole of the foot outward. It tilts the foot sideways rather than lifting the toes.
Elevation lifts a body part such as the shoulders or the mandible superiorly. The ankle movements have their own names, dorsiflexion and plantar flexion.

questions.q: Pointing the toes downward, as when standing on tiptoe, is which movement?
questions.why: Plantar flexion bends the foot at the ankle toward the sole (the plantar surface), pointing the toes down. It happens when you stand on tiptoe or push off during walking. Its opposite is dorsiflexion, which lifts the toes toward the shin.
notes: Dorsiflexion lifts the toes upward toward the shin. Pick it for walking on the heels.
Inversion turns the sole of the foot inward. It tilts the foot sideways rather than pointing the toes down.
Correct. Pointing the toes down is plantar flexion.
Protraction moves a body part forward, as when you jut the jaw forward. It would be the answer for forward movement of the mandible or scapula.

questions.q: Turning the sole of the foot to face medially, or inward, is which movement?
questions.why: Inversion turns the sole of the foot to face medially, toward the other foot. Most ankle sprains happen when the foot is forced too far into inversion. The opposite movement, turning the sole outward, is eversion.
notes: Dorsiflexion lifts the toes toward the shin. It bends the foot up rather than turning the sole inward.
Eversion turns the sole to face laterally, away from the midline. Pick it for the outward turn.
Correct. Turning the sole inward is inversion.
Plantar flexion points the toes downward, as on tiptoe. It bends the foot down rather than turning the sole.

questions.q: Turning the sole of the foot to face laterally, or outward, is which movement?
questions.why: Eversion turns the sole of the foot to face laterally, away from the midline. It is the opposite of inversion, which turns the sole inward. These side-to-side movements happen mainly at the joints between the tarsal bones rather than at the ankle hinge.
notes: Plantar flexion points the toes down at the ankle. It bends the foot down rather than turning the sole.
Rotation turns a bone around its own long axis, such as the humerus or femur. The foot's sideways turning has its own names, inversion and eversion.
Inversion turns the sole to face medially, toward the other foot. Pick it for the inward turn.
Correct. Turning the sole outward is eversion.

questions.q: Lifting a body part superiorly, such as shrugging the shoulders, is which movement?
questions.why: Elevation moves a body part upward, as when you shrug the shoulders or close the mouth by raising the mandible. Depression is the opposite, lowering the part again. These terms are used mainly for the scapula and the mandible.
notes: Protraction moves a body part forward in the horizontal plane, as when you jut the jaw out. It would be the answer for forward movement.
Circumduction moves the distal end of a limb in a circle. It would fit a question about drawing circles with the arm.
Correct. Shrugging the shoulders upward is elevation.
Depression lowers a body part, as when you drop the shoulders or open the mouth. Pick it for the downward movement.

questions.q: Moving a body part anteriorly in the horizontal plane, such as jutting the jaw forward, is which movement?
questions.why: Protraction moves a body part forward in the horizontal plane. Jutting the mandible forward and reaching the arms forward, which slides the scapulae around the chest wall, are both protraction. Retraction is the opposite, pulling the part back.
notes: Correct. Moving the jaw forward is protraction.
Elevation lifts a body part upward, such as shrugging the shoulders. It would be the answer for a superior movement.
Rotation turns a bone around its own long axis. It does not slide a part forward.
Retraction pulls a body part backward, as when you squeeze the shoulder blades together. Pick it for the backward movement.

questions.q: Pulling a body part posteriorly in the horizontal plane, such as squaring the shoulders back, is which movement?
questions.why: Retraction moves a body part backward in the horizontal plane. Squeezing the shoulder blades together and pulling the jaw back after jutting it forward are examples. It is the opposite of protraction.
notes: Protraction moves a body part forward, as when you reach forward or jut the jaw. Pick it for the forward movement.
Depression lowers a body part, such as dropping the shoulders or opening the mouth. It would be the answer for a downward movement.
Correct. Pulling the shoulders back is retraction.
Supination turns the forearm so the palm faces anteriorly. It is a forearm rotation, not a backward slide.

questions.q: Moving the thumb across the palm to touch the tips of the other fingers is which movement?
questions.why: Opposition moves the thumb across the palm so its tip meets the tips of the other fingers. It happens at the carpometacarpal joint of the thumb, a saddle joint, and it is what lets us grip and handle small objects.
notes: Circumduction moves the distal end of a part in a circle. The thumb can circumduct, but touching the fingertips is a specific movement with its own name.
Correct. Bringing the thumb across to touch the fingertips is opposition.
Supination turns the forearm so the palm faces anteriorly. It moves the whole hand, not the thumb alone.
Abduction moves a part away from the midline. Moving the thumb away from the palm is abduction of the thumb, not opposition.

questions.q: A patient rolls the ankle so the sole turns inward, and then a therapist turns it outward. Name the two movements in order.
questions.why: Turning the sole inward, toward the other foot, is inversion. Turning it outward is eversion. Rolled ankles usually happen in inversion, which is why the lateral side of the ankle, including the lateral malleolus and its ligaments, is so often injured.
notes: This reverses the order. Inward comes first in the scenario, and inward is inversion.
Dorsiflexion and plantar flexion bend the foot up and down at the ankle. They would fit lifting the toes and then pointing them.
Pronation and supination are forearm movements in this course, turning the palm back and forward. They would be the answer for turning the palm down and then up.
Correct. Inward is inversion, then outward is eversion.

questions.q: Starting in anatomical position, you rotate the forearm so the palm faces backward, then return it. Which sequence of movements is this?
questions.why: In anatomical position the palm faces anteriorly, which is the supinated position. Turning the palm to face posteriorly is pronation, and returning it to face forward is supination. The radius crosses over the ulna in pronation and lies parallel to it in supination.
notes: Correct. Pronation turns the palm back, and supination returns it.
This reverses the order. Turning away from anatomical position comes first, and that first movement is pronation.
Protraction and retraction move a part forward and back, like the jaw or the scapula. They would fit reaching forward and squaring the shoulders.
Inversion and eversion turn the sole of the foot in and out. They would be the answer for foot movements.

questions.q: Reaching the arms forward, then squaring the shoulders back, moves the scapulae through which pair of movements?
questions.why: Reaching forward slides the scapulae forward around the chest wall, which is protraction. Squaring the shoulders back pulls the scapulae toward the spine, which is retraction. Both happen in the horizontal plane.
notes: Rotation turns a bone around its long axis, and circumduction moves a distal end in a circle. Neither describes sliding the scapulae forward and back.
Correct. Forward is protraction, and back is retraction.
This reverses the order. The forward reach comes first, and forward movement is protraction.
Elevation and depression lift and lower the scapulae, as in shrugging and dropping the shoulders. Pick them for up-and-down motion.

questions.q: The cruciate ligaments lie inside the knee's articular capsule. Ligaments in this position are classified as what?
questions.why: Intracapsular ligaments lie inside the articular capsule. The anterior and posterior cruciate ligaments of the knee are the main examples, and synovial folds keep them out of the synovial cavity itself. They cross each other in an X, which is what cruciate means.
notes: Extracapsular ligaments lie outside the capsule, like the collateral ligaments of the knee. Pick it if the question described a ligament on the outer side of the joint.
Collateral ligaments are the extracapsular ligaments on the medial and lateral sides of the knee. They are the cruciates' counterparts outside the capsule.
Articular discs, or menisci, are fibrocartilage pads between the bones, not ligaments. They would be the answer for the C-shaped and O-shaped pads of the knee.
Correct. Ligaments inside the capsule are intracapsular.

questions.q: Which knee ligament crosses within the joint and stops the tibia from sliding backward, which matters most on stairs and inclines?
questions.why: The posterior cruciate ligament, or PCL, is an intracapsular ligament that crosses inside the knee. It stops the tibia from sliding backward under the femur. That job matters most when walking down stairs or inclines, when the femur tends to slide forward on the tibia.
notes: The tibial collateral ligament runs along the medial side of the knee, outside the capsule. It would be the answer for the medial ligament torn in the unhappy triad.
The oblique popliteal ligament strengthens the back of the knee joint from outside. It does not cross within the joint, so it would fit a question about the posterior surface of the capsule.
The anterior cruciate ligament also crosses inside the knee, but it stops the tibia from sliding forward. Pick it if the question asked which ligament is torn most often in serious knee injuries.
Correct. The posterior cruciate ligament stops backward sliding of the tibia.

questions.q: Which knee structure is the more circular, almost O-shaped fibrocartilage disc on the lateral side of the joint?
questions.why: The knee has two menisci resting on the tibial condyles. The lateral meniscus is more circular, close to an O shape, while the medial meniscus is C-shaped. Both are fibrocartilage pads that improve the fit of the femur on the tibia and absorb shock.
notes: The medial meniscus is the C-shaped disc on the medial side. Pick it if the question asked for the C-shaped meniscus or the one torn in the unhappy triad.
Correct. The lateral meniscus is the more circular disc on the lateral side.
The fibular collateral ligament is on the lateral side too, but it is a ligament outside the capsule, not a cartilage disc. It would be the answer for the lateral extracapsular ligament.
The transverse ligament is the band that joins the two menisci at the front. It would be the answer for what connects the medial and lateral menisci.

questions.q: Which band joins the medial and lateral menisci of the knee to each other?
questions.why: The transverse ligament is a short band that runs across the front of the knee joint and connects the medial meniscus to the lateral meniscus. It ties the front edges of the two menisci together. It is easy to confuse with the transverse humeral ligament at the shoulder, which holds a tendon in place instead.
notes: Correct. The transverse ligament joins the two menisci.
The patellar ligament runs from the patella to the tibial tuberosity on the front of the knee. Pick it if the question asked about the continuation of the quadriceps tendon.
The arcuate popliteal ligament strengthens the lower lateral part of the back of the knee. It would be the answer for posterior reinforcement on the lateral side.
The posterior cruciate ligament crosses inside the knee and stops the tibia from sliding backward. It connects the tibia to the femur, not the menisci to each other.

questions.q: An athlete twists a knee, and it is not swollen right away but becomes puffy several hours later. What does this delayed swelling most likely indicate?
options: Fat from the articular fat pads
questions.why: The timing of knee swelling gives a clue to its cause. Swelling that appears immediately is blood from torn vessels. Swelling that builds up over hours is excess synovial fluid, produced as the irritated synovial membrane reacts to the injury.
notes: Articular fat pads are cushions of adipose tissue inside some joints. They do not leak fat into the joint to cause swelling after an injury.
Sodium urate crystals cause gouty arthritis, which flares without an injury, often at the base of the big toe. They would not explain swelling after a twist.
Correct. Delayed swelling is excess synovial fluid.
Blood from torn vessels causes swelling right away, within minutes of the injury. Pick it if the knee swelled immediately.

questions.q: When the elbow is fully flexed, the forearm muscles press against the muscles of the arm and stop further bending. Which factor limiting range of motion is at work?
questions.why: Several factors set the limits of joint movement: the shape and fit of the bones, the tension of the ligaments, contact between soft body parts, and hormones. When the bulk of the forearm meets the bulk of the arm, the soft tissue itself blocks further flexion. That is contact of soft parts, which is why very muscular people often cannot flex the elbow as far.
notes: Correct. Soft tissue pressing against soft tissue is contact of soft parts.
Hormones can loosen joints, as when relaxin loosens the pubic symphysis late in pregnancy. They would be the answer for a change in joint looseness over time, not a mechanical block.
Bone shape limits motion when the bones themselves meet or fit tightly, as when the olecranon of the ulna locks into its fossa during full extension. It would be the answer for that bony stop.
Ligament tension limits motion when ligaments are pulled taut and stop the bones from moving farther. Pick it if a stretched ligament were the limit.

questions.q: Which shoulder ligament holds the tendon of the long head of the biceps brachii in place between the greater and lesser tubercles?
questions.why: The transverse humeral ligament is a narrow band that bridges the groove between the greater and lesser tubercles of the humerus. The tendon of the long head of the biceps brachii runs in that groove, and the ligament holds it in place. It is one of the supporting structures of the shoulder joint.
notes: Correct. The transverse humeral ligament holds the long head of the biceps tendon in its groove.
The glenoid labrum is a rim of fibrocartilage around the glenoid cavity that deepens the socket. It would be the answer for what enlarges the shoulder socket.
The glenohumeral ligaments are three thickenings of the anterior capsule that steady the joint near the limits of motion. They would be the answer for reinforcement of the front of the capsule.
The coracohumeral ligament runs from the coracoid process to the greater tubercle and strengthens the top of the capsule. Pick it if the question asked about the superior capsule.

questions.q: Which shoulder ligament runs from the coracoid process to the greater tubercle of the humerus and strengthens the superior part of the capsule?
questions.why: The coracohumeral ligament is named for the two bones it connects, the coracoid process of the scapula and the humerus. It attaches to the greater tubercle and reinforces the top of the shoulder's articular capsule. Even so, the shoulder's ligaments add little strength overall, and most stability comes from the rotator cuff.
notes: Correct. The coracohumeral ligament runs from the coracoid process to the greater tubercle.
The transverse humeral ligament bridges the greater and lesser tubercles to hold the biceps tendon. Pick it if the question asked what keeps the long head of the biceps in its groove.
The tibial collateral ligament is a knee ligament on the medial side of the joint. It would be the answer for a question about the knee, not the shoulder.
The glenohumeral ligaments are three thickenings on the front of the capsule, not a band from the coracoid process. They would be the answer for anterior reinforcement.

questions.q: The acromioclavicular joint, where the acromion of the scapula meets the clavicle, has flat surfaces that glide slightly. Which type of synovial joint is it?
questions.why: The acromioclavicular joint joins the acromion of the scapula to the lateral end of the clavicle at the top of the shoulder. Its flat articular surfaces slide on each other, which makes it a plane joint. Small gliding movements here let the scapula shift as the arm moves.
notes: Correct. The acromioclavicular joint is a plane joint.
A ball-and-socket joint is the glenohumeral joint just below the acromioclavicular joint. Pick it if the question asked about the shoulder joint itself.
A hinge joint has a convex surface in a concave one and allows flexion and extension, like the elbow. It would be the answer for a joint that bends in one plane.
A pivot joint allows only rotation in a ring of bone and ligament, like the atlantoaxial joint. It would be the answer for a joint that turns.

questions.q: The talocrural joint, where the talus meets the tibia and fibula, is which type of synovial joint?
questions.why: The talocrural joint is the ankle joint. The talus fits between the tibia and the two malleoli, and the joint moves in one plane, allowing dorsiflexion and plantar flexion. Movement in one plane makes it a hinge joint.
notes: A pivot joint allows only rotation, like the atlantoaxial joint. It would be the answer for a joint that turns around one axis.
A ball-and-socket joint moves in every direction, like the hip. The ankle is built to block sideways motion, so it is not a ball-and-socket joint.
Correct. The talocrural joint is a hinge joint.
A plane joint has flat surfaces that glide, like the intertarsal joints just below the ankle. Pick it for the joints between the tarsal bones.

questions.q: The manubriosternal joint is joined by a disc of fibrocartilage and lies in the midline. Which type of cartilaginous joint is it?
questions.why: A symphysis is a cartilaginous joint joined by a broad, flat disc of fibrocartilage, and it is slightly movable. All symphyses lie in the midline of the body. The manubriosternal joint, between the manubrium and the body of the sternum, is one example, along with the pubic symphysis and the joints between vertebral bodies.
notes: A plane joint is a synovial joint with gliding surfaces and a joint cavity. The manubriosternal joint has no cavity, so it is not synovial.
Correct. The manubriosternal joint is a symphysis.
A synchondrosis is joined by hyaline cartilage and is immovable. Pick it for the joint between the first rib and the manubrium or for a growth plate.
A suture is a fibrous joint found only between skull bones. It is not a cartilaginous joint.

questions.q: The first rib is joined to the manubrium by hyaline cartilage, and the joint is immovable. Which type of joint is it?
questions.why: A synchondrosis is a cartilaginous joint in which hyaline cartilage joins the bones, and it is immovable. Besides the epiphyseal growth plate, the joint between the first rib and the manubrium is a classic example. Its rigidity helps anchor the top of the rib cage.
notes: A syndesmosis is a fibrous joint held by a ligament, like the distal tibiofibular joint. It would be the answer for bones united by a ligament, not by cartilage.
A symphysis is joined by fibrocartilage and is slightly movable, like the manubriosternal joint just below. Pick it if the question described a fibrocartilage disc.
A gomphosis is the peg-in-socket fibrous joint of a tooth. It would be the answer for teeth in their sockets.
Correct. The first rib joins the manubrium at a synchondrosis.

questions.q: What is the specific name for extension that continues past the anatomical position, as when you tip your head back to look at the ceiling?
questions.why: Extension increases the angle between bones and returns a part to anatomical position. When the movement keeps going beyond anatomical position, it is called hyperextension. Tipping the head back to look straight up and swinging the arm back behind the body are examples.
notes: Correct. Extension beyond anatomical position is hyperextension.
Circumduction moves the distal end of a part in a circle. It would be the answer for rolling the head in a circle, not tipping it straight back.
Lateral flexion bends the head or trunk sideways in the frontal plane. Pick it if the question described tilting an ear toward the shoulder.
Rotation turns a bone around its own long axis, as when you shake the head no. It would be the answer for turning the head side to side.

questions.q: Bending the trunk sideways in the frontal plane, as when you reach down to touch the side of your knee, is which movement?
questions.why: Lateral flexion is bending the trunk or the head sideways, in the frontal plane. It occurs at the joints of the vertebral column, such as when you tilt your trunk to one side or bring an ear toward a shoulder. Ordinary flexion, by contrast, bends forward in the sagittal plane.
notes: Hyperextension is extension past anatomical position, as in bending backward. It would be the answer for leaning back, not sideways.
Abduction moves a limb away from the midline, as when you raise an arm out to the side. The trunk's sideways bending has its own name, lateral flexion.
Correct. Bending the trunk sideways is lateral flexion.
Rotation turns a part around its long axis, as when you twist the trunk to look behind you. It would be the answer for twisting, not bending.

questions.q: Which movement is a simple back-and-forth or side-to-side sliding of one bone surface on another, with no change in the angle between the bones?
questions.why: Gliding is the simplest movement at a synovial joint. Flat or slightly curved surfaces slide over each other back and forth or side to side, and the angle between the bones does not change. It happens at plane joints, such as the intercarpal and intertarsal joints.
notes: Rotation turns a bone around its own long axis. It would be the answer for turning the head or the humerus in place.
Correct. Sliding without changing the angle is gliding.
Circumduction moves the distal end of a part in a circle, combining several angular movements. It changes angles throughout, so it is not gliding.
Flexion decreases the angle between bones, so it is an angular movement, not a slide. Pick it for bending the elbow or knee.

questions.q: Why does warming up before exercise make the joints move more easily?
options: Movement drains synovial fluid out of the joint so the bones touch
Warming up shortens the ligaments so the joint is tighter
Synovial fluid is gel-like at rest and becomes thinner with movement
Warming up adds new articular cartilage to the bone ends
questions.why: Synovial fluid, made of hyaluronic acid and interstitial fluid, is thick and gel-like when a joint has been at rest. As the joint moves, the fluid thins and spreads as a slippery film between the cartilage surfaces. That is why a few minutes of easy movement before exercise makes the joints feel looser.
notes: Movement spreads synovial fluid over the joint surfaces rather than draining it. Bone ends touching without fluid would increase friction.
Ligaments do not shorten during a warm-up, and a tighter joint would move less freely, not more.
Correct. Synovial fluid thins with movement, which eases the joints.
Articular cartilage does not grow during a warm-up. Its thickness changes only slowly over time, so this cannot explain a quick change in how the joint feels.
questions.answerText: Synovial fluid is gel-like at rest and becomes thinner with movement

questions.q: A person described as double-jointed can bend some joints much farther than usual. What explains this, and what is the trade-off?
options: Shallower sockets in every joint, which make them stiffer
An extra joint in each finger, which makes the fingers weaker
Greater ligament flexibility, which makes the joints less stable
Extra synovial fluid, which makes the cartilage wear faster
questions.why: Double-jointed people do not have extra joints. Their ligaments are more flexible than usual, so the bones can move farther before the ligaments become taut. Because ligament tension is one of the main things holding a joint together, these joints are less stable and dislocate more easily.
notes: A shallow socket would allow more motion, not stiffness, and double-jointedness is about ligaments, not socket shape. This choice mixes two separate ideas.
Double-jointed people have the normal number of joints and phalanges. The name is misleading, which is why students often take it literally.
Correct. Looser ligaments allow more motion but less stability.
Extra synovial fluid is a sign of joint irritation or injury, not the cause of unusual flexibility. It would be the answer for delayed swelling after a knee injury.
questions.answerText: Greater ligament flexibility, which makes the joints less stable

questions.q: A car crash dislocates a person's knee, pushing the tibia forward on the femur. Which vessel behind the knee is most at risk of damage?
questions.why: A dislocated knee is a displacement of the tibia relative to the femur, most often anteriorly. The popliteal artery runs through the popliteal fossa directly behind the knee joint, so it can be stretched or torn when the bones shift. Damage to it can cut off blood flow to the leg and foot, which makes a knee dislocation an emergency.
notes: The femoral artery runs through the thigh and becomes the popliteal artery only as it passes behind the knee. Pick it if the injury were in the thigh.
The dorsalis pedis artery runs on the top of the foot, far from the knee. It is a pulse point for checking blood flow to the foot, not the vessel injured at the knee.
Correct. The popliteal artery lies directly behind the knee and is at risk in a dislocation.
The great saphenous vein is a superficial vein running up the medial side of the leg and thigh. It is not tucked behind the knee joint like the popliteal artery.

questions.q: A bone turning around its own long axis, as when you shake your head no, is which movement?
questions.why: Rotation is the turning of a bone around its own long axis. Shaking the head no rotates the atlas around the dens of the axis. In the limbs, rotation toward the midline is medial rotation and rotation away from it is lateral rotation.
notes: Circumduction moves the distal end of a part in a circle, so the part sweeps out a cone. In rotation the part stays in place and only turns.
Correct. Turning around the long axis is rotation.
Lateral flexion tilts the head or trunk sideways, bringing an ear toward a shoulder. It would be the answer for tilting, not turning.
Abduction moves a limb away from the midline. It would be the answer for raising the arm out to the side.

questions.q: Lowering the mandible to open the mouth, or dropping the shoulders after a shrug, is which movement?
questions.why: Depression moves a body part inferiorly, as when you lower the mandible to open the mouth or drop the shoulders. Elevation is the opposite movement, lifting the part upward. These terms are used mainly for the mandible and the scapula.
notes: Plantar flexion points the toes down at the ankle. It applies to the foot, not the mandible or shoulders.
Correct. Lowering the mandible or the shoulders is depression.
Retraction pulls a part backward in the horizontal plane, as when you square the shoulders. It would be the answer for a backward movement.
Elevation lifts a body part upward, as in shrugging the shoulders or closing the mouth. Pick it for the upward movement.

questions.q: A student argues that any joint without a synovial cavity must be immovable. Which joint disproves this, and how is it classified?
options: An adult skull suture, which is fibrous and immovable.
The elbow joint, which is synovial and freely movable.
The distal tibiofibular joint, fibrous but slightly movable.
The epiphyseal plate, which is cartilaginous and immovable.
questions.why: Structure and function are separate classifications, so check one joint against both. The distal tibiofibular joint is a syndesmosis: it has no synovial cavity and is held by a ligament, so it is fibrous. It still allows slight movement, which makes it an amphiarthrosis and disproves the claim.
notes: An adult suture has no cavity and is immovable, so it fits the student's claim rather than disproving it.
The elbow has a synovial cavity, so it says nothing about joints without one.
Correct. A syndesmosis has no cavity, yet it is slightly movable, an amphiarthrosis.
The epiphyseal plate is a synchondrosis with no cavity, and it is immovable, so it supports the claim.
questions.answerText: The distal tibiofibular joint, fibrous but slightly movable.

questions.q: A lab model shows two bone ends capped with smooth cartilage, enclosed by a capsule around a fluid-filled space. Before you learn the joint's name, what can you say about its functional class?
options: It is a diarthrosis, because all synovial joints move freely.
It is an amphiarthrosis, since cartilage allows only slight give.
It is a synarthrosis, since the capsule binds the bones tightly.
It cannot be classed until its synovial type is known.
questions.why: Use the structure to reach the function. A fluid-filled cavity inside an articular capsule, with articular cartilage on the bone ends, makes this a synovial joint. All synovial joints are diarthroses, freely movable, so the functional class is known before the joint is named.
notes: Correct. A capsule around a fluid-filled cavity makes it synovial, and every synovial joint is a diarthrosis.
Slightly movable joints are syndesmoses and symphyses, which have no cavity. Articular cartilage in a synovial joint does not bind the bones.
Immovable joints are sutures and gomphoses, with no cavity. The capsule here encloses a fluid-filled cavity that allows movement.
The synovial type sets the axes of movement, not the functional class. Every synovial type is a diarthrosis.
questions.answerText: It is a diarthrosis, because all synovial joints move freely.

questions.q: In a gomphosis, which ligament holds the tooth in its bony socket?
questions.why: A gomphosis is a fibrous joint in which a cone-shaped peg, the tooth, is held in a bony socket by the periodontal ligament. It is immovable, a synarthrosis.
notes: The anterior tibiofibular ligament unites the distal tibia and fibula in a syndesmosis, not a tooth in its socket.
Correct. The periodontal ligament holds a tooth in its socket in a gomphosis.
The interosseous membrane is a syndesmosis, a sheet of dense connective tissue binding the shafts of the radius and ulna, or the tibia and fibula. It does not hold a tooth.
The transverse ligament joins the two menisci of the knee to each other.

questions.q: The growth plate and the joint between the first rib and the manubrium are both joined by hyaline cartilage. A student calls both symphyses because they are cartilaginous. What is the correct type, and what decides it?
options: Both are symphyses, because they are slightly movable.
The plate is a synchondrosis; the rib joint is a symphysis.
Both are synchondroses, because hyaline cartilage joins the bones.
Both are syndesmoses, because a band of tissue joins them.
questions.why: The two cartilaginous joint types are told apart by the cartilage that joins the bones. A synchondrosis is joined by hyaline cartilage and is immovable, as at the growth plate and the first rib with the manubrium. A symphysis is joined by a broad, flat disc of fibrocartilage and is slightly movable.
notes: Symphyses are joined by fibrocartilage and are slightly movable. These joints are hyaline and immovable.
Both joints are joined by hyaline cartilage, so both are synchondroses. A symphysis needs a fibrocartilage disc.
Correct. Hyaline cartilage joining the bones defines a synchondrosis.
Syndesmoses are fibrous joints united by a ligament. These joints are held by cartilage, so they are cartilaginous.
questions.answerText: Both are synchondroses, because hyaline cartilage joins the bones.

questions.q: The skull of an 8-year-old shows a suture running down the middle of the frontal bone. What is this suture, and what does its presence tell you?
options: A sagittal suture, joining the two parietal bones.
A coronal suture, joining the frontal and parietal bones.
A metopic suture, a frontal suture kept past about age six.
A synostosis, a suture that has already fused into bone.
questions.why: Identify the joint, then interpret its age. A suture in the frontal bone is a frontal suture, and when it is still present past about age six it is called a metopic suture. Like all sutures, it is a fibrous joint found only between bones of the skull.
notes: The sagittal suture runs along the midline between the two parietal bones, behind the frontal bone, not through it.
The coronal suture runs across the top of the skull between the frontal and parietal bones, not down the middle of the frontal bone.
Correct. The metopic suture is a frontal suture that persists past about age six.
A synostosis is a joint where two bones have fused completely. A visible suture line means the frontal halves have not fused.
questions.answerText: A metopic suture, a frontal suture kept past about age six.

questions.q: From anatomical position, a person raises the arm out to the side until it is overhead, then lowers it back to the side. Which two movements occur, and at which type of joint?
options: Abduction then adduction, at a ball-and-socket joint.
Adduction then abduction, at a ball-and-socket joint.
Flexion then extension, at a hinge joint.
Elevation then depression, at a plane joint.
questions.why: Name the movements by their direction relative to the midline. Raising the arm out to the side moves it away from the midline, which is abduction, and lowering it back is adduction. The shoulder, where this happens, is a ball-and-socket joint.
notes: Correct. Moving away from the midline is abduction, moving back is adduction, and the shoulder is a ball-and-socket joint.
The joint is right, but the order is reversed. Moving away from the midline comes first, and that is abduction.
Flexion and extension change the angle in the sagittal plane, as when the arm moves forward and back. The shoulder is not a hinge joint.
Elevation and depression lift and lower a part, such as shrugging the shoulders. Raising the arm sideways is abduction.
questions.answerText: Abduction then adduction, at a ball-and-socket joint.

questions.q: From anatomical position, a person turns the forearm so the palm faces posteriorly. Which movement is this, and what happens to the forearm bones?
options: Supination, with the radius crossing over the ulna.
Pronation, with the ulna crossing over the radius.
Pronation, with the radius crossing over the ulna.
Medial rotation, with neither forearm bone moving.
questions.why: Start in anatomical position with the palm facing anteriorly, which is supination. Turning the palm to face posteriorly is pronation. In pronation the radius crosses over the ulna, using the proximal and distal radioulnar joints.
notes: Supination turns the palm to face anteriorly, the anatomical position. In supination the radius and ulna lie side by side.
The movement is right, but the radius is the bone that crosses over in pronation.
Correct. Turning the palm to face posteriorly is pronation, and the radius crosses over the ulna.
Medial rotation turns a bone around its long axis toward the midline. Turning the palm is pronation, which moves the radius.
questions.answerText: Pronation, with the radius crossing over the ulna.

questions.q: A person walks on the heels with the toes lifted, then rises onto tiptoe. Which two ankle movements occur, in order, and what type of joint is the ankle?
options: Plantar flexion then dorsiflexion, at a hinge joint.
Inversion then eversion, at a plane joint.
Dorsiflexion then plantar flexion, at a pivot joint.
Dorsiflexion then plantar flexion, at a hinge joint.
questions.why: Walking on the heels bends the foot up at the ankle, which is dorsiflexion. Rising onto tiptoe points the toes down, which is plantar flexion. The ankle is a hinge joint, which moves in one axis of flexion and extension.
notes: The joint is right, but the order is reversed. Lifting the toes is dorsiflexion and comes first here.
Inversion and eversion turn the sole inward and outward. They are not the up and down movements of heel and toe walking.
The movements are right, but pivot joints allow only rotation, as at the atlantoaxial joint. The ankle is a hinge joint.
Correct. Lifting the toes is dorsiflexion, pointing them down is plantar flexion, and the ankle is a hinge joint.
questions.answerText: Dorsiflexion then plantar flexion, at a hinge joint.

questions.q: Which type of synovial joint is the shoulder joint?
questions.why: In a ball-and-socket joint, a ball fits a cup and the joint moves around three axes. The shoulder and the hip are the two examples, and the shoulder is the most freely movable joint in the body.
notes: Hinge joints move in one axis, flexion and extension, as at the elbow, ankle, and interphalangeal joints.
A saddle joint has surfaces that are each concave and convex. The carpometacarpal joint of the thumb is the example.
Correct. The shoulder is a ball-and-socket joint.
A condyloid joint fits an oval projection into an oval depression, as at the radiocarpal and metacarpophalangeal joints.

questions.q: Which type of synovial joint are the intercarpal joints between the wrist bones?
questions.why: Plane joints have flat or slightly curved surfaces that glide across each other. The intercarpal and intertarsal joints are the standard examples.
notes: Pivot joints fit a rounded surface into a ring of bone and ligament for rotation, as at the atlantoaxial and radioulnar joints.
Hinge joints allow only flexion and extension, as at the elbow and ankle. The small carpal surfaces glide instead.
Correct. The intercarpal joints are plane joints with flat surfaces that glide.
The only saddle joint example is the carpometacarpal joint of the thumb, not the joints between the carpals.

questions.q: Which type of synovial joint is the radiocarpal joint at the wrist?
questions.why: A condyloid joint fits an oval projection into an oval depression and moves around two axes. The radiocarpal joint at the wrist and the metacarpophalangeal joints are the examples.
notes: Correct. The radiocarpal joint is a condyloid joint.
Plane joints have flat surfaces that glide, as between the carpals themselves. The radiocarpal joint is condyloid.
Pivot joints allow only rotation, as at the atlantoaxial and radioulnar joints.
Ball-and-socket joints are triaxial, as at the shoulder and hip. The wrist joint is condyloid and biaxial.
